About This Translation

What this document is

This book is a complete English translation of the Language Basics (语言基础) section of OI Wiki — the collaborative knowledge base used by Chinese informatics olympiad contestants. It covers everything the wiki’s language track covers: C++ fundamentals, the C++ standard library (STL), advanced C++, and crash courses for Python, Java and Pascal users. OI Wiki is where most Chinese IOI/NOI contestants learn the language side of the sport, and this translation lets you read exactly what they read.

Source and license

The source is https://oi-wiki.org/lang/, taken from the OI Wiki repository (github.com/OI-wiki/OI-wiki), snapshot c11199f (2026-08-30). OI Wiki content is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license (CC BY-SA 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). This translation is a derivative work under the same license: credit goes to the OI Wiki contributors for the original content; the English rendering is provided for your IOI preparation and may be shared under the same terms.

Translation fidelity

The translation is sentence-for-sentence faithful: nothing was added, removed, reordered or silently “fixed.” Specifically:

  • Every sentence, list item, table cell, footnote and reference entry of the original appears here.
  • Code is untouched — only comments inside code blocks were translated. Program output shown in text blocks was translated where the original printed Chinese messages.
  • Formulas are untouched — every $…$ math expression is byte-identical to the source, now typeset properly.
  • Links to other wiki pages were dropped from cross-references (they would be dead ends in print); the wording keeps the reference. Links to external sites (cppreference, GCC docs, LOJ, etc.) are preserved.
  • Each chapter header shows the exact source page path so you can check the original online.

How to read the page furniture

The wiki uses collapsible colored boxes (admonitions) and side-by-side language tabs. Here, all admonitions are expanded, and tabs are shown as labeled blocks (the label bar, e.g. C++ or Python, names the language of the code below it). A “▾” marker in an admonition title means the box is collapsible on the wiki. Footnotes are numbered per chapter and collected at the chapter’s end.

OI Wiki · Language Basics

Introduction

oi-wiki.org/lang/index.md

This chapter will introduce programming-related knowledge, including a C++ tutorial from beginner to advanced level and brief introductions to some other languages.

A program is the vehicle that carries algorithms and data structures, and the tool for solving OI problems.

In OI, the most commonly used programming language is C++.

Learning to program is the most fundamental part of learning OI.

Chapter 1 · C++ Fundamentals

Hello, World!

oi-wiki.org/lang/helloworld.md

disqus:

Environment Setup#

To do one's work well, one must first sharpen one's tools.

Integrated Development Environments#

IDEs are relatively easy to use, so beginners generally choose an IDE to write their code. The most common one in competitions is Dev-C++ (if the contest environment runs Windows, this IDE is usually provided as well).

Compilers#

Windows#

The GNU compiler is recommended. You need to go to MinGW Distro to download MinGW and install it. In addition, on Windows you can also choose the Microsoft Visual C++ compiler, which needs to be downloaded and installed from the Visual Studio page.

macOS#

Execute the following in the terminal:

xcode-select --install

Linux#

Use g++ -v to check whether g++ has been installed.

It can be installed with the following command:

sudo apt update && sudo apt install g++

Compiling Code on the Command Line#

Once they become proficient, some people also use the more flexible command line to compile their code; this way they no longer depend on an IDE, but instead write code with the text editor they are familiar with.

g++ test.cpp -o test -lm

g++ is the compiler for the C++ language (the compiler for the C language is gcc), -o is used to specify the file name of the executable, and the compile option -lm is used to link the math library libm, so that code using math.h compiles and runs correctly.

Note: C++ programs do not need -lm to compile and run correctly. The C++ compile options for NOI/NOIP problems over the years all included -lm, so it is added here as well.

Your First Piece of Code#

Let's begin the journey into C++ with this sample program~

Note: before you start writing, make sure to switch to an English input method.

The C++ language

#include <iostream>  // include the header file

int main() {                     // define the main function
  std::cout << "Hello, world!";  // use the cout function in the standard namespace
  return 0;  // returns 0, ending the main function. The compiler usually adds this line automatically, so it can usually be omitted
}

The C language

#include <stdio.h>  // include the header file

int main() {                // define the main function
  printf("Hello, world!");  // output Hello, world!
  return 0;                 // returns 0, ending the main function
}

Note: C is shown here only for reference. C++ is largely compatible with C and has many new features, which can help contestants achieve twice the result with half the effort during a contest. For details, see Differences between C++ and Other Common Languages

Chapter 2 · C++ Fundamentals

C++ Syntax Basics

oi-wiki.org/lang/basic.md

Code Skeleton#

If you don't want to dig into the principles behind it, you can simply memorize this "skeleton" as a beginner:

#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  // do something...
  return 0;
}

noteWhat is include?

#include is actually a preprocessing directive; it means "placing" a file at the position of this statement, and the file being "placed" is called a header file. In other words, during compilation, the compiler "copies" the contents of the header file iostream and "pastes" them at the position of the #include <iostream> statement. This way, you can use the objects provided by iostream, such as std::cin, std::cout, and std::endl.

If you have learned C, you will find that the C++ headers we have encountered so far generally do not carry the .h suffix, while the C headers xx.h have all become cxx, e.g. stdio.h has become cstdio. Because C++ directly uses the header files of C in order to stay compatible with C, the c prefix is used to distinguish C++ headers from C headers.

Generally speaking, which headers you should #include should be determined by the needs of the C++ program you are going to write. But if you #include extra headers, this only increases compilation time and has almost no impact on the running time. So far we have only encountered the two headers iostream and cstdio; if you only need scanf and printf, you can leave out #include <iostream>.

Can you #include header files you wrote yourself? The answer is: yes.

You can write a header file yourself, such as myheader.h. Then put it in the same directory as your code, and #include "myheader.h" will do. Note that custom headers need to be included using quotation marks rather than angle brackets. Of course, you can also use the compile command -I <header_file_path> to tell the compiler where to find header files, so the headers do not need to be placed in the same directory as the code.

noteWhat is <code>main()</code>?

You can understand it as: when the program runs, the code in main() gets executed.

In fact, the main function is called by the system or by an external program. For example, when you call your program from the command line, you are calling the main function of your program (before that, the construction of the global variables is completed first).

The final return 0; indicates that the program ran successfully. By default, a return value of 0 when the program ends means everything is normal; otherwise, the return value is an error code (on Windows, the hexadecimal form of this error code can be looked up on the Windows Error Codes website). Who is this value returned to? It is precisely the system or external program that called the program you wrote; it receives this return value when your program ends. If you do not write a return statement, the default return value of a program that ends normally is also 0.

In C or C++, a non-zero return value of the program causes a runtime error (RE).

Comments#

In C++ code, there are two ways to write comments:

  1. Inline comments

    They start with //; everything after it on the line is a comment.

  2. Block comments

    They start with /* and end with */; everything in between is a comment, and it can span multiple lines.

Comments have no effect on the running of a program. They can be used to explain what the program means, and they can also be used to keep a segment of code from executing (while still keeping it in the source file).

In engineering development, comments make later maintenance and reading by others easier.

In OI, few people write many comments, but comments can help you organize your thoughts while writing code, or make later review easier. Moreover, if you are going to write editorials or tutorials, a moderate amount of comments makes it easier for readers to read and understand the intent of the code. We hope everyone will develop the good habit of writing comments.

Input and Output#

cin and cout#

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int x, y;                          // declare variables
  std::cin >> x >> y;                // read x and y
  std::cout << y << std::endl << x;  // output y, then a newline, then x
  return 0;                          // end of the main function
}

noteWhat is a variable?

You can refer to the variables page.

noteWhat is <code>std</code>?

std is the namespace used by the C++ standard library. Namespaces are used to avoid name collisions.

For detailed information about namespaces, you can refer to the namespaces page.

scanf and printf#

scanf and printf are actually functions provided by the C language. In most cases, they are faster than cin and cout, and they make it convenient to control the input and output format.

noteInput and output optimization

For the specific differences between cin/cout and scanf/printf, as well as input and output optimization, please refer to the Input and output optimization page.

#include <cstdio>

int main() {
  int x, y;
  scanf("%d%d", &x, &y);   // read x and y
  printf("%d\n%d", y, x);  // output y, then a newline, then x
  return 0;
}

Here, %d means the variable being read or output is a variable of a signed integer type (int).

Similarly:

  1. %s means a string.
  2. %c means a character.
  3. %lf means a double-precision floating-point number (double).
  4. %lld means a long integer type (long long). Depending on the system, it may also be %I64d.
  5. %u means an unsigned integer type (unsigned int).
  6. %llu means an unsigned long integer type (unsigned long long); it may also be %I64u.

Besides the type specifiers, there are also some ways to control the format. Many of them are rarely used; two commonly used ones are listed below:

  1. %1d means an integer of length 1. When reading, digits can be read in one by one even without spaces. When printing, if the specified length is greater than the number of digits of the number, spaces are used for padding in front of the number. If the specified length is less than the number of digits, it has no effect.
  2. %.6lf, used for output, keeps six decimal places.

You can fill in other numbers at the corresponding places of these two operators; for example, %.3lf means keeping three decimal places.

noteWhat are &#x27;double-precision floating-point numbers&#x27; and &#x27;long integer types&#x27;?

These represent types of variables. As above, they will be explained all together in variables.

noteWhy is there an <code>&amp;</code> operator in <code>scanf</code>?

Here, & is actually the address-of operator; it returns the address of the variable in memory. And the parameters that scanf receives are exactly the addresses of variables. The details can probably only be made fully clear in pointers; for now, you just need to remember this.

noteWhat is <code>\n</code>?

\n is an escape character; it represents a newline.

Escape characters are used to represent characters that cannot be typed directly, such as the newline character, which cannot be typed directly because string literals cannot contain line breaks; the quotation mark, which cannot be typed because it has a special meaning; and the backslash, which cannot be typed because it is what marks escape characters.

Commonly used escape characters include:

  1. \t represents the tab character.

  2. \\ represents \.

  3. \" represents ".

  4. \0 represents the null character, used to mark the end of a C-style string.

  5. \r represents a carriage return. On Linux, the newline character is \n; on Windows, it is \r\n. In OI, if your output needs a newline, using \n is enough. But when reading input, if you read character by character, the newline characters may cause some problems, so you need to be careful. For example, gets treats \n as the end of the string; in that case, if the newline is \r\n, the \r will be left at the end of the string.

  6. In particular, %% represents %; it can only be used in printf or scanf. In other string literals, simply using % is fine.

noteWhat is a literal?

A "literal" is a piece of the program that directly serves as a value in the code; for example, 3 is an int literal, and 'c' is a char literal. The "hello world" in the program we wrote above is also a string literal.

Literals that appear without explanation or reason are also called "magic numbers"; if the code is meant to be read by people, this is a strongly discouraged practice.

Some Extensions#

Whitespace Characters in C++#

In C++, all whitespace characters (spaces, tabs, newlines), whether multiple or single, are treated the same. (Of course, whitespace inside quotation marks, being part of a string, does not count.)

Therefore, you can freely use any code style (except that inline comments, string literals, and preprocessing directives must stay on a single line), for example:

--8<-- "docs/lang/code/basic/basic_1.cpp:main"

Of course, doing this is not recommended.

A code style that is also widely used, but differs from the one OI Wiki requires:

--8<-- "docs/lang/code/basic/basic_2.cpp:main"

The #define Directive#

#define is a kind of preprocessing directive, used to define macros; it is essentially text replacement. For example:

#include <iostream>
#define n 233

// n is not a variable; the compiler textually replaces every n in the code with 233, but an n that is part
// of an identifier will not be replaced, e.g. fn does not become f233. Likewise, n inside strings is not replaced

int main() {
  std::cout << n;  // outputs 233
  return 0;
}

noteWhat is an identifier?

An identifier is a sequence of characters that can be used as a variable name. For example, abcd and abc1 are legal identifiers, while 1a and c+b are not.

An identifier must start with an English letter or an underscore, and only English letters, underscores, and digits are allowed in the rest. Note that keywords (such as int, for, if) cannot be used as identifiers.

noteWhat is a preprocessing directive?

A preprocessing directive is a command accepted by the preprocessor, used to perform preliminary textual transformations on the code, such as the file-inclusion operation #include and macro processing #define. For GCC, the output of the preprocessing stage, the .i file, is not kept by default. The -E option can be used to keep the output file.

Macros can take parameters; a macro with parameters can be used like a function:

#include <iostream>
#define sum(x, y) ((x) + (y))
#define square(x) ((x) * (x))

int main() {
  std::cout << sum(1, 2) << ' ' << 2 * sum(3, 5) << std::endl;  // outputs 3 16
}

But macros with parameters are different from functions. Because macros are text replacement, they can cause many problems. For example:

#include <iostream>
#define sum(x, y) x + y
// this should be #define sum(x, y) ((x) + (y))
#define square(x) ((x) * (x))

int main() {
  std::cout << sum(1, 2) << ' ' << 2 * sum(3, 5) << std::endl;
  // the output is 3 11, because #define is text replacement: the later statement was replaced by 2 * 3 + 5
  int i = 1;
  std::cout << square(++i) << ' ' << i;
  // the output is undefined, because ++i is executed twice
  // and modifying the same variable multiple times in the same statement is undefined behavior (there are exceptions)
}

Using #define is risky (because the scope of a #define is the whole program, text may be replaced unintentionally, and #undef is needed to cancel the definition in time), so it should be used with caution. The more recommended practice is: declare constants with the const qualifier, and use functions instead of macros.

However, in OI, #define still has its uses (the following two usages are not recommended, as they make the code less standardized):

  1. #define int long long + signed main(). Usually used to avoid errors caused by forgetting to use long long, or, when debugging, to rule out the possibility that an error was caused by forgetting to use long long. (It may also increase the constant factor or even cause TLE, or cause MLE by exceeding the memory limit.)
  2. #define For(i, l, r) for (int i = (l); i <= (r); ++i), #define pb push_back, #define mid ((l + r) / 2), used to shorten the code.

That said, #define also has its advantages; for example, combined with preprocessing directives such as #ifdef it can work wonders, as in:

#ifdef LINUX
// code for linux
#else
// code for other OS
#endif

You can use -DLINUX at compile time to control the code that gets compiled, without modifying the source file. This has one more advantage: the executable compiled with -DLINUX does not contain the code of other operating systems; that code has already been deleted during preprocessing.

#define can also use the # and ## operators, which greatly facilitates debugging.

Chapter 3 · C++ Fundamentals

Variables

oi-wiki.org/lang/var.md

Data Types#

The type system of C++ consists of the following parts:

  1. Fundamental types (the representative keyword/type is given in parentheses)
    1. void type (void)
    2. (since C++11) the null pointer type (std::nullptr_t)
    3. Arithmetic types
      1. Integer types (int)
      2. Boolean type (bool)
      3. Character types (char)
      4. Floating-point types (float, double)
  2. Compound types1

Boolean Type#

A variable of type bool can only take one of two values: true and false.

Typically, a bool variable occupies 111 byte (typically, 111 byte = 888 bits) of storage.

tipTip

The number of bits in a byte can be obtained through the macro constant CHAR_BIT in the header <climits> (C++) / <limits.h> (C).

noteThe Boolean type in C

See also the differences between C++ and other commonly used languages - bool.

The C language originally had no Boolean type; it was not until C99 that the keyword _Bool was introduced as the Boolean type, and it is regarded as an unsigned integer type.

noteNote

Since C23, the bool type of the C language is no longer defined using the integer zero and non-zero values; instead, it is defined as a type capable of storing the two constants true and false.

For convenience, stdbool.h provides the three macros bool, true, and false, defined as follows:

#define bool _Bool
#define true 1
#define false 0

These macros were removed in C23, and since C23 true, false, and bool have been introduced as keywords, while _Bool is retained as an alternative spelling7.

In addition, since C23 the width of the Boolean type can also be obtained through the macro constant BOOL_WIDTH in <limits.h>.

Integer Types#

Used to store integers. The most fundamental integer type is int.

warningNote

For historical reasons, the Boolean type and the character types are treated as special integer types in C++.

In almost all cases, character types other than signed char and unsigned char should not be used as integer types.

Integer types generally come in 5 tiers by width: char, short, int, long, long long.

The C++ standard guarantees 1 == sizeof(char) <= sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long)

For historical reasons, there are several prevailing models for the widths of integer types. To solve this problem, C99/C++11 introduced fixed-width integer types.

noteThe size of the <code>int</code> type

The C++ standard specifies that int is at least 161616 bits.

In fact, on the vast majority of current platforms, int is 323232 bits.

The int keyword can be modified with the following modifier keywords:

Signedness:

  • signed: denotes a signed integer (the default);
  • unsigned: denotes an unsigned integer.

Size:

  • short: denotes an integer of at least 161616 bits;
  • long: denotes an integer of at least 323232 bits;
  • (since C++11) long long: denotes an integer of at least 646464 bits.

The following table gives, in general, the widths and representable range sizes of the integer types (on a few platforms, the representable ranges of some types may differ from the table below):

Type name Equivalent type Width (C++ standard) Width (common) Width (less common)
signed char signed char 888 - -
unsigned char unsigned char 888 - -
short,short int,signed short,signed short int short int ≥16\geq 16≥16 161616 -
unsigned short,unsigned short int unsigned short int ≥16\geq 16≥16 161616 -
int,signed,signed int int ≥16\geq 16≥16 323232 161616 (common in the Win16 API)
unsigned,unsigned int unsigned int ≥16\geq 16≥16 323232 161616 (common in the Win16 API)
long,long int,signed long,signed long int long int ≥32\geq 32≥32 323232 646464 (common on 64-bit Linux, macOS)
unsigned long,unsigned long int unsigned long int ≥32\geq 32≥32 323232 646464 (common on 64-bit Linux, macOS)
long long,long long int,signed long long,signed long long int long long int ≥64\geq 64≥64 646464 -
unsigned long long,unsigned long long int unsigned long long int ≥64\geq 64≥64 646464 -

When the width is xxx, the representable range of a signed type is −2x−1∼2x−1−1-2^{x-1}\sim 2^{x-1}-1−2x−1∼2x−1−12, and the representable range of an unsigned type is 0∼2x−10 \sim 2^x-10∼2x−1. Specifically, we have the following table:

Width Representable range
888 signed: −27∼27−1-2^{7}\sim 2^{7}-1−27∼27−1, unsigned: 0∼28−10 \sim 2^{8}-10∼28−1
161616 signed: −215∼215−1-2^{15}\sim 2^{15}-1−215∼215−1, unsigned: 0∼216−10 \sim 2^{16}-10∼216−1
323232 signed: −231∼231−1-2^{31}\sim 2^{31}-1−231∼231−1, unsigned: 0∼232−10 \sim 2^{32}-10∼232−1
646464 signed: −263∼263−1-2^{63}\sim 2^{63}-1−263∼263−1, unsigned: 0∼264−10 \sim 2^{64}-10∼264−1

noteEquivalent type spellings

When no ambiguity is introduced, some modifier keywords may be omitted, or the order of the modifier keywords may be rearranged. This means that the same type can have multiple equivalent spellings.

For example, int, signed, int signed, and signed int denote the same type, and unsigned long and unsigned long int denote the same type.

In addition, some compilers implement extended integer types. For example, GCC implements 128-bit integers: the signed version __int128_t and the unsigned version __uint128_t. If you want to use these types during a contest, please read the contest rules carefully to determine whether the use of extended integer types is allowed or supported.

warningNote

The STL does not necessarily provide adequate support for extended integer types, so extra care is required when using extended integer types.

noteSample code
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

int f1(int n) {
  return abs(n);  // Good
}

int f2(int n) {
  return std::abs(n);  // Good
}

__int128_t f3(__int128_t n) {
  return abs(n);  // Bad
}

// Wrong
// __int128_t f4(__int128_t n) {
//   return std::abs(n);
// }

int main() {
  std::cout << "f1: " << f1(-42) << std::endl;
  std::cout << "f2: " << f2(-42) << std::endl;
  // std::cout << "f3: " << f3(-42) << std::endl; // Wrong
  // std::cout << "f4: " << f4(-42) << std::endl; // Wrong
  return 0;
}
The sample code above has the following problems:

  1. __int128_t f3(__int128_t) uses the C-style absolute value function, whose signature is int abs(int), so n is first forcibly converted to int and only then is the abs function called.
  2. __int128_t f4(__int128_t) uses the C++-style absolute value function, for which there is no function overload with the signature __int128_t std::abs(__int128_t), so it fails to compile.
  3. C++ stream output does not support __int128_t or __uint128_t.

Here is one solution:

noteThe corrected code
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

__int128_t abs(__int128_t n) { return n < 0 ? -n : n; }

std::ostream &operator<<(std::ostream &os, __uint128_t n) {
  if (n > 9) os << n / 10;
  os << (int)(n % 10);
  return os;
}

std::ostream &operator<<(std::ostream &os, __int128_t n) {
  if (n < 0) {
    os << '-';
    n = -n;
  }
  return os << (__uint128_t)n;
}

int f1(int n) { return abs(n); }

int f2(int n) { return std::abs(n); }

__int128_t f3(__int128_t n) { return abs(n); }

int main() {
  std::cout << "f1: " << f1(-42) << std::endl;
  std::cout << "f2: " << f2(-42) << std::endl;
  std::cout << "f3: " << f3(-42) << std::endl;
}

Character Types#

They are divided into "narrow character types" and "wide character types". Since wide character types are almost never used in competitive programming, only narrow character types are introduced here.

A narrow character type is typically 888 bits wide; in fact, the underlying storage is still an integer, and the one-to-one correspondence between characters and integers is usually established via ASCII encoding. There are three such types:

  • signed char: the type for representing signed characters, with a range of −128∼127-128 \sim 127−128∼127.
  • unsigned char: the type for representing unsigned characters, with a range of 0∼2550 \sim 2550∼255.

  • char has the same representation and alignment as one of signed char or unsigned char, but is always a distinct type.

    The signedness of char depends on the compiler and the target platform: on ARM and PowerPC the default is usually unsigned, while on x86 and x64 the default is usually signed.

    GCC allows -fsigned-char or -funsigned-char to be added to the compiler options to specify that char be treated as signed char or unsigned char; for other compilers, please consult their documentation. Note that specifying a signedness different from the architecture's default may break the ABI and cause the program to malfunction.

warningNote

Unlike the other integer types, char, signed char, and unsigned char are three distinct types.

In general, signed char and unsigned char should not be used to store characters; in the vast majority of cases, both of these types are treated as integer types.

Floating-Point Types#

Used to store "real numbers" (note that these are not real numbers in the strict sense, but approximations of real numbers under certain rules), including the following three:

  • float: single-precision floating-point type. Matches the IEEE-754 binary32 format if supported.
  • double: double-precision floating-point type. Matches the IEEE-754 binary64 format if supported.
  • long double: extended-precision floating-point type. Matches the IEEE-754 binary128 format if supported, otherwise the IEEE-754 binary64 extended format if supported, otherwise some non-IEEE-754 extended floating-point format with better precision than binary64 and a range at least as good as that of binary64, otherwise the IEEE-754 binary64 format.
Floating-point format Width Largest positive number Precision (significant digits)
IEEE-754 binary32 format 323232 3.4×10383.4\times 10^{38}3.4×1038 6∼96\sim 96∼9
IEEE-754 binary64 format 646464 1.8×103081.8\times 10^{308}1.8×10308 15∼1715\sim 1715∼17
IEEE-754 binary64 extended format ≥80\geq 80≥80 ≥1.2×104932\geq 1.2\times 10^{4932}≥1.2×104932 ≥18∼21\geq 18\sim 21≥18∼21
IEEE-754 binary128 format 128128128 1.2×1049321.2\times 10^{4932}1.2×104932 33∼3633\sim 3633∼36

The most negative number of an IEEE-754 floating-point format is the negation of the largest positive number.

Because the float type has a small representable range and low precision, the double type is commonly used to represent floating-point numbers in practice.

In addition, floating-point types can support some special values:

  • Infinity (positive or negative): INFINITY.
  • Negative zero: -0.0; for example, 1.0 / 0.0 == INFINITY, 1.0 / -0.0 == -INFINITY.
  • Not a Number (NaN): std::nan, NAN; it can generally be produced by operations such as 0.0 / 0.0. It compares unequal to any value (including itself); since C++11, std::isnan can be used to determine whether a floating-point number is NaN.

Void Type#

The void type is the no-type. Unlike the types above, a variable cannot be declared as void. However, a function's return type is allowed to be void, indicating that the function has no return value.

Null Pointer Type#

Please refer to the corresponding section on pointers

Fixed-Width Integer Types#

Since C++11, support for fixed-width integers is provided, as follows:

  • <cstdint>: provides several fixed-width integer types, as well as macro constants such as the maximum and minimum values of each fixed-width integer type.
  • <cinttypes>: provides format macro constants for the fixed-width integer types, for use with the std::fprintf family of functions and the std::fscanf family of functions.

The fixed-width integers are as follows:

  • intN_t: the signed integer type whose width is exactly NNN bits, e.g. int32_t.
  • int_fastN_t: the fastest signed integer type whose width is at least NNN bits, e.g. int_fast32_t.
  • int_leastN_t: the smallest signed integer type whose width is at least NNN bits, e.g. int_least32_t.

The unsigned versions are obtained simply by adding the letter u in front of the signed versions, e.g. uint32_t, uint_least8_t.

The standard mandates that the following 16 types be implemented:

int_fast8_t,int_fast16_t,int_fast32_t,int_fast64_t,

int_least8_t,int_least16_t,int_least32_t,int_least64_t,

uint_fast8_t,uint_fast16_t,uint_fast32_t,uint_fast64_t,

uint_least8_t,uint_least16_t,uint_least32_t,uint_least64_t.

The vast majority of compilers additionally implement the following 8 types on top of these:

int8_t,int16_t,int32_t,int64_t,

uint8_t,uint16_t,uint32_t,uint64_t.

Where a corresponding type is implemented, the C++ standard mandates that macro constants be implemented for the maximum value, the minimum value, and the width of that type. The format is: take the type name, remove the trailing _t, convert it to uppercase, and append a suffix:

  • _MAX denotes the maximum value; e.g. INT32_MAX is the maximum value of int32_t.
  • _MIN denotes the minimum value; e.g. INT32_MIN is the minimum value of int32_t.

warningNote

Fixed-width integer types are essentially type aliases of ordinary integer types, so mixing fixed-width integer types and ordinary integer types may hurt cross-platform compilation. For example:

noteSample code
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  long long a;
  int64_t b;
  std::cin >> a >> b;
  std::cout << std::max(a, b) << std::endl;
  return 0;
}
int64_t is usually long long int on 64-bit Windows, while it is usually long int on 64-bit Linux, so this code does not compile with GCC on 64-bit Linux but compiles with MSVC on 64-bit Windows, because std::max requires the two arguments passed in to be of the same type.

In addition, since C++17 the <limits> header provides the std::numeric_limits class template, which is used to query the properties of the various arithmetic types, such as the maximum value, the minimum value, whether the type is an integer type, and whether it is signed.

#include <cstdint>
#include <limits>

std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max();  // the maximum value of int32_t, 2'147'483'647
std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::min();  // the minimum value of int32_t, -2'147'483'648

std::numeric_limits<double>::min();  // the minimum value of double, approximately 2.22507e-308
std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon();  // the difference between 1.0 and the next representable value of double,
                                         // approximately 2.22045e-16

Type Conversion#

Sometimes (for example, when a function accepts a parameter of type int but a variable of type double is passed in), we need to convert from one type to another.

The type conversion mechanism in C++ is fairly complex; here we mainly introduce the two kinds of conversion for fundamental data types: numeric promotion and numeric conversion.

Numeric Promotion#

During a numeric promotion, the value itself remains unchanged.

noteNote

Default argument promotion is performed when values are passed through a C-style variadic argument domain. For example:

noteSample code
#include <stdarg.h>
#include <stdio.h>

void test(int tot, ...) {
  va_list valist;
  int i;

  // initialize the variable argument list
  va_start(valist, tot);

  for (i = 0; i < tot; ++i) {
    // get the value of the i-th variable
    double xx = va_arg(valist, double);  // Correct
    // float xx = va_arg(valist, float); // Wrong

    // print the underlying storage content of the i-th variable
    printf("i = %d, value = 0x%016llx\n", i, *(long long *)(&xx));
  }

  // clean up the memory of the variable argument list
  va_end(valist);
}

int main() {
  float f;
  double fd, d;
  f = 123.;   // 0x42f60000
  fd = 123.;  // 0x405ec00000000000
  d = 456.;   // 0x407c800000000000
  test(3, f, fd, d);
}
When test is called, f is promoted to double, so its underlying storage content is the same as that of fd, and the output is

i = 0, value = 0x405ec00000000000
i = 1, value = 0x405ec00000000000
i = 2, value = 0x407c800000000000

If double xx = va_arg(valist, double); is changed to float xx = va_arg(valist, float);, GCC should give a warning similar to the following:

In file included from test.c:2:
test.c: In function 'test':
test.c:14:35: warning: 'float' is promoted to 'double' when passed through '...'
  14 |         float xx = va_arg(valist, float);
     |                                   ^
test.c:14:35: note: (so you should pass 'double' not 'float' to 'va_arg')
test.c:14:35: note: if this code is reached, the program will abort

In that case, the program will terminate before producing any output.

This also explains why printf's %f can match both float and double.

Integer Promotion#

A prvalue of a small integer type (such as char) can be converted to a prvalue of a larger integer type (such as int).

Specifically, arithmetic operators do not accept types smaller than int as their arguments, and after the lvalue-to-rvalue conversion, integer promotion is applied automatically where applicable.

Specifically, the rules are as follows:

  • If the source type is signed char or signed short / short, it can be promoted to int.
  • If the source type is unsigned char or unsigned short, then if int can hold the entire range of values of the source type, it can be promoted to int; otherwise, it can be promoted to unsigned int. (Since C++20, char8_t also follows this rule)
  • The promotion rule for char depends on whether its underlying type is signed char or unsigned char.
  • The bool type can be converted to int: false becomes 0, and true becomes 1.
  • If the range of values of the target type contains that of the source type, and the range of the source type cannot be contained by int or unsigned int, then the source type can be promoted to the target type.3

warningNote

char->short is not a numeric promotion, because char must first be promoted to int / unsigned int, and what follows is int / unsigned int->short, which does not satisfy the conditions for a numeric promotion.

For example (in the following, assume int is 32 bits, unsigned short is 16 bits, signed char and unsigned char are 8 bits, and bool is 1 bit):

  • (signed char)'\0' - (signed char)'\xff' first promotes (signed char)'\0' to (int)0 and (signed char)'\xff' to (int)-1, then performs the arithmetic between int values, and the final result is (int)1.
  • (unsigned char)'\0' - (unsigned char)'\xff' first promotes (unsigned char)'\0' to (int)0 and (unsigned char)'\xff' to (int)255, then performs the arithmetic between int values, and the final result is (int)-255.
  • false - (unsigned short)12 first promotes false to (int)0 and (unsigned short)12 to (int)12, then performs the arithmetic between int values, and the final result is (int)-12.

Floating-Point Promotion#

A floating-point value of smaller width can be promoted to a floating-point value of larger width (for example, when a variable of type float and a variable of type double are involved in an arithmetic operation, the float variable is promoted to a double variable), and its value is unchanged.

Numeric Conversion#

During a numeric conversion, the value may change.

warningNote

Numeric promotion takes precedence over numeric conversion. For example, bool->int is a numeric promotion, not a numeric conversion.

Integer Conversion#

  • If the target type is an unsigned integer type of width xxx, the result of the conversion is the original value  mod 2x\bmod 2^xmod2x.

    • If the width of the target type is greater than the width of the source type:

      • If the source type is signed, then in general sign extension is performed first, followed by the conversion.

        For example:

        • When converting (short)-1 ((short)0b1111'1111'1111'1111) to the unsigned int type, sign extension is performed first, yielding 0b1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111, and then the integer conversion is performed, with the result (unsigned int)4'294'967'295 ((unsigned int)0b1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111).
        • When converting (short)32'767 ((short)0b0111'1111'1111'1111) to the unsigned int type, sign extension is performed first, yielding 0b0000'0000'0000'0000'0111'1111'1111'1111, and then the integer conversion is performed, with the result (unsigned int)32'767 ((unsigned int)0b0000'0000'0000'0000'0111'1111'1111'1111).

      • If the source type is unsigned, zero extension must be performed first, followed by the conversion.

        For example, when converting (unsigned short)65'535 ((unsigned short)0b1111'1111'1111'1111) to the unsigned int type, zero extension is performed first, yielding 0b0000'0000'0000'0000'1111'1111'1111'1111, and then the integer conversion is performed, with the result (unsigned int)65'535 ((unsigned int)0b0000'0000'0000'0000'1111'1111'1111'1111).

    • If the width of the target type is not greater than the width of the source type, truncation must be performed first, followed by the conversion.

      For example, when converting (unsigned int)4'294'967'295 ((unsigned int)0b1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111) to the unsigned short type, truncation is performed first, yielding 0b1111'1111'1111'1111, and then the integer conversion is performed, with the result (unsigned short)65'535 ((unsigned short)0b1111'1111'1111'1111).

  • If the target type is a signed integer type of width xxx, then in general the result of the conversion can be regarded as the original value  mod 2x\bmod 2^xmod2x.4

    For example, when converting (unsigned int)4'294'967'295 ((unsigned int)0b1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111'1111) to the short type, the result is (short)-1 ((short)0b1111'1111'1111'1111).

  • If the target type is bool, this is a Boolean conversion.

  • If the source type is bool, then false is converted to 0 of the corresponding type, and true is converted to 1 of the corresponding type.

Floating-Point Conversion#

Converting a floating-point value of larger width to a floating-point type of smaller width rounds the value to the nearest value representable in the target type.

Floating-Integral Conversion#

  • When a floating-point value is converted to an integer, the entire fractional part of the floating-point value is discarded.

    If the target type is bool, this is a Boolean conversion.

  • When an integer is converted to a floating-point value, it is rounded to the nearest value representable in the target type.

    If the value cannot fit into the target type, the behavior is undefined.

    If the source type is bool, then false is converted to zero and true is converted to one.

Boolean Conversion#

When a value of another type is converted to the bool type, zero is converted to false and non-zero values are converted to true.

Defining Variables#

To put it simply5, defining a variable requires a type specifier (which indicates the type of the variable) and the name of the variable to be defined.

For example, the following statements are all variable definitions.

int oi;
double wiki;
char org = 'c';

In the program fragments we have encountered so far, variables defined in places wrapped in curly braces are local variables, while variables defined in places not wrapped in curly braces are global variables. There are exceptions in practice, but you do not need to know them yet.

Global variables that are not given an initial value at their definition will be initialized to 000. Local variables do not have this property; you need to assign them an initial value manually, otherwise bugs that are hard to find may occur.

Variable Scope#

A scope is a block of code in which a variable can take effect.

The scope of a global variable begins at the place of its definition6 and ends at the end of the file.

The scope of a local variable begins at the place of its definition and ends at the end of the code block.

A code block is made up of several statements enclosed in a pair of curly braces.

int g = 20;  // define a global variable

int main() {
  int g = 10;         // define a local variable
  printf("%d\n", g);  // print g
  return 0;
}

If a variable with the same name is defined in a block nested inside a code block, the variable of the same name in the outer block cannot be accessed inside the inner block.

For example, in the code above, the value printed for ggg will be 101010. Therefore, to avoid unexpected errors, please try to avoid cases where a local variable has the same name as a global variable.

Constants#

A constant is a fixed value that does not change during the execution of the program.

The value of a constant cannot be modified after it is defined. Simply add the const keyword at the definition.

const int a = 2;
a = 3;

If the value of a constant is modified, an error is reported at the compilation stage: error: assignment of read-only variable 'a'.

Chapter 4 · C++ Fundamentals

Operators

oi-wiki.org/lang/op.md

author: aofall, greyqz, Ir1d, Link-cute, Marcythm, ouuan, Shen-Linwood, sshwy, StudyingFather

Arithmetic operators#

Operator Function
+ (unary) Positive
- (unary) Negative
* (binary) Multiplication
/ Division
% Modulo
+ (binary) Addition
- (binary) Subtraction

noteUnary and binary operators

A unary operator (also called a monadic operator) is an operator with only one operand, while a binary operator (also called a dyadic operator) has two operands. For example, in 1 + 2 the plus sign is a binary operator: it has two operands, 1 and 2. In addition, C++ has exactly one ternary operator, ?:.

Among the arithmetic operators, there are two unary operators (positive and negative) and five binary operators (multiplication, division, modulo, addition, and subtraction), and the unary operators have the highest precedence.

Among these, the modulo operator % computes the remainder obtained when two integers are divided, that is, it takes the remainder.

When - is used as a binary operator it acts as the subtraction operator, as in 2-1; when it is used as a unary operator it acts as the negation operator, as in -1.

The usage is as follows.

op=x-y*z

The computed value of op follows the precedence rules of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division in mathematics: operations with higher precedence are carried out first, operations with the same precedence are carried out according to their associativity, and parentheses raise precedence.

Type conversion in arithmetic operations#

For binary arithmetic operators, when the two variables involved in the operation have the same type, no type conversion takes place, and the result of the operation will be held in the type of the variables involved; otherwise a type conversion takes place so that the two variables have the same type. See type conversion for the conversion rules.

For example, for an integer (int) variable xxx and another variable yyy of double-precision floating-point (double) type:

  • the result of x/3 will be of integer type;
  • the result of x/3.0 will be of double-precision floating-point type;
  • the result of x/y will be of double-precision floating-point type;
  • the result of x*1/3 will be of integer type;
  • the result of x*1.0/3 will be of double-precision floating-point type;

Bitwise operators#

See also: bitwise operations.

Operator Function
~ Bitwise NOT
& (binary) Bitwise AND
| Bitwise OR
^ Bitwise XOR
<< Bitwise left shift
>> Bitwise right shift

For the meaning of bitwise operations, refer to the bitwise operations page. Note that the precedence of the bitwise operators is lower than that of the arithmetic operators (except for NOT), and bitwise AND, bitwise OR, and XOR have lower precedence than the comparison operators (see the complete table of C++ operator precedence for details), so take extra care when using them and add parentheses when necessary.

In shift operations, the behavior is undefined if either of the following occurs:

  1. the right operand (i.e. the shift count) is negative;
  2. the right operand is greater than or equal to the number of bits of the left operand;

For example, for a variable a of type int32_t, both a<<-1 and a<<32 are undefined.

For left shifts of signed non-negative values, you must make sure the shifted result can be represented in the type of the original value; otherwise the behavior is also undefined.1 Performing a left shift on a negative value is undefined as well.2

For right shifts, the extra bits on the right side will be discarded, while the left side is more complicated: for unsigned numbers, 000 is filled in on the left3; for signed numbers, the value of the highest bit (which is really just the sign bit: 000 for non-negative numbers, 111 for negative numbers) is used for filling4.

Increment/decrement operators#

Sometimes we need to increase a variable by 1 (increment) or decrease it by 1 (decrement); this is where the increment operator ++ and the decrement operator -- come in handy.

The increment/decrement operators can be placed before or after the variable: placed before the variable they are called prefix, and placed after the variable they are called suffix. When used on their own, there is no need to distinguish prefix from suffix; if the value of the expression is used, however, care is required — see the examples below. For details, refer to the examples given in the reference page.

i = 100;

op1 = i++;  // op1 = 100: first op1 = i, then i = i + 1

i = 100;

op2 = ++i;  // op2 = 101: first i = i + 1, then assign to op2

i = 100;

op3 = i--;  // op3 = 100: first assign to op3, then i = i - 1

i = 100;

op4 = --i;  // op4 = 99: first i = i - 1, then assign to op4

Compound assignment operators#

Compound assignment operators are actually a shorthand form of expressions. They can be divided into the compound arithmetic operators +=, -=, *=, /=, %= and the compound bitwise operators &=, |=, ^=, <<=, >>=.

For example, op = op + 2 can be written as op += 2, op = op - 2 can be written as op -= 2, and op= op * 2 can be written as op *= 2.

Conditional operator#

The conditional operator can be seen as shorthand for the if statement: in a ? b : c, if the expression a holds, the result of the conditional expression is b; otherwise the result of the conditional expression is c.

Comparison operators#

Operator Function
> Greater than
>= Greater than or equal to
< Less than
<= Less than or equal to
== Equal to
!= Not equal to

In particular, note that the equality operator == must be distinguished from the assignment operator =; this is especially important in conditional statements.

if (op=1) and if (op==1) look similar, but their actual behavior differs enormously. The first statement assigns to op; when the assigned value is non-zero it counts as true, so the condition of the expression is always satisfied and no real check is performed; the second statement is the one that actually tests the value of op.

Logical operators#

Operator Function
&& Logical AND
|| Logical OR
! Logical NOT 
Result = op1 && op2;  // Result is true when both op1 and op2 are true

Result = op1 || op2;  // Result is true when one of op1 or op2 is true

Result = !op1;  // Result is true when op1 is false

The built-in operators && and || perform short-circuit evaluation (if the result is already known after evaluating the first operand, the second is not evaluated); overloaded operators do not have this property and always evaluate both operands.

Comma operator#

The comma operator can separate multiple expressions; the separated expressions are evaluated one by one from left to right, and the value of the whole expression is the value of the last expression. Among all operators, the comma expression has the lowest precedence.

exp1, exp2, exp3;  // The final value is the result of exp3.

Result = 1 + 2, 3 + 4, 5 + 6;
// The value of Result is 3 rather than 11, because the assignment operator "="
// has higher precedence than the comma operator, so the assignment is performed before the comma operation.

Result = (1 + 2, 3 + 4, 5 + 6);

// To make Result take the result of the comma operation, the whole expression
// should be wrapped in parentheses to raise its precedence; only then is the value of Result 11.

Member access operators#

Operator Function
[] Array subscript
. Object member
& (unary) Take address / obtain reference
* (unary) Indirection / dereference
-> Pointer member

These operators are used to access the members or memory of objects; except for the last one, all of the operators above can be overloaded. For content related to &, *, and ->, read the pointer and reference tutorials. Two rarely used operators, .* and ->*, are also omitted here; for their specific usage, see the C++ language manual.

auto result1 = v[1];  // Get the object at index 2 in v
auto result2 = p.q;   // Get the q member of object p
auto result3 = p -> q;  // Get the q member of the object pointed to by pointer p, equivalent to (*p).q
auto result4 = &v;      // Get a pointer to v
auto result5 = *v;      // Get the object pointed to by pointer v
