References and notes#

Footnotes
  1. Before C++20, if the original value is of a signed type and the shifted result can be represented by the unsigned version of the original type, that result is converted to the corresponding signed value; otherwise the behavior is undefined; the left shift of an unsigned number discards the bits shifted out of the result type. Since C++20, it is specified that a << b is the value of a⋅2ba\cdot 2^ba⋅2b modulo 2N2^N2N (NNN being the width in bits of the result type); that is, whether the value is signed or unsigned, a left shift simply discards the bits shifted out of the result type (i.e. an arithmetic left shift / logical left shift).
  2. Before C++20. For the behavior since C++20, see [^note1].
  3. That is, a logical right shift.
  4. That is, an arithmetic right shift. Before C++20, the right shift of signed values was implementation-defined, and most implementations adopted arithmetic right shift. Since C++20, it is specified that a >> b is ⌊a/2b⌋\lfloor a/2^b\rfloor⌊a/2b⌋, so the right shift of a signed value is an arithmetic right shift.
← PreviousVariablesNext →Branching
Chapter 5 · C++ Fundamentals

Branching · Control Flow

oi-wiki.org/lang/branch.md

By default, a program executes sequentially in the order the code is written; sometimes we need to execute certain statements selectively, and this is where branching comes in. Choosing suitable branching statements can improve the efficiency of a program.

The if statement#

The basic if statement#

The following is the structure of the basic if statement.

if (condition) {
  body;
}

The if statement evaluates the condition: if the result is true (non-zero), the statement is executed; otherwise it is not executed.

If the body contains only a single statement, the curly braces can be omitted.

The if...else statement#

if (condition) {
  body1;
} else {
  body2;
}

The if...else statement is similar to the if statement, except that no condition is written after else. When the condition of the if statement is satisfied, the statements inside the if are executed; when the condition of the if statement is not satisfied, the statements inside the else are executed. Likewise, when the body consists of only one statement, the curly braces can be omitted.

The else if statement#

if (condition1) {
  body1;
} else if (condition2) {
  body2;
} else if (condition3) {
  body3;
} else {
  body4;
}

The else if statement is a combination of if and else: it tests multiple conditions and selects among different statement branches. The final else statement does not need a condition. For example, if condition 1 is true, body 1 is executed; if condition 3 is true while condition 1 and condition 2 are both false, body 3 is executed; only when all the conditions are false is body 4 executed.

In fact, this construct is equivalent to the else clause of the first if containing only a single if statement, with the curly braces omitted so that they are written together. If the conditions are parallel to one another, writing it this way makes the logic of the code clearer.

Logically, it roughly corresponds to the following passage:

When solving a quadratic equation in one variable, the relationship between the roots of the equation and the discriminant:

  • if (Δ<0\Delta<0Δ<0) the equation has no solution;
  • otherwise, if (Δ=0\Delta=0Δ=0) the equation has two identical real solutions;
  • otherwise the equation has two distinct real solutions;

The switch statement#

switch (selector) {
  case label1:
    body1;
  case label2:
    body2;
  default:
    body3;
}

When the switch statement executes, the value of the selector is computed first; then, based on the value of the selector, the corresponding label is chosen, and execution starts from that label. The selector must be an expression of integer type, and the labels must all be constants of integer type. For example:

int i = 1;  // Here the data type of i is integer, which satisfies the requirement for an integer type expression

switch (i) {
  case 1:
    cout << "OI WIKI" << endl;
}
char i = 'A';

// Here the data type of i is character type, but char
// is also one of the integer types, which satisfies the requirement for an integer type expression
switch (i) {
  case 'A':
    cout << "OI WIKI" << endl;
}

In a switch statement, break statements must also be added as needed to interrupt execution; otherwise, once the corresponding case is selected, the statements in all the following cases and in the default will be run. See the example below for details.

char i = 'B';

switch (i) {
  case 'A':
    cout << "OI" << endl;
    break;

  case 'B':
    cout << "WIKI" << endl;

  default:
    cout << "Hello World" << endl;
}

After the code above runs, the output is WIKI and Hello World; if you do not want the statements in the branches below to be run, you need a break — see the example below for details.

char i = 'B';

switch (i) {
  case 'A':
    cout << "OI" << endl;
    break;

  case 'B':
    cout << "WIKI" << endl;
    break;

  default:
    cout << "Hello World" << endl;
}

After the code above runs, the output is WIKI: because of the break, the statements that follow are no longer executed. The last statement does not need a break, because there are no statements below it.

The entry numbers must not be repeated, but they may be reversed. That is to say, the order of the entry numbers does not matter. The cases (including default) may appear in any order. For example:

char i = 'B';

switch (i) {
  case 'B':
    cout << "WIKI" << endl;
    break;

  default:
    cout << "Hello World" << endl;
    break;

  case 'A':
    cout << "OI" << endl;
}

Curly braces can also be added optionally to the case clauses of a switch. Note, however, that if you need to define variables inside a switch statement, the curly braces must be added. For example:

char i = 'B';

switch (i) {
  case 'A': {
    int i = 1, j = 2;
    cout << "OI" << endl;
    ans = i + j;
    break;
  }

  case 'B': {
    int qwq = 3;
    cout << "WIKI" << endl;
    ans = qwq * qwq;
    break;
  }

  default: {
    cout << "Hello World" << endl;
  }
}
noteHow to understand switch

In the text above, terms such as "case clause" and "case sub-clause" were used a lot. In fact, at the level of the underlying implementation, a switch is equivalent to a set of jump statements. This is also why clever tricks like Duff's Device exist; those who wish to learn about it can study it on their own.

← PreviousOperatorsNext →Loops
Chapter 6 · C++ Fundamentals

Loops · Control Flow

oi-wiki.org/lang/loop.md

Sometimes we need to do the same thing many times; to avoid writing too much repetitive code, we need loops.

Sometimes the number of iterations is not a constant, in which case we cannot repeat the code multiple times and must use a loop.

The for statement#

The following is the structure of the for statement:

for (initialization; condition; update) {
  loop body;
}

Order of execution:

e.g. reading n numbers:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
  cin >> a[i];
}

Of the three parts of the for statement, any one of them can be omitted. Among these, omitting the condition is equivalent to the condition always being true.

The while statement#

The following is the structure of the while statement:

while (condition) {
  loop body;
}

Order of execution:

e.g. verifying the 3x+1 conjecture:

while (x > 1) {
  if (x % 2 == 1) {
    x = 3 * x + 1;
  } else {
    x = x / 2;
  }
}

The do...while statement#

The following is the structure of the do...while statement:

do {
  loop body;
} while (condition);

Order of execution:

The difference from the while statement is that the do...while statement executes the loop body first and then performs the test.

e.g. enumerating permutations:

do {
  // do someting...
} while (next_permutation(a + 1, a + n + 1));

The relationship between the three statements#

// for statement

for (statement1; statement2; statement3) {
  statement4;
}

// while statement

statement1;
while (statement2) {
  statement4;
  statement3;
}

These are equivalent when there is no continue statement (see below) in statement4, but the latter form is rarely used.

// while statement

statement1;
while (statement2) {
  statement1;
}

// do...while statement

do {
  statement1;
} while (statement2);

These two forms are also equivalent when there is no continue statement in statement1.

while (1) {
  // do something...
}

for (;;) {
  // do something...
}

Both of these forms loop forever. (You can use break (see below) to exit.)

As you can see, the three statements can replace one another, but in general, the choice of statement follows these principles:

  1. Use the for statement when the loop involves a fixed incremental step (most commonly, enumeration);
  2. Use the while statement when only the termination condition of the loop is known;
  3. When using a while statement, if the loop body should be executed first and the test performed afterwards, use the do...while statement. It is rarely used; a common scenario is user input.

The break and continue statements#

The purpose of the break statement is to exit the loop.

The purpose of the continue statement is to skip the rest of the loop body. The following is an example of using the continue statement in a do...while statement:

do {
  // do something...
  continue;  // equivalent to goto END;
// do something...
END:;
} while (statement);

Both the break and continue statements can be used in the loop bodies of all three loop statements.

In general, the break and continue statements are used to make the logic of the code clearer, for example:

// The logic is less clear, and the nesting of braces is complicated

for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
  if (i != x) {
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
      if (j != x) {
        // do something...
      }
    }
  }
}

// The logic is clearer, and the nesting of braces is simple and clear

for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
  if (i == x) continue;
  for (int j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
    if (j == x) continue;
    // do something...
  }
}
// The condition of the for statement is complicated and does not reflect the essence of "enumeration"

for (int i = l; i <= r && i % 10 != 0; ++i) {
  // do something...
}

// The for statement is used for enumeration, and break expresses "until when"

for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) {
  if (i % 10 == 0) break;
  // do something...
}
// Statements are duplicated, and the order is unnatural

statement1;
while (statement3) {
  statement2;
  statement1;
}

// No duplicated statements, and the order is natural

while (1) {
  statement1;
  if (!statement3) break;
  statement2;
}
← PreviousBranchingNext →Arrays
Chapter 7 · C++ Fundamentals

Arrays · Compound Data Types

oi-wiki.org/lang/array.md

An array is a container that holds objects of the same type. The objects stored in an array have no names; instead, they are accessed through their positions. The size of an array is fixed, and the length of an array cannot be changed arbitrarily.

Defining Arrays#

An array is declared in the form a[d], where a is the name of the array and d is the number of elements in the array. At compile time, d should be known — that is, d should be an integral constant expression.

unsigned int d1 = 42;
const int d2 = 42;
int arr1[d1];  // error: d1 is not a constant expression
int arr2[d2];  // correct: arr2 is an array of length 42

You cannot assign one array directly to another:

int arr1[3];
int arr2 = arr1;  // error
arr2 = arr1;      // error

Larger arrays should be defined as global variables whenever possible. Local variables are created on the stack, so an overly large array (larger than the stack size) will overflow the stack, which in turn causes an RE. If an array is declared in the global scope, it is created in the static storage area.

Accessing Array Elements#

Elements of an array can be accessed with the subscript operator []; array indices (the values inside the square brackets) start from 0. Take an array with 10 elements as an example: its indices are 0 to 9, not 1 to 10. In OI, however, for convenience we usually make the array a bit larger, leave the first element of the array unused, and access array elements starting from subscript 1.

Example 1: Read an integer nnn from standard input, then read nnn numbers and store them in an array. Here, n≤1000n\leq 1000n≤1000.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int arr[1001];  // the subscript range of array arr is [0, 1001)

int main() {
  int n;
  cin >> n;
  for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    cin >> arr[i];
  }
}

Example 2: (continued from Example 1) Compute the sum of the elements in the array arr and output the sum. It is guaranteed that the sum of all elements in the array is less than or equal to 231−12^{31} - 1231−1.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int arr[1001];

int main() {
  int n;
  cin >> n;
  for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    cin >> arr[i];
  }

  int sum = 0;
  for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    sum += arr[i];
  }

  printf("%d\n", sum);
  return 0;
}

Accessing Out-of-Bounds Subscripts#

The subscript idx\mathit{idx}idx of an array must satisfy 0≤idx<size0\leq \mathit{idx}< \mathit{size}0≤idx<size; if the subscript is not within this range, it is undefined behavior, which can have unpredictable consequences, such as a segmentation fault, or modifying variables other than the intended ones, and so on.

Multidimensional Arrays#

A multidimensional array is, in essence, an "array of arrays": the elements of the outer array are arrays. A two-dimensional array requires two dimensions in its definition: the length of the array, and the length of the elements inside the array. Two indices must be written when accessing a two-dimensional array:

int arr[3][4];  // an array of length 3 whose elements are "arrays of length 4
                // with int elements"
arr[2][1] = 1;  // accessing the two-dimensional array

We often process two-dimensional arrays with nested for loops.

Example: Read two numbers nnn and mmm from standard input, denoting the height and width of a black-and-white image, respectively, where n,m≤1000n,m\leq 1000n,m≤1000. Each of the next nnn lines of data contains mmm numbers separated by spaces, representing the brightness value at that position. Now we read this image and store it in a two-dimensional array.

const int MAXN = 1001;
int pic[MAXN][MAXN];
int n, m;

cin >> n >> m;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
  for (int j = 1; j <= m; ++j) cin >> pic[i][j];

Likewise, you can define three-dimensional, four-dimensional, and even higher-dimensional arrays.

← PreviousLoopsNext →Structs
Chapter 8 · C++ Fundamentals

Structs · Compound Data Types

oi-wiki.org/lang/struct.md

author: Ir1d, cjsoft, Lans1ot

A struct can be viewed as a composite of a series of elements called members.

It can be viewed as a user-defined data type.

noteNote

The struct described on this page is different from the struct in C; in C++, struct has been extended into a class specifier similar to class.

Defining a Struct#

struct Object {
  int weight;
  int value;
} e[array_length];

const Object a;
Object b, B[array_length], tmp;
Object *c;

The example above defines a struct named Object, with two members value, weight, both of type int.

After the }, a constant a of data type Object, a variable b, a variable tmp, an array B, and a pointer c are defined. For any type that already exists, the approach shown here can be used to define constants, variables, pointers, arrays, and so on.

About pointers: you need not force yourself to master them.

Defining Pointers#

If you are defining a pointer to a built-in type, it is done just as pointers are normally defined.

If you are defining a struct pointer, use StructName* in the definition.

struct Edge {
  /*
  ...
  */
  Edge* nxt;
};

The example above is for illustration only; there is no need to dwell on its practical meaning.

Accessing/Modifying Members#

You can access members with variable_name.member_name. For example, cout << var.v can be used to output the member v of var.

You can also access members with pointer_name->member_name, or with (*pointer_name).member_name. For example, (*ptr).v = tmp or ptr->v = tmp assigns the value tmp to the member v of the struct that the struct pointer ptr points to.

Why Do We Need Structs?#

First of all, all roads lead to Rome — the same effect can be achieved without using structs. But structs can explicitly bundle members (in competitive programming, usually variables) together; for instance, the Object struct in this example puts value,weight together (the actual point of defining this struct is to represent the weight and value of an item). The benefit of this is that it restricts the usage of the members. Imagine not using structs and having two arrays value[], Value[] — it would be easy to mix them up. Using a struct reduces the chance of mistakes involving variable usage.

Moreover, different structs (struct types, such as the Object struct), or different struct variables (instances of a struct, such as the e array above), can have members with the same name (e.g. tmp.value,b.value); members with the same name are independent of one another (each has its own memory — for instance, modifying tmp.value does not affect the value of b.value). The benefit of this is that you can use the same or similar variables to describe an item. For example, Object has the member variable value; we could also define a Car struct that likewise has a member named value. Without structs, we might have to define arrays with different names such as valueOfObject[],valueOfCar[] to distinguish them.

If you want to describe something in more detail, you can also define member functions. Please refer to Class for details.

More Operations?#

See Class for details.

Notes#

To access memory more efficiently, when the compiler processes the actual storage of the members in a struct, it may align the members at certain byte positions, which means there can be gaps inside the struct. Therefore, the space occupied by the struct may be larger than the sum of the space occupied by all of its members.

References#

  1. Class - zh.cppreference.com
  2. Data structures - cplusplus.com
  3. Alignment - Microsoft Docs
← PreviousArraysNext →Unions
Chapter 9 · C++ Fundamentals

Unions · Compound Data Types

oi-wiki.org/lang/union.md

A union is a special class type that can hold only one of its non-static data members at a time.

Unions were officially added to the entry level of the NOI syllabus in 2023.

Defining a Union#

The class specifier for declaring a union is similar to the declaration of a class or struct:

union MyUnion {
  int x;
  long long y;
} x;

Defining a union is similar to defining a struct. With the definition above, MyUnion can likewise be used as a user-defined type. The name MyUnion can be omitted.

Accessing/Modifying Members#

As with structs, you can likewise use variable_name.member_name for access.

The size of the memory space occupied by a union is no less than the size of its largest member, and all members share the same memory space and address. When one member is assigned to, due to the shared memory, the other members of the union are all overwritten. That is, a union can only hold the value of one member at any given moment.

For more uses of unions, see cppreference: union declaration.

← PreviousStructsNext →Pointers
Chapter 10 · C++ Fundamentals

Pointers · Compound Data Types

oi-wiki.org/lang/pointer.md

author: tsagaanbar, Enter-tainer, Xeonacid

Variable Addresses and Pointers#

In a program, our data all has the address at which it is stored. During each actual run of the program, the storage location of a variable in physical memory is not necessarily the same. Nevertheless, while programming, we can still use certain statements to obtain the address of data in memory.

An address is data, too. The type of variable used to store addresses has a special name — the "pointer variable", sometimes simply called a "pointer".

noteThe size of a pointer variable

The size of a pointer variable differs across environments. On a 32-bit machine, an address is represented as a 32-bit binary integer, so a pointer is 4 bytes in size. On a 64-bit machine, an address is represented as a 64-bit binary integer, so a pointer becomes 8 bytes in size.

An address is merely ordinary data, like a tick mark on a ruler; to deal with different types of data, "pointer variables" also come in different types. For example, there can be a pointer variable of int type, where the address stored in it (that is, the value the pointer variable stores) corresponds to the starting address of a 32-bit region of space; there can also be a pointer variable of char type, where the stored address corresponds to the starting address of an 8-bit region of space.

In fact, a user can also declare a pointer variable that points to a pointer variable.

Suppose the user has defined a struct:

struct ThreeInt {
  int a;
  int b;
  int c;
};

Then a pointer variable of type ThreeInt corresponds to a region of space of 3 × 32 = 96 bits.

Declaring and Using Pointers#

In C/C++, the type of a pointer variable is the type name followed by an asterisk *. For example, the type name of a pointer variable of int type is int*.

We can use the & symbol to obtain the address of a variable.

To access the region of space corresponding to the address stored in a pointer variable (also called the space the pointer points to), the pointer variable must be dereferenced, using the * symbol.

int main() {
  int a = 123;  // a: 123
  int* pa = &a;
  *pa = 321;  // a: 321
}

The same goes for struct variables. To access a member of the struct a pointer points to, you must first dereference the pointer, then use the . member access operator. However, it is recommended to use the more convenient notation of the "arrow" operator ->.

struct ThreeInt {
  int a;
  int b;
  int c;
};

int main() {
  ThreeInt x{1, 2, 3}, y{6, 7, 8};
  ThreeInt* px = &x;
  (*px) = y;    // x: {6,7,8}
  (*px).a = 4;  // x: {4,7,8}
  px->b = 5;    // x: {4,5,8}
}

Pointer Offsets#

Pointer variables can also be added to and subtracted from integers. For an int pointer, each addition of 1 (an increment of 1) offsets the address it points to by 32 bits (that is, 4 bytes); if 2 is added, the address it points to is offset by 2 × 32 = 64 bits. Likewise, for a char pointer, each increment offsets the address it points to by 8 bits (that is, 1 byte).

Accessing Arrays with Pointer Offsets#

As we said earlier, an array is a contiguous region of storage. And in C/C++, using an array name directly gives the starting address of the array.

int main() {
  int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};
  int* p = a;  // p points to a[0]
  *p = 4;      // a: [4, 2, 3]
  p = p + 1;   // p points to a[1]
  *p = 5;      // a: [4, 5, 3]
  p++;         // p points to a[2]
  *p = 6;      // a: [4, 5, 6]
}

When accessing elements of an array through a pointer, "pointer offsets" are often needed — in other words, access is done through a base address (the starting address of the array) plus an offset.

We often use the [] operator to access the element at a specified offset in an array, e.g. a[3] or p[4]. This notation is equivalent to doing arithmetic on the pointer and then dereferencing it: p[4] and *(p + 4) are two equivalent spellings.

Null Pointers#

Before C++11, C++ used the NULL macro to denote the null pointer constant just as C did; the implementation of NULL in C++ was generally as follows:

// before C++11
#define NULL 0

noteThe definition of <code>NULL</code> in C

Before C23, the C language had two definitions of NULL, differing only in type: one is an integer constant expression, and the other is a constant expression converted to the void * type; but both have the value 0, and the compiler may choose either implementation.

Mixing null pointers and the integer 0 leads to many problems in C++, for example:

int f(int x);
int f(int* p);

When calling f(NULL), the type of the function actually called is int(int) rather than int(int *).

noteThe problems <code>NULL</code> causes in C

Compared with C++, because there are two definitions, the problems NULL causes in C are more serious: in a function that takes variadic arguments, if the function's author wants to accept a pointer but the caller passes a NULL defined as an integer, undefined behavior results, because when the passed variadic argument is used inside the function, a type conversion must be performed, and conversion from an integer type to a pointer type is undefined behavior.1

To solve these problems, C++11 introduced the nullptr keyword as the null pointer constant.

C++ specifies that nullptr can be implicitly converted to any pointer type, and the result of such a conversion is the null pointer value of that type.

The type of nullptr is std::nullptr_t, called the null pointer type; a possible implementation is as follows:

namespace std {
typedef decltype(nullptr) nullptr_t;
}

In addition, starting with C++11 the implementation of the NULL macro has been changed to:

// since C++11
#define NULL nullptr
noteC&#x27;s improvement of the null pointer constant

For similar reasons, C23 also introduced nullptr as the null pointer constant, along with nullptr_t as its type.1

Advanced Uses of Pointers#

Using pointers, the programmer can manipulate data everywhere in the running program, without being restricted by scope.

Using Pointer-Type Parameters#

In C/C++, the arguments used when calling a function (procedure) are all passed into the subroutine by copy (except for references, which will be introduced later). By default, a function can only return its result to the caller through its return value. But if a function wants to modify data outside itself, or if the amount of data in some struct/class is rather large and should not be copied, then by passing in the address of the external data, the function gains the ability to access or even modify the external data.

The my_swap function below receives two pointers to int and, using an intermediate variable inside the function, accomplishes the swap of the values of two int variables.

void my_swap(int *a, int *b) {
  int t;
  t = *a;
  *a = *b;
  *b = t;
}

int main() {
  int a = 6, b = 10;
  my_swap(&a, &b);
  // after the call, the value of the variable a in the main function becomes 10, and the value of b becomes 6
}

C++ introduced the concept of references, which are easier to use and safer than pointers. For details, see C++: References and Differences between C and C++: Pointers and References.

Dynamic Instantiation#

Beyond this, writing programs often involves dynamic memory allocation — that is, the program dynamically requests from, or returns to, the operating system the memory needed to store data at run time. When the program requests memory by calling an operating system interface, the operating system returns the address of the space the program requested. To use this space, we need to store the address of this space in a pointer variable.

In C++, we use the new operator to obtain a region of memory, and the delete operator to release the space a pointer points to.

int* p = new int(1234);
/* ... */
delete p;

The statements above use the new operator to request a region of space the size of an int from the operating system, initialize the value in it to 1234, and declare an int pointer p pointing to this space.

Likewise, new can also be used to allocate new objects:

class A {
  int a;

 public:
  A(int a_) : a(a_) {}
};

int main() {
  A* p = new A(1234);
  /* ... */
  delete p;
}

As shown above, a "new expression" will attempt to allocate a region of space of the corresponding size, attempt to construct the object in this space, and return the address of this space.

struct ThreeInt {
  int a;
  int b;
  int c;
};

int main() {
  ThreeInt* p = new ThreeInt{1, 2, 3};
  /* ... */
  delete p;
}

noteList-initialization

The {} operator can be used to initialize structs that have no constructor. In addition, using the {} operator makes the initialization form of variables uniform. See "list initialization (since C++11)" for details.

Note that when memory requested with new is no longer being used, it must be released with delete. A region of memory must not be released twice or more. And applying delete to the null pointer nullptr is legal.

Dynamically Creating Arrays#

The new[] operator can also be used to create arrays. In this case, the new[] operator returns the base address of the array — that is, the address of the array's first element — and we can store this address in a pointer of the corresponding type. When releasing it, the delete[] operator is required.

size_t element_cnt = 5;
int *p = new int[element_cnt];
delete[] p;

The elements of the array are stored contiguously, i.e. p + 1 points to the successor element of p.

Two-Dimensional Arrays#

When storing data in matrix form, a data type like the "two-dimensional array" may come into use. Semantically speaking, a two-dimensional array is an array of arrays. And computer memory can be viewed as one very long one-dimensional array. To store a two-dimensional array in computer memory, there is then the question of whether it is "contiguous" or not.

By "contiguous" we mean that the end of any row of the two-dimensional array and the beginning of the next row are adjacent in physical address; in other words, the entire two-dimensional array can be viewed as a one-dimensional array. Otherwise, the two are not necessarily adjacent physically.

For a "contiguous" two-dimensional array, a single loop with a constantly incrementing pointer suffices to traverse all the data in the array. For a non-contiguous two-dimensional array, since the rows are not contiguous, one must first obtain the address of the beginning of a row, and then access the elements within that row.

noteStorage of two-dimensional arrays

This way of storing data row by row is called row-major storage; correspondingly, data can also be stored column by column. Due to the characteristics of computer memory access, accessing contiguous data generally yields higher efficiency. Therefore, you should choose "row-major" or "column-major" storage according to how the data might be used.

Dynamically Creating Two-Dimensional Arrays#

In C/C++, we can use a statement like the one below to declare a two-dimensional array with N rows and M columns whose space is physically contiguous.

noteDescribing the dimensions of an array

A more general way is to speak of the n-th dimension. For the "row-major" storage form, the length of the array's first dimension is N, and the length of its second dimension is M.

int a[N][M];

This form of declaration requires N and M to be constant expressions that can be determined at compile time.

In C/C++, the first element of an array has subscript 0, so an expression like a[r][c] stands for the (c + 1)-th element of the (r + 1)-th row of the two-dimensional array a; we also say the subscript of this element is (r,c).

In actual use, however, the size of a (two-dimensional) array may not be fixed, and dynamic memory allocation is needed.

A common approach is to declare a one-dimensional array of length N × M, and access the element with subscript (r, c) of the two-dimensional array via the subscript r * M + c.

int* a = new int[N * M];

This approach guarantees that the two-dimensional array is contiguous.

noteLinear storage of arrays at the physical level

In fact, data in memory can all be viewed as stored linearly; therefore, under certain rules, by dynamically allocating the space of a one-dimensional array, an n-dimensional array can be stored on it.

In addition, memory can also be obtained and used following the concept of the "array of arrays". For an array that stores several arrays, what is actually stored is an array of the base addresses of those arrays — that is, an array storing several pointer variables.

We need a variable to store the base address of this "array of arrays" — that is, the address of a pointer. This variable is then a "pointer to a pointer", sometimes also called a "double pointer", for example:

int** a = new int*[5];

Next, we need to request space for each of the arrays:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  a[i] = new int[5];
}

At this point, we have finished obtaining the memory. As for releasing memory obtained in this way, a reverse operation must be performed: first release each array, then release the array storing the base addresses of these arrays, for example:

for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  delete[] a[i];
}
delete[] a;

Note that for a two-dimensional array obtained this way, its space cannot be guaranteed to be contiguous.

There is one more approach, which makes use of the "pointer to an array".

noteThe difference between an array name and the address of the array&#x27;s first element

As we said before, in C/C++, using an array name directly gives a value equal to the address of the array's first element. But the type of the variable that the array name denotes is actually the whole array, not a single element.

int main() { int a[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; }

Conceptually, the type of the identifier a in the code is int[5]; in practice, the address pointed to by a + 1 is offset from the address pointed to by a by the length of 5 int variables.

int main() {
  int(*a)[5] = new int[5][5];
  int* p = a[2];
  a[2][1] = 1;
  delete[] a;
}

This approach also yields contiguous memory, but the form a[n] can be used directly to obtain the base address of the (n + 1)-th row of the array; therefore, using the form a[r][c], the element with subscript (r, c) can be accessed.

Since a pointer to an array is also a definite data type, the lengths of all dimensions other than the array's first must be constants that can be determined at compile time. Otherwise, the compiler would be unable to translate expressions such as a[n] (a being a pointer to an array).

Pointers to Functions#

For an introduction to functions, please see the C++ Functions chapter.

Put simply, to call a function, you need to know the function's parameter types and count, as well as its return type; these are collectively called the interface type.

Functions can be called through function pointers. Sometimes, several functions share the same interface type; using function pointers, the function to be called can be chosen dynamically according to how the program runs. In other words, without modifying a function, merely by changing the argument passed into it (the function pointer), the behavior of that function can be changed.

Suppose we have several binary-operation functions on the int type; then the function's parameters are 2 ints, and its return value is also an int. Below is an example that uses a function pointer:

#include <iostream>

int (*binary_int_op)(int, int);

int foo1(int a, int b) { return a * b + b; }

int foo2(int a, int b) { return (a + b) * b; }

int main() {
  int choice;
  std::cin >> choice;
  if (choice == 1) {
    binary_int_op = foo1;
  } else {
    binary_int_op = foo2;
  }

  int m, n;
  std::cin >> m >> n;
  std::cout << binary_int_op(m, n);
}

note<code>&amp;</code>, <code>*</code>, and function pointers

In C, writings such as void (*p)() = foo;, void (*p)() = &foo;, void (*p)() = *foo;, and void (*p)() = ***foo all give the same result.

Since a function (such as foo) can be implicitly converted to a pointer to that function, the writing void (*p)() = foo; is valid.

The & operator can obtain the address of an object, and this holds for functions too, so the writing void (*p)() = &foo; is also valid.

Applying the * operator to a function pointer yields the function the pointer points to; as for a writing like **foo, *foo yields the function foo, which is then immediately implicitly converted back into a pointer to foo. By the same reasoning, what **foo yields in the end is still a function pointer pointing to foo; the user may use as many *s as they like, and the result is the same.

Similarly, when calling, using statements like (*p)() and p() is the same — the * operator can be omitted.

Reference: Why do function pointer definitions work with any number of ampersands '&' or asterisks '*'? - stackoverflow.com

The typedef keyword can be used to declare the type of a function pointer.

typedef int (*p_bi_int_op)(int, int);

This way, we can use the type p_bi_int_op afterwards — that is, a pointer to a function that "takes 2 int parameters and also returns int".

Using std::function, functions can be referenced more conveniently. (to be continued)

Using function pointers, "callback functions" can be implemented. (to be continued)

References and Notes#

Footnotes

Chapter 11 · C++ Fundamentals

Functions

oi-wiki.org/lang/func.md

author: Ir1d, tsagaanbar, yang-lile

Declaring a Function#

A function in programming is generally a collection of statements. We can also call it a "subroutine". In programming, if there are some repeated processes, we can extract them and turn them into a function. A function can receive several values, which are called the function's parameters. A function can also return some value, which is called the function's return value.

To declare a function, we need the return type, the name of the function, and the parameter list.

// Return type: int
// Name of the function: some_function
// Parameter list: int, int
int some_function(int, int);

As shown above, we have declared a function named some_function, which takes two parameters of type int and whose return type is also int. We can consider that this function will perform some operations on the two integers passed in and return a result of the same type.

Implementing a Function: Writing the Function's Definition#

A declaration of the function alone is not enough: it only lets us know the interface type of the function when calling it (that is, what data it receives and what data it returns), but it lacks the concrete internal implementation, namely the function's definition. We can write code that implements the function somewhere else after the declaration (it can also be implemented in a separate file, but then the separately compiled files must be provided together at link time).

If the function has a return value, a return statement is needed to return the value to the caller. As soon as execution reaches a return statement, the current function ends immediately, and the statements after it are not executed.

int some_function(int, int);  // declaration

/* some other code here... */

int some_function(int x, int y) {  // definition
  int result = 2 * x + y;
  return result;
  result = 3;  // this statement is never executed
}

In the definition, we give names to the variables in the function's parameter list. This way, we can use these variables in the function definition.

Within the same file, we can also directly merge the declaration and the definition into one — in other words, completing the definition at the point of declaration.

int some_function(int x, int y) { return 2 * x + y; }

If a function does not need a return value, its return type is marked as void; if a function needs no parameters, the parameter list can be left empty. Likewise, a function with no return value also stops executing when it reaches a return; statement.

void say_hello() {
  cout << "hello!\n";
  cout << "hello!\n";
  cout << "hello!\n";
  return;
  cout << "hello!\n";  // this statement is never executed
}

Calling a Function#

As with variables, a function must be declared before it can be used. The act of using a function is called a "call". We can call other functions from inside any function, including the function itself. A function calling itself is called recursion.

In most languages, a function call is written as the function's name followed by a pair of parentheses (), as in foo(). If the function requires parameters, we fill in the arguments it needs, in order, inside the parentheses, separated by commas, as in foo(1, 2). A function call is also an expression, and the function's return value is the value of the expression.

The parameters written in a function's declaration can be understood as variables usable inside the current invocation of the function; their values are initialized from the values passed at the call site. Consider the following example:

void foo(int, int);

/* ... */

void foo(int x, int y) {
  x = x * 2;
  y = y + 3;
}

/* ... */

a = 1;
b = 1;
// Before the call: a = 1, b = 1
foo(a, b);  // call foo
            // After the call: a = 1, b = 1

In the example above, foo(a, b) is a call to foo. At the time of the call, the variables x and y in foo are initialized from the values of a and b at the call site. Therefore, modifications to the variables x and y inside foo do not affect the values of the variables at the call site.

If we need to modify the values of variables inside the function (subroutine), we have to use "pass by reference".

void foo(int& x, int& y) {
  x = x * 2;
  y = y + 3;
}

/* ... */

a = 1;
b = 1;
// Before the call: a = 1, b = 1
foo(a, b);  // call foo
            // After the call: a = 2, b = 4

In the code above, we see that an & (ampersand) has been added after the int in the function's parameter list; this denotes a reference to int. When foo is called, the call-site variables a and b respectively initialize the two references to int, x and y, inside foo. The x and y inside foo can be understood as "aliases" of the call-site variables a and b: operations on x and y inside foo are operations on a and b at the call site.

The main Function#

In particular, every C/C++ program needs to have a function named main. Every program starts running from the main function.

The main function can also have parameters; through the parameters of main, we can obtain the instructions passed to this program from the outside (namely, the "command-line arguments"), so as to respond differently.

Below is a piece of code that calls a function (subroutine):

// hello_subroutine.cpp

#include <iostream>

void say_hello() {
  std::cout << "hello!\n";
  std::cout << "hello!\n";
  std::cout << "hello!\n";
}

int main() {
  say_hello();
  say_hello();
}

File I/O

oi-wiki.org/lang/file-op.md

author: Ir1d, cqnuljs, akakw1, MingqiHuang, Chrogeek, henrytbtrue, Planet6174, StudyingFather

The Concept of a File#

A file is a collection of related data gathered together for a specific purpose. C/C++ regards every file as an ordered stream of bytes; every file ends with the end-of-file marker (EOF). To operate on a file, a program should first open the file; whenever a file has been opened (remember to close the files you open), the file is associated with a stream, and this stream is in fact a sequence of bytes.

C/C++ divides files into text files and binary files. A text file is simply a plain text file (the key point), while a binary file is a file in some special format, or an executable code file, among others.

Steps for File Operations#

  1. Open the file, point the file pointer at the file, and decide the mode in which the file is opened;
  2. Read from and write to the file (the operations mainly used during contests; some other operations are omitted for now);
  3. Close the file after you are done using it.

The freopen Function#

Overview#

This function redirects a specified input/output stream to a file in a specified manner. It is contained in the header stdio.h (cstdio). The function can change the input/output environment without changing the original appearance of the code, but when using it you should ensure that the stream is reliable.

The function mainly has three modes: reading, writing, and appending.

Syntax#

FILE* freopen(const char* filename, const char* mode, FILE* stream);

Parameter Description#

  • filename: the name of the file to open
  • mode: the mode in which the file is opened, indicating the file's access permissions
  • stream: the file pointer; usually the standard file streams (stdin/stdout) or the standard error output stream (stderr)
  • Return value: a file pointer pointing to the opened file

File Open Modes (optional)#

  • r: opens the file in read-only mode; the file must exist; only reading data is allowed (commonly used)
  • r+: opens the file in read/write mode; the file must exist; reading and writing data are allowed
  • rb: opens a binary file in read-only mode; the file must exist; only reading data is allowed
  • rb+: opens a binary file in read/write mode; the file must exist; reading and writing data are allowed
  • rt+: opens a text file in read/write mode; reading and writing data are allowed
  • w: opens the file in write-only mode; if the file does not exist, a new file is created, otherwise the contents are emptied; only writing data is allowed (commonly used)
  • w+: opens the file in read/write mode; if the file does not exist, a new file will be created, otherwise the contents are emptied; reading and writing data are allowed
  • wb: opens a binary file in write-only mode; if the file does not exist, a new file will be created, otherwise the contents are emptied; only writing data is allowed
  • wb+: opens a binary file in read/write mode; if the file does not exist, a new file will be created, otherwise the contents are emptied; reading and writing data are allowed
  • a: opens the file in write-only mode; if the file does not exist, a new file will be created; written data will be appended to the end of the file (the EOF marker is preserved)
  • a+: opens the file in read/write mode; if the file does not exist, a new file will be created; written data will be appended to the end of the file (the EOF marker is not preserved)
  • at+: opens a text file in read/write mode; written data will be appended to the end of the file
  • ab+: opens a binary file in read/write mode; written data will be appended to the end of the file

Usage#

To read the contents of a file:

freopen("data.in", "r", stdin);
// data.in is the name of the file to read; it must be placed in the same directory as the executable

To output to a file:

freopen("data.out", "w", stdout);
// data.out is the name of the output file; it is in the same directory as the executable

Closing the standard input/output streams

fclose(stdin);
fclose(stdout);
noteNote

Functions such as printf/scanf/cin/cout use stdin/stdout by default; after stdin/stdout is redirected, these functions will read from / write to the file being redirected to

Template#

#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

int main(void) {
  freopen("data.in", "r", stdin);
  freopen("data.out", "w", stdout);
  /*
  The code in between needs no changes; just use cin and cout directly
  */
  fclose(stdin);
  fclose(stdout);
  return 0;
}

The fopen Function (optional)#

This function is roughly the same as freopen: it opens the specified file and returns a pointer to the opened file

Function Prototype#

FILE* fopen(const char* path, const char* mode)

The meanings of the parameters are the same as for freopen

Available Reading/Writing Functions (Basic)#

  • fread/fwrite
  • fgetc/fputc
  • fscanf/fprintf
  • fgets/fputs

Usage#

FILE *in, *out;  // define file pointers
in = fopen("data.in", "r");
out = fopen("data.out", "w");
/*
do what you want to do
*/
fclose(in);
fclose(out);

C++ ifstream/ofstream File Input/Output Streams#

Usage#

To read the contents of a file:

ifstream fin("data.in");
// data.in is the relative or absolute location of the file to read

To output to a file:

ofstream fout("data.out");
// data.out is the relative or absolute location of the output file

Closing the standard input/output streams

fin.close();
fout.close();

Template#

#include <fstream>
using namespace std;  // both types are in the std namespace

ifstream fin("data.in");
ofstream fout("data.out");

int main(void) {
  /*
  In the code in between, just change cin to fin and cout to fout
  */
  fin.close();
  fout.close();
  return 0;
}

References#

  1. A Complete Guide to the Informatics Olympiad

Chapter 13 · The C++ Standard Library

Overview of the C++ Standard Library

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/index.md

The C++ Standard#

The first thing to introduce is the version of C++ itself. Since C++ is just a language, and different compilers implement C++ in different ways, standardization is needed to constrain how compilers implement it, so that C++ code behaves consistently across different compilers. Since its birth in 1985, C++ has seen a total of 7 official C++ standards published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), namely, in order: C++98, C++03, C++11 (also known as C++0x), C++14 (also known as C++1y), C++17 (also known as C++1z), C++20 (also known as C++2a), and C++23 (also known as C++2b). C++ standard drafts are available on the open-std website, and the progress of the latest standard can be viewed at Current Status : Standard C++. In addition, there are some supplementary standards, such as C++ TR1.

Each version of the C++ standard specifies not only the syntax and language features of C++, but also an implementation specification for the library built into C++; this library is the C++ standard library. The C++ standard library contains implementations of a large amount of commonly used code, such as input and output, basic data structures, memory management, multithreading support, and so on. Mastering the C++ standard library is a necessary step toward writing more modern C++ code. Detailed documentation of the C++ standard library is available on the cppreference website; the documentation covers the usage, efficiency, caveats, and so on of the types and functions in the standard library — make good use of it.

It should be noted that different online judge (OJ) platforms differ in the C++ versions they support; for example, the latest ICPC contest rules support the C++20 standard. According to a resolution of the NOI Scientific Committee, since September 1, 2021, NOI Linux 2.0 has been used as the standard environment for NOI-series contests and events such as CSP-J/S. The g++ 9.3.0 specified in NOI Linux 2.0 has a default supported standard of C++14, and also supports the C++17 standard, which satisfies the needs of the vast majority of contestants. Therefore, when learning C++, pay attention to the standard supported by your contest, so as to avoid compilation errors during a contest.

The Standard Template Library (STL)#

The STL, i.e. the Standard Template Library, is part of the C++ standard library; it contains some generic, templated data structures and algorithms. Because of its templated nature, it is compatible with custom data types and saves you from a great deal of reinventing the wheel. Both NOI and ICPC contests allow the use of the STL, so putting the STL to good use lets you avoid writing needless algorithms and take full advantage of the compiler's optimization of the template library to improve efficiency. For a detailed introduction to the STL, please see the corresponding pages: STL containers and STL algorithms.

noteWhat is reinventing the wheel

Reinventing the wheel (Reinventing_the_wheel) means re-inventing algorithms that already exist, or re-writing readily available, already-optimized code. Reinventing the wheel usually costs a great deal of time and effort, and the result is still not as good as what others have made. But if it is for the sake of learning or practice, reinventing the wheel is necessary.

The Boost Library#

Boost is another long-renowned open-source C++ utility library besides the standard library; its code is portable, high-quality, high-performance, and highly reliable. The number of modules in Boost is very large and its functionality is comprehensive, and it enjoys complete cross-platform support, so it is regarded as a de facto standard library for C++. Quite a few features of the C++ standard also come from Boost, such as smart pointers, metaprogramming, and date and time. Although Boost cannot be used in OI, many of the off-the-shelf components ("wheels") in Boost can be used to verify algorithms or for stress testing: for example, Boost.Geometry has an implementation of R-trees, Boost.Graph has graph-related algorithms, and Boost.Intrusive provides a set of intrusive containers whose usage is similar to that of STL containers. Interested readers can search online for tutorials on their own.

References#

  1. C++ reference
  2. C++ Reference Manual
  3. Wikipedia - C++
  4. Boost official website
  5. Boost tutorial website

Overview of STL Containers · STL Containers

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/container.md

Classification#

Sequence Containers#

  • Vector (vector): a sequential list where elements can be added efficiently at the back.
  • Array (array) C++11: a fixed-length sequential list, a simple wrapper around C-style arrays.
  • Deque (deque): a sequential list where elements can be added efficiently at either end.
  • List (list): a linked list that can be traversed in both directions.
  • Forward list (forward_list): a linked list that can be traversed in only one direction.

Associative Containers#

  • Set (set): a container that stores distinct elements in order. Its implementation is a red-black tree made up of nodes, where each node contains one element, and the nodes are arranged by some predicate that compares element values.
  • Multiset (multiset): a container that stores elements in order. It allows equal elements to exist.
  • Map (map): a set of {key, value} pairs, arranged by some predicate that compares keys.
  • Multimap (multimap): a multiset of {key, value} pairs; that is, a map in which keys may be equal.
noteWhat is a predicate (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predicate_%28mathematical_logic%29"><strong>Predicate</strong></a>)?

A predicate is simply a function whose return value is true or false. Predicates are used often in STL containers, as template parameters.

Unordered (Associative) Containers#

  • Unordered (multi)set (unordered_set/unordered_multiset) C++11: differs from set/multiset in that its elements are unordered — it only cares about "whether an element exists" — and it is implemented with hashing.
  • Unordered (multi)map (unordered_map/unordered_multimap) C++11: differs from map/multimap in that its keys are unordered — it only cares about "the correspondence between keys and values" — and it is implemented with hashing.

Container Adapters#

Container adapters are not actually containers. They lack some of the characteristics of containers (e.g., having iterators, having a clear() function, ...).

"An adapter is a mechanism that makes one thing's behavior resemble another thing's behavior"; a container adapter wraps a container and makes it exhibit a different behavior.

  • Stack (stack): a last-in-first-out (LIFO) container; by default it is a wrapper around the deque (deque).
  • Queue (queue): a first-in-first-out (FIFO) container; by default it is a wrapper around the deque (deque).
  • Priority queue (priority_queue): a queue in which the order of the elements is determined by some predicate acting on the pairs of stored values; by default it is a wrapper around the vector (vector).

Common Features#

Container Declaration#

All take the form containerName<typeName,...> name, but the number and form of the template parameters (the parameters inside <>) vary with the specific container.

The fundamental reason: the STL is precisely the "Standard Template Library", so all containers are class templates.

Iterators#

Please refer to the Iterators page.

Common Functions#

=: has an assignment operator as well as a copy constructor.

begin(): returns an iterator pointing to the first element.

end(): returns an iterator pointing to the element after the last one. end() does not point to any element, but it is the successor of the last element.

size(): returns the number of elements in the container.

max_size(): returns the maximum number of elements the container can theoretically store. It varies with the container type and the type of the stored variables.

empty(): returns whether the container is empty.

swap(): swaps two containers.

clear(): clears the container.

==/!=/</>/<=/>=: compares two containers by lexicographical order. (When comparing element values, each element of a map counts as a set<pair<key, value>>; unordered containers do not support </>/<=/>=.)

← PreviousOverview of the C++ Standard LibraryNext →Iterators
Chapter 15 · The C++ Standard Library

Iterators · STL Containers

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/iterator.md

In the STL, an iterator is an object used to access and examine the elements of STL containers; its behavior is similar to that of a pointer, but it encapsulates some validity checks and provides a uniform access format. Similar concepts exist in many other high-level languages, such as Python's __iter__ function and C#'s IEnumerator.

Basic Usage#

Iterators may sound rather obscure, but an iterator itself can be viewed as a pointer to data. An iterator mainly supports two operators: increment (++) and dereference (the unary * operator); the increment is used to move the iterator, and the dereference can fetch or modify the element it points to.

The type of an iterator pointing to an element of an STL container container is generally container::iterator.

Iterators can be used to traverse a container; for example, the following two for loops have the same effect:

vector<int> data(10);

for (int i = 0; i < data.size(); i++)
  cout << data[i] << endl;  // access elements using subscripts

for (vector<int>::iterator iter = data.begin(); iter != data.end(); iter++)
  cout << *iter << endl;  // access elements using iterators
// Since C++11, auto iter = data.begin() can be used to simplify the code above
tipUsing <code>auto</code> in contests

Most contestants like to use auto in place of verbose iterator declarations. According to the Supplementary Notice on Programming Language Usage Restrictions in NOI-Series Events released in September 2021, NOI-series contests (including CSP J/S) will be judged using C++14, a version that already supports the auto keyword.

Classification#

In the STL's definition, iterators are classified in order into the following categories based on the operations they support:

  • InputIterator (input iterator): only requires support for copying, increment, and dereference access.
  • OutputIterator (output iterator): only requires support for copying, increment, and dereference assignment.
  • ForwardIterator (forward iterator): on top of InputIterator, supports dereference access over multiple passes through the iterator, and guarantees that the results of multiple accesses are consistent.
  • BidirectionalIterator (bidirectional iterator): on top of ForwardIterator, supports decrement (i.e., access in reverse).
  • RandomAccessIterator (random-access iterator): on top of BidirectionalIterator, supports addition and subtraction operations and comparison operations (i.e., random access).

  • ContiguousIterator (contiguous iterator): on top of RandomAccessIterator, requires that, for a dereferenceable iterator, a + n be such that *(a + n) is equivalent to *(std::address_of(*a) + n) (i.e., contiguous storage, where a is a contiguous iterator and n is an integral value).

    ContiguousIterator was officially introduced in C++17.

tipWhy are input iterators called input iterators?

"Input" means "input can be obtained from the iterator", while "output" means "one can output to the iterator".

The agent of "input" and "output" is the other parts of the program, not the iterator itself.

These categories of iterators are not mutually exclusive. In fact, apart from output iterators, the categories earlier in the list subsume those later in the list. For example, wherever a forward iterator is required, a bidirectional iterator can be used just as well. Starting from forward iterators, if such iterators also implement the functionality of output iterators (i.e., allow write operations), they are called mutable iterators. From this, categories such as "mutable random-access iterator" can be derived.

Different STL containers support different iterator types; keep this in mind when using them.

Pointers to arrays satisfy all the requirements of contiguous iterators (or of random-access iterators, for C++14 and earlier), and can be used as contiguous iterators.

Related Functions#

Many STL functions use iterators as parameters.

std::advance(it, n) can be used to advance the iterator it by n steps; if n is negative, this corresponds to moving backward, in which case the iterator must satisfy the bidirectional iterator requirements, otherwise the behavior is undefined.

Since C++11, std::next(it) can be used to obtain the successor of the forward iterator it (the iterator it itself is left unchanged), and std::next(it, n) to obtain the n-th successor of the forward iterator it.

Since C++11, std::prev(it) can be used to obtain the predecessor of the bidirectional iterator it (the iterator it itself is left unchanged), and std::prev(it, n) to obtain the n-th predecessor of the bidirectional iterator it.

STL containers generally support access starting from one end or from both ends, as well as support for the const qualifier. For example, a container's begin() function can obtain an iterator pointing to the container's first element; the rbegin() function can obtain a reverse iterator pointing to the container's last element; the cbegin() function can obtain a const iterator pointing to the container's first element; and the end() function can obtain an iterator pointing to the container's past-the-end position (the "past-the-end position" is not the last element — it can be regarded as the successor of the last element; the predecessor of the "past-the-end position" is the last element in the container, and it does not itself point to any element).

More usage can be found at Iterator library - cppreference.com.

author: MingqiHuang, Xeonacid, greyqz, i-Yirannn, ChenZ01

vector#

std::vector is a contiguous-memory, variable-length array (also called a list) data structure provided by the STL. It provides insertion and deletion with linear complexity, as well as random access with constant complexity.

Why use vector#

As contestants, we pursue program efficiency far more than engineering-level stability. Because vector handles memory dynamically, its time efficiency is lower than that of static arrays in some cases, and it is even worse when the OJ server does not necessarily have full optimization enabled. So when storing data in the ordinary way, vector is usually not chosen. Below are several excellent features of vector; in situations where these features are needed, vector can be of great help to us.

vector can allocate memory dynamically#

Often we cannot allocate that much space in advance (e.g., precomputing the divisors of all numbers in 1\~n). Even though we may know that the total amount of data is within what the space allows, a single piece of data may still be very large. In such cases we need vector to keep memory usage within a suitable range. vector also supports dynamic growth; this feature comes in handy when memory is very tight.

vector overloads the comparison operators and the assignment operator#

vector overloads six comparison operators, implemented in lexicographic order, which makes it convenient for us to determine whether two containers are equal (the complexity is linear in the size of the container). For example, you can use vector<char> to implement string comparison (of course, using std::string is still faster and more convenient). In addition, vector also overloads the assignment operator, which makes copying arrays more convenient.

Convenient initialization of vector#

Since vector overloads the = operator, we can conveniently perform whole-vector assignment. In addition, since C++11, vector also supports list-initialization, for example vector<int> data {1, 2, 3};.

Usage of vector#

The following introduces common usage; for details, see the C++ documentation.

Constructors#

See the following code for usage examples (assuming you have already used using for the relevant types in the std namespace):

// 1. Create an empty vector; constant complexity
vector<int> v0;
// 1+. This line of code ensures constant time complexity when inserting the first 3 elements into the vector
v0.reserve(3);
// 2. Create a vector with an initial space of 3, whose elements have the default value 0; linear complexity
vector<int> v1(3);
// 3. Create a vector with an initial space of 3, whose elements have the default value 2; linear complexity
vector<int> v2(3, 2);
// 4. Create a vector with an initial space of 3, whose elements have the default value 1,
// and use the allocator of v2; linear complexity
vector<int> v3(3, 1, v2.get_allocator());
// 5. Create vector v4 as a copy of v2, whose elements are the same as those of v2; linear complexity
vector<int> v4(v2);
// 6. Create vector v5 as a copy of v4, whose content is {v4[1], v4[2]}; linear complexity
vector<int> v5(v4.begin() + 1, v4.begin() + 3);
// 7. Move v2 into the newly created vector v6, with no copy occurring; constant complexity; requires C++11
vector<int> v6(std::move(v2));  // alternatively, v6 = std::move(v2);

noteTest code
// The following is test code; interested readers may compile and run it themselves.
cout << "v1 = ";
copy(v1.begin(), v1.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
cout << "v2 = ";
copy(v2.begin(), v2.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
cout << "v3 = ";
copy(v3.begin(), v3.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
cout << "v4 = ";
copy(v4.begin(), v4.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
cout << "v5 = ";
copy(v5.begin(), v5.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
cout << "v6 = ";
copy(v6.begin(), v6.end(), ostream_iterator<int>(cout, " "));
cout << endl;
You can use the methods above to construct a vector; this is enough for our purposes.

Element access#

vector provides the following methods for element access

  1. at()

    v.at(pos) returns a reference to the element at index pos in the container. If the array access is out of bounds, an exception of type std::out_of_range is thrown.

  2. operator[]

    v[pos] returns a reference to the element at index pos in the container. No bounds checking is performed.

  3. front()

    v.front() returns a reference to the first element.

  4. back()

    v.back() returns a reference to the last element.

  5. data()

    v.data() returns a pointer to the first element in the contiguous memory space that v uses internally to store its data.

Iterators#

vector provides the following iterators

  1. begin()/cbegin()

    Returns an iterator pointing to the first element, where *begin = front.

  2. end()/cend()

    Returns an iterator pointing to the placeholder at the end of the container; note that there is no element there.

  3. rbegin()/crbegin()

    Returns a reverse iterator pointing to the first element of the reversed array, which can be understood as the last element of the forward container.

  4. rend()/crend()

    Returns an iterator pointing to the position after the last element of the reversed array, corresponding to the position before the first element of the container; there is no element there.

Among the iterators listed above, those containing the character c are read-only iterators, and you cannot modify the values of elements in a vector through a read-only iterator. If a vector itself is read-only, then its ordinary iterators and its read-only iterators are completely equivalent. Read-only iterators have been supported since C++11.

Length and capacity#

vector has the following functions related to the length and capacity of the container. Note that the length (size) of a vector refers to the number of valid elements, while the capacity refers to the length of the memory it actually allocates; for the relevant details, see the implementation details section later in this page.

Length-related:

  • empty() returns a bool value, namely v.begin() == v.end(); true means empty, and false means non-empty.

  • size() returns the length of the container (the number of elements), namely std::distance(v.begin(), v.end()).

  • resize(n) changes the length of the vector to n. If n is greater than the current length, elements are appended; if the argument provides the element to be appended, the argument is used, otherwise the default value is used; if n is less than the current length, the first n elements are kept and the elements after them are deleted.

  • max_size() returns the maximum possible length of the container.

    Capacity-related:

  • reserve() makes the vector reserve a certain amount of memory space, avoiding unnecessary memory allocation and copying.

  • capacity() returns the capacity of the container, i.e., the number of elements for which the current vector has already allocated space.

  • shrink_to_fit() makes the capacity of the vector equal to its length, removing the capacity that the vector does not use.

Element insertion, deletion, and modification#

  • clear() Clears all elements
  • insert() Supports inserting an element at a given iterator position; multiple elements can be inserted. The complexity is linear in the distance from pos to the end, not constant
  • erase() Deletes the element at a given iterator or in a given range, returning the iterator of the last deleted element. The complexity is the same as insert.
  • push_back() Inserts an element at the end, with an amortized complexity of constant, and a worst case of linear complexity.
  • pop_back() Deletes the last element, with constant complexity.
  • swap() Swaps with another container; this operation is of constant complexity, not linear.

Implementation details of vector#

Under the hood, vector is still a fixed-length array; the reason it can grow dynamically is that it adds operations that prevent the number of elements from overflowing. First, it should be noted that the number of elements in a vector (its length) nnn and the maximum number of elements its allocated memory can hold (its capacity) NNN are not the same, and vector stores these two quantities separately. When an element is added to the vector, if n>Nn>Nn>N is found, the container allocates an array of size 2N2N2N, then copies the old data from its original position into the new array, and then releases the original memory. Although the asymptotic complexity of this operation is O(n)O(n)O(n), it can be shown that its amortized complexity is O(1)O(1)O(1). Deleting an element at the end and accessing an element both still have O(1)O(1)O(1) overhead. Therefore, as long as the size of the vector is estimated appropriately and good use is made of resize() and reserve(), the efficiency of vector will not differ much from that of a fixed-length array.

vector<bool>#

The standard library specifically provides a vector specialization for bool, in which each "bool" occupies only 1 bit, and dynamic growth is supported. However, the return type of its operator[] is not bool& but vector<bool>::reference. Therefore, use vector<bool> with caution; consider using deque<bool> or vector<char> instead. And if you need to save space, use bitset directly.

array(C++11)#

std::array is a contiguous-memory, fixed-length array data structure provided by the STL. It is essentially a direct wrapper around a native array.

Why use array#

array is actually the STL's encapsulation of the array. Compared with vector, it sacrifices dynamic growth, but in exchange gains performance almost identical to that of a native array (provided that full optimization is enabled). Therefore, in cases where C++11 features can be used, almost everywhere a native array can be used, fixed-length arrays can be directly replaced with array, while dynamically allocated arrays can be replaced with vector.

Member functions#

Implicitly defined member functions#

Function Purpose
operator= Overwrites each element of the array with the corresponding element from another array

Element access#

Function Purpose
at Accesses the specified element, while performing bounds checking
operator[] Accesses the specified element, without performing bounds checking
front Accesses the first element
back Accesses the last element
data Returns a pointer to the first element of the array in memory

at throws std::out_of_range if pos >= size() is encountered.

Capacity#

Function Purpose
empty Checks whether the container is empty
size Returns the number of elements it holds
max_size Returns the maximum number of elements it can hold

Since every array is a fixed-size container, the value returned by size() equals the value returned by max_size().

Operations#

Function Purpose
fill Fills the container with the specified value
swap Swaps the contents

Note that swapping two arrays is Θ(size)\Theta(\text{size})Θ(size), not O(1)O(1)O(1) as with regular STL containers.

Non-member functions#

Function Purpose
operator== etc. Compares the values in the array in lexicographic order
std::get Accesses an element of the array
std::swap The specialized std::swap algorithm

The following is an example of using array:

// 1. Create an empty array with length 3; constant complexity
std::array<int, 3> v0;
// 2. Create an array with the specified constants; constant complexity
std::array<int, 3> v1{1, 2, 3};

v0.fill(1);  // Fill the array

// Access the array
for (int i = 0; i != arr.size(); ++i) cout << arr[i] << " ";

deque#

std::deque is the double-ended queue data structure provided by the STL. It provides insertion and deletion with linear complexity, as well as random access with constant complexity.

Usage of deque#

The following introduces common usage; for details, see the C++ documentation. The iterator functions of deque are the same as those of vector, so they are not described in detail here.

Constructors#

See the following code (assuming you have already used using for the relevant types in the std namespace):

// 1. Define an empty int deque v0
deque<int> v0;
// 2. Define an int deque v1 and set its initial size to 10; linear complexity
deque<int> v1(10);
// 3. Define an int deque v2 and initialize it to ten 1s; linear complexity
deque<int> v2(10, 1);
// 4. Copy the existing deque v1; linear complexity
deque<int> v3(v1);
// 5. Create deque v4 as a copy of v2, whose content is v4[0] to v4[2]; linear complexity
deque<int> v4(v2.begin(), v2.begin() + 3);
// 6. Move v2 into the newly created deque v5, with no copy occurring; constant complexity; requires C++11
deque<int> v5(std::move(v2));

Element access#

Same as vector, but the underlying memory cannot be accessed. For its efficient element access speed, see the implementation details section.

  • at() Returns a reference to the element at the given position in the container, performing bounds checking, with constant complexity.
  • operator[] Returns a reference to the element at the given position in the container. It does not perform bounds checking, with constant complexity.
  • front() Returns a reference to the first element.
  • back() Returns a reference to the last element.

Iterators#

Same as vector.

Length#

Same as vector, but there are no reserve() and capacity() functions. (The shrink_to_fit() function is still available)

Element insertion, deletion, and modification#

Same as vector, with additional functions for adding elements at the head of the queue.

  • clear() Clears all elements
  • insert() Supports inserting an element at a given iterator position; multiple elements can be inserted. The complexity is linear in the smaller of the distances from pos to the two ends.
  • erase() Deletes the element at a given iterator or in a given range, returning the iterator of the last deleted element. The complexity is the same as insert.
  • push_front() Inserts an element at the head, with constant complexity.
  • pop_front() Deletes the head element, with constant complexity.
  • push_back() Inserts an element at the end, with constant complexity.
  • pop_back() Deletes the last element, with constant complexity.
  • swap() Swaps with another container; this operation is of constant complexity, not linear.

Implementation details of deque#

The underlying implementation of deque is usually several non-contiguous buffers, while the memory within each buffer is contiguous. Each buffer also records a head pointer and a tail pointer, which are used to mark the range of the valid data. Once a buffer is filled, a new buffer is allocated before or after it to store more data. For a more detailed explanation, see how deque is implemented in The Annotated STL Sources.

list#

std::list is the doubly linked list data structure provided by the STL. It provides random access with linear complexity, as well as insertion and deletion with constant complexity.

Usage of list#

The usage of list is basically the same as that of deque, but the complexities of insertion/deletion operations and access are different. For details, see the C++ documentation. The functions of list related to iterators, length, and element insertion, deletion, and modification are the same as those of deque, so they are not described in detail here.

Element access#

Since the implementation of list is a linked list, it does not provide a random access interface. If you need to access a middle element, you need to use an iterator.

  • front() Returns a reference to the first element.
  • back() Returns a reference to the last element.

Operations#

The list type also provides some STL algorithm functions implemented specifically for its characteristics. Since these algorithms require random access iterators, list provides special implementations so that they are convenient to use. These algorithms include splice(), remove(), sort(), unique(), merge(), etc.

forward_list (C++11)#

std::forward_list is the singly linked list data structure provided by the STL, with reduced space overhead compared to std::list.

Usage of forward_list#

The usage of forward_list is almost identical to that of list, but its iterators are one-directional only, so its specific usage is not described in detail. For details, see the C++ documentation
