Chapter 17 · The C++ Standard Library

Associative Containers · STL Containers

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/associative-container.md

set#

set is an associative container that contains a sorted set of objects of key type; search, removal, and insertion have logarithmic complexity. Internally, set is typically implemented with a red-black tree. The properties of balanced binary trees make set well suited to cases where you need to handle lookup, insertion, and deletion at the same time.

Similar to sets in mathematics, a set never contains two elements with the same value. If you need a collection that can hold equal elements, you need to use multiset. The way multiset is used is basically the same as the way set is used.

Insertion and Deletion Operations#

  • insert(x) inserts the element x into the set when the container has no equivalent element.
  • erase(x) removes all elements with value x and returns the number of removed elements.
  • erase(pos) removes the element at iterator pos; the iterator is required to be valid.
  • erase(first,last) removes all elements in the range [first,last)[first,last)[first,last).
  • clear() empties the set.
noteThe return value of <code>insert</code>

The return type of the insert function is pair<iterator, bool>, where iterator is an iterator pointing to the inserted element (or to the element that was already in the container and is equal to the inserted value), and the bool indicates whether the insertion succeeded. Since elements in a set are unique, if an element with an equal value already exists in the set, the insertion fails and false is returned; otherwise the insertion succeeds and true is returned. The same is true of insert in map.

Iterators#

set provides the following iterators:

  1. begin()/cbegin() Returns an iterator pointing to the first element, where *begin = front.
  2. end()/cend() Returns an iterator pointing to the placeholder at the end of the array; note that there is no element there.
  3. rbegin()/crbegin() Returns a reverse iterator pointing to the first element of the reversed array, which can be understood as the last element of the forward container.
  4. rend()/crend() Returns an iterator pointing to the position one past the last element of the reversed array, corresponding to the position just before the beginning of the container; there is no element there.

Among the iterators listed above, those containing the character c are read-only iterators; you cannot use a read-only iterator to modify the values of elements in a set. If a set is itself read-only, then its ordinary iterators and its read-only iterators are completely equivalent. Read-only iterators have been supported since C++11.

Lookup Operations#

  • count(x) returns the number of elements in the set with key x.
  • find(x) returns an iterator to the element with key x if such an element exists in the set, and end() otherwise.
  • lower_bound(x) returns an iterator to the first element not less than the given key. If no such element exists, end() is returned.
  • upper_bound(x) returns an iterator to the first element greater than the given key. If no such element exists, end() is returned.
  • empty() returns whether the container is empty.
  • size() returns the number of elements in the container.

warningThe time complexity of <code>lower_bound</code> and <code>upper_bound</code>

The time complexity of the lower_bound and upper_bound that come with set is O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn).

But if you use the lower_bound and upper_bound functions from the algorithm library to query elements in a set, the time complexity is O(n)O(n)O(n).

warningThe time complexity of <code>nth_element</code>

set does not provide its own nth_element. Using the nth_element from the algorithm library to find the kkk-th largest element has time complexity O(n)O(n)O(n).

If you need to implement the O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) lookup of the kkk-th largest element that balanced binary trees provide, you have to hand-write your own balanced binary tree or weighted segment tree, or choose to use the balanced binary tree in the pb_ds library.

Usage Examples#

Using set in Greedy Algorithms#

In greedy algorithms, there is often a need for operations like find and remove the smallest element greater than or equal to a certain value. This kind of operation can easily be done with set.

// elements currently available
set<int> available;
// the value that elements must be greater than or equal to
int x;

// find the smallest element greater than or equal to x
set<int>::iterator it = available.lower_bound(x);
if (it == available.end()) {
  // no such element exists, so do the corresponding operations ...
} else {
  // such an element is found; remove it from the currently available elements
  available.erase(it);
  // do the corresponding operations ...
}

map#

map is an ordered key-value pair container, and the keys of its elements are unique. Search, removal, and insertion operations have logarithmic complexity. map is usually implemented as a red-black tree.

Imagine the following scenario: we now need to store some key-value pairs, for example, the scores corresponding to students' names: Tom 0, Bob 100, Alan 100. But since array subscripts can only be non-negative integers, we cannot use names as subscripts to store them; in this case, the simplest way is to use the map in the STL.

map overloads operator[], so any type that has operator < defined can be used as a subscript (in a map this is called the key, that is, the index):

map<Key, T> yourMap;

Here, Key is the key type and T is the value type. The following is an example of using map:

map<string, int> mp;

No two elements in a map have the same key, while multimap allows multiple elements to share the same key. The way multimap is used is basically the same as the way map is used.

warningWarning

Precisely because multimap allows multiple elements to share the same key, multimap does not provide a way to access the corresponding value given a key.

Insertion and Deletion Operations#

  • You can directly perform lookup or insertion operations via subscript access, e.g. mp["Alan"]=100.
  • Inserting an element can also be accomplished by inserting a value of type pair<Key, T> into the map, e.g. mp.insert(pair<string,int>("Alan",100));;
  • The erase(key) function removes all elements with key key. The return value is the number of removed elements.
  • erase(pos): removes the element at iterator pos; the iterator is required to be valid.
  • erase(first,last): removes all elements in the range [first,last)[first,last)[first,last).
  • The clear() function empties the whole container.
noteNotes on subscript access

When using subscript access to access an element in a map, if the map does not contain an element with the corresponding key, a new element is automatically inserted into the map, and its value is set to the default value (for integers, the value is zero; for types with a default constructor, the default constructor is called to initialize it).

When subscript access is performed too frequently, a large number of meaningless elements will appear in the container, which affects the efficiency of the map. Therefore, it is generally recommended to use the find() function to look for the element with a specific key.

Query Operations#

  • count(x): returns the number of elements in the container with key x. The complexity is O(log⁡(size)+ans)O(\log(size)+ans)O(log(size)+ans) (logarithmic in the size of the container, plus the number of matches).
  • find(x): if the container contains an element with key x, returns an iterator to that element; otherwise returns end().
  • lower_bound(x): returns an iterator to the first element not less than the given key.
  • upper_bound(x): returns an iterator to the first element greater than the given key. If all elements in the container are less than or equal to the given key, returns end().
  • empty(): returns whether the container is empty.
  • size(): returns the number of elements in the container.

Usage Examples#

Using map to Store Complex States#

In search algorithms, we sometimes need to store some fairly complex states (such as coordinates, values that cannot be discretized, strings, etc.) as well as the answers related to them (such as the minimum number of steps to reach the state). map can be used to implement this: the key is the state, and the value is the related answer. The following example shows how to use map to store states represented as string.

// store states and their corresponding answers
map<string, int> record;

// a newly searched state and its corresponding answer
string status;
int ans;
// check whether the corresponding state has appeared before
map<string, int>::iterator it = record.find(status);
if (it == record.end()) {
  // this state has not been searched yet; add it to the state record
  record[status] = ans;
  // do the corresponding operations ...
} else {
  // this state has already been searched; do the corresponding operations ...
}

Traversing Containers#

You can use iterators to traverse all the elements of an associative container.

set<int> s;
using si = set<int>::iterator;
for (si it = s.begin(); it != s.end(); it++) cout << *it << endl;

Note that after dereferencing an iterator of a map, what you get is a key-value pair of type pair<Key, T>.

In C++11, using a range-based for loop makes the code much more concise:

set<int> s;
for (auto x : s) cout << x << endl;

For any associative container, the time complexity of traversing the container with iterators is O(n)O(n)O(n).

Custom Comparison#

By default, the comparison function of set is < (for non-built-in types, the < operator needs to be overloaded). However, in some special cases, we may want to customize the comparison used inside set.

This problem can be solved by passing in a custom comparator.

Specifically, we need to define a class and overload the () operator in it.

For example, if we want to maintain a set that stores integers with larger values first, we can implement it like this:

struct cmp {
  bool operator()(int a, int b) const { return a > b; }
};

set<int, cmp> s;

For other associative containers, custom comparison can be implemented in a similar way; we will not repeat the details here.

← PreviousSequence ContainersNext →Unordered Associative Containers
Chapter 18 · The C++ Standard Library

Unordered Associative Containers · STL Containers

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/unordered-container.md

Overview#

Since the C++11 standard, four unordered associative containers implemented based on hashing have been officially incorporated into the C++ Standard Template Library (STL), namely: unordered_set, unordered_multiset, unordered_map, unordered_multimap.

noteUsage when the compiler does not support C++11

Before C++11, the unordered associative containers were part of the TR1 extensions of C++. So, if the compiler does not support C++11, you need to add the tr1/ prefix to the header names and use the std::tr1 namespace. For example, #include <unordered_map> needs to be changed to #include <tr1/unordered_map>; std::unordered_map needs to be changed to std::tr1::unordered_map (if you use using namespace std;, it is tr1::unordered_map).

They have much in common with the corresponding associative containers in terms of functionality, functions, and so on, but the biggest difference is that ordinary associative containers are generally implemented with red-black trees, and their internal elements are sorted in a specific order, whereas these unordered associative containers store elements by hashing, and their internal elements are not sorted in any specific order; therefore, when you access elements in an unordered associative container, the access order is not guaranteed either.

The characteristics of hash-based storage enable unordered associative containers to complete most operations (including lookup, insertion, and deletion) in constant time complexity on average, which is better than the time complexity of associative containers, which grows logarithmically with the container size.

warningWarning

In the worst case, the time complexity of operations such as insertion, deletion, and lookup on unordered associative containers becomes linear in the container size! This situation usually arises when a large number of hash collisions occur inside the container.

Meanwhile, since operations on unordered associative containers usually have fairly large constants, their efficiency is sometimes not much better than that of ordinary associative containers.

Therefore, unordered associative containers should be used with caution, and abuse should be avoided as much as possible (for example, being too lazy to discretize and directly using unordered_map<int, int> as an ordinary array with unlimited space).

Since unordered associative containers have a lot in common with the corresponding associative containers in terms of usage and operations, we will not introduce the various operations of unordered associative containers here; for this content, readers can refer to the associative containers page.

Creating Hash Collisions#

As mentioned above, in the worst case, the time complexity of some operations on unordered associative containers is linear in the container size.

When the hash function is fixed, data can be constructed so that a large number of hash collisions occur inside the container, causing the complexity to reach its upper bound.

In the standard library implementation, the hash value of each element is obtained by taking the value modulo a prime; more specifically, it is one of the primes in this list (for g++ 6 and earlier compilers, this prime is usually 126271126271126271; for g++ 7 and later compilers, this prime is usually 107897107897107897).

Therefore, by inserting multiples of these moduli into the container, one can achieve the goal of creating a large number of hash collisions.

Custom Hash Functions#

Using a custom hash function can effectively avoid the large number of hash collisions caused by constructed data.

To use a custom hash function, you need to define a struct and overload the () operator in it, like this:

struct my_hash {
  size_t operator()(int x) const { return x; }
};

Of course, to make sure the hash function cannot be cracked quickly (for example, by hacking submissions that use unordered associative containers on Codeforces), you can try adding some randomization functions (such as the time) to the hash function to increase the difficulty of cracking it.

For example, this blog post gives the following hash function:

struct my_hash {
  static uint64_t splitmix64(uint64_t x) {
    x += 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15;
    x = (x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9;
    x = (x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111eb;
    return x ^ (x >> 31);
  }

  size_t operator()(uint64_t x) const {
    static const uint64_t FIXED_RANDOM =
        chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count();
    return splitmix64(x + FIXED_RANDOM);
  }

  // Hash function for std::pair<int, int> as the key type
  size_t operator()(pair<uint64_t, uint64_t> x) const {
    static const uint64_t FIXED_RANDOM =
        chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count();
    return splitmix64(x.first + FIXED_RANDOM) ^
           (splitmix64(x.second + FIXED_RANDOM) >> 1);
  }
};

After writing your custom hash function, you can pass the custom hash function into the container with definitions like unordered_map<int, int, my_hash> my_map; or unordered_map<pair<int, int>, int, my_hash> my_pair_map;.

← PreviousAssociative ContainersNext →Container Adapters
Chapter 19 · The C++ Standard Library

Container Adapters · STL Containers

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/container-adapter.md

author: Xeonacid, ksyx, Early0v0

Stack#

The STL stack (std::stack) is a last-in-first-out (LIFO) container adapter. It only supports querying or deleting the most recently added element (the top element of the stack); it does not support random access, and, in order to keep the data strictly ordered, it does not support iterators.

Header#

#include <stack>

Definition#

std::stack<TypeName> s;  // Uses the default underlying container deque; the data type is TypeName
std::stack<TypeName, Container> s;  // Uses Container as the underlying container
std::stack<TypeName> s2(s1);        // Constructs s2 from a copy of s1

Member functions#

All of the following functions have constant complexity

  • top() Accesses the top element of the stack (if the stack is empty, an error occurs here)
  • push(x) Inserts the element x into the stack
  • pop() Deletes the top element of the stack
  • size() Queries the number of elements in the container
  • empty() Queries whether the container is empty

Simple example#

std::stack<int> s1;
s1.push(2);
s1.push(1);
std::stack<int> s2(s1);
s1.pop();
std::cout << s1.size() << " " << s2.size() << std::endl;  // 1 2
std::cout << s1.top() << " " << s2.top() << std::endl;    // 2 1
s1.pop();
std::cout << s1.empty() << " " << s2.empty() << std::endl;  // 1 0

Queue#

The STL queue (std::queue) is a first-in-first-out (FIFO) container adapter. It only supports querying or deleting the first added element (the front element of the queue); it does not support random access, and, in order to keep the data strictly ordered, it does not support iterators.

Header#

#include <queue>

Definition#

std::queue<TypeName> q;  // Uses the default underlying container deque; the data type is TypeName
std::queue<TypeName, Container> q;  // Uses Container as the underlying container

std::queue<TypeName> q2(q1);  // Constructs q2 from a copy of q1

Member functions#

All of the following functions have constant complexity

  • front() Accesses the front element of the queue (if the queue is empty, an error occurs here)
  • push(x) Inserts the element x into the queue
  • pop() Deletes the front element of the queue
  • size() Queries the number of elements in the container
  • empty() Queries whether the container is empty

Simple example#

std::queue<int> q1;
q1.push(2);
q1.push(1);
std::queue<int> q2(q1);
q1.pop();
std::cout << q1.size() << " " << q2.size() << std::endl;    // 1 2
std::cout << q1.front() << " " << q2.front() << std::endl;  // 1 2
q1.pop();
std::cout << q1.empty() << " " << q2.empty() << std::endl;  // 1 0

Priority queue#

The priority queue std::priority_queue is a heap, usually a binary heap.

Header#

#include <queue>

Definition#

std::priority_queue<TypeName> q;             // The data type is TypeName
std::priority_queue<TypeName, Container> q;  // Uses Container as the underlying container
std::priority_queue<TypeName, Container, Compare> q;
// Uses Container as the underlying container and Compare as the comparison type

// Uses vector as the underlying container by default
// The comparison type is less<TypeName> (in this case its top() returns the maximum)
// If you want top() to return the minimum, you can set the comparison type to greater<TypeName>
// Note: you cannot skip Container and pass in Compare directly

// Since C++11, if you customize Compare with a lambda function,
// you need to pass it in as an argument to the constructor, e.g.:
auto cmp = [](const std::pair<int, int> &l, const std::pair<int, int> &r) {
  return l.second < r.second;
};
std::priority_queue<std::pair<int, int>, std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>,
                    decltype(cmp)>
    pq(cmp);

Member functions#

All of the following functions have constant complexity

  • top() Accesses the top element of the heap (the priority queue cannot be empty at this point)
  • empty() Queries whether the container is empty
  • size() Queries the number of elements in the container

All of the following functions have logarithmic complexity

  • push(x) Inserts an element and sorts the underlying container
  • pop() Deletes the top element of the heap (the priority queue cannot be empty at this point)

Simple example#

std::priority_queue<int> q1;
std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>> q2;
// Since C++11, the space can be omitted
std::priority_queue<int, std::deque<int>, std::greater<int>> q3;
// q3 is a min-heap
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) q1.push(i);
// Elements in q1: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
std::cout << q1.top() << std::endl;
// Output: 5
q1.pop();
// Elements in the heap: [1, 2, 3, 4]
std::cout << q1.size() << std::endl;
// Output: 4
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) q3.push(i);
// Elements in q3: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
std::cout << q3.top() << std::endl;
// Output: 1

Chapter 20 · The C++ Standard Library

STL Algorithms

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/algorithm.md

The STL provides about 100 template functions that implement algorithms, most of which are included in <algorithm>, with some others included in <numeric> and <functional>. For a complete list of functions, please refer to the reference manual; for sorting-related topics, you can refer to the corresponding page on sorting.

  • find: sequential search. find(v.begin(), v.end(), value), where value is the value to be found.

  • reverse: reverses an array or string. reverse(v.begin(), v.end()) or reverse(a + begin, a + end).

  • unique: removes adjacent duplicate elements in a container. unique(ForwardIterator first, ForwardIterator last); the return value is an iterator pointing to the end of the container after duplicates are removed, and the size of the original container is unchanged. Used together with sort, it can remove duplicates from the entire container.

  • random_shuffle: randomly shuffles an array. random_shuffle(v.begin(), v.end()) or random_shuffle(v + begin, v + end).

    warningThe <code>random_shuffle</code> function has been removed in the latest C++ standard

    random_shuffle has been deprecated since C++14 and removed since C++17.

    In C++11 and later standards, you can use the shuffle function to replace the original random_shuffle. It is used as shuffle(v.begin(), v.end(), rng) (the last argument passed in is the random number generator to be used; in general, the Mersenne Twister pseudo-random number generator mt19937 seeded with the true random number generator random_device is used).

    // #include <random>
std::mt19937 rng(std::random_device{}());
std::shuffle(v.begin(), v.end(), rng);
    - sort: sorting. sort(v.begin(), v.end(), cmp) or sort(a + begin, a + end, cmp), where end is the position one past the last element of the array to be sorted, and cmp is a custom comparison function.

  • stable_sort: stable sorting, used in the same way as sort().

  • nth_element: partitions within the specified range; that is, it finds the nnn-th largest element in the sequence, making all the numbers to its left less than it and all the numbers to its right greater than it. nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + n, v.end(), cmp) or nth_element(a + begin, a + begin + n, a + end, cmp).

  • binary_search: binary search. binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), value), where value is the value to be found.

  • merge: merges in sorted order two (already sorted) sequences onto the insert iterator of a third sequence. merge(v1.begin(), v1.end(), v2.begin(), v2.end() ,back_inserter(v3)).

  • inplace_merge: merges in place into one sorted sequence the two ranges [first,middle), [middle,last) (already sorted by the less-than operator). inplace_merge(v.begin(), v.begin() + middle, v.end()).

  • lower_bound: performs a binary search on a sorted sequence and returns an iterator to the position of the first element greater than or equal to xxx. If no such element exists, the end iterator is returned. lower_bound(v.begin(),v.end(),x).

  • upper_bound: performs a binary search on a sorted sequence and returns an iterator to the position of the first element greater than xxx. If no such element exists, the end iterator is returned. upper_bound(v.begin(),v.end(),x).

    warningThe time complexity of <code>lower_bound</code> and <code>upper_bound</code>

    In an ordinary array, both of these functions have time complexity O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn), but in set and other associative containers, directly calling lower_bound(s.begin(),s.end(),val) has time complexity O(n)O(n)O(n).

    set and other associative containers already have lower_bound and similar functions built in (called like s.lower_bound(val)), and calling them this way has time complexity O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn).

    - next_permutation: changes the current permutation to the next permutation in the sequence of all permutations. If the current permutation is already the last permutation in the sequence of all permutations (elements arranged completely from largest to smallest), the function returns false and changes the permutation to the first permutation in the sequence of all permutations (elements arranged completely from smallest to largest); otherwise, the function returns true. next_permutation(v.begin(), v.end()) or next_permutation(v + begin, v + end).

  • prev_permutation: changes the current permutation to the previous permutation in the sequence of all permutations. Used in the same way as next_permutation.

  • partial_sum: computes prefix sums. Let the source container be xxx and the target container be yyy; then let y[i]=x[0]+x[1]+⋯+x[i]y[i]=x[0]+x[1]+\dots+x[i]y[i]=x[0]+x[1]+⋯+x[i]. partial_sum(src.begin(), src.end(), back_inserter(dst)).

Usage Examples#

  • Use next_permutation to generate all permutations of 111 to 999. Example problem: Luogu P1706 Full Permutation Problem

    noteImplementation
    int N = 9, a[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9};
do {
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) cout << a[i] << " ";
  cout << endl;
} while (next_permutation(a, a + N));
    - Use lower_bound and upper_bound to find, in the sorted array aaa, the boundaries between the elements less than xxx, equal to xxx, and greater than xxx.

    noteImplementation
    int N = 10, a[] = {1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 7, 7, 9, 9}, x = 5;
int i = lower_bound(a, a + N, x) - a, j = upper_bound(a, a + N, x) - a;
// a[0] ~ a[i - 1] are the elements less than x, a[i] ~ a[j - 1] are the elements equal to x,
// and a[j] ~ a[N - 1] are the elements greater than x
cout << i << " " << j << endl;
    - Use partial_sum to compute the prefix sums of the elements in srcsrcsrc and store them in dstdstdst.

    noteImplementation
    vector<int> src = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, dst;
// Compute the prefix sums of the elements in src: dst[i] = src[0] + ... + src[i]
// The back_inserter function acts on the dst container and provides an iterator
partial_sum(src.begin(), src.end(), back_inserter(dst));
for (unsigned int i = 0; i < dst.size(); i++) cout << dst[i] << " ";
    - Use lower_bound to find the element in the sorted array aaa closest to xxx. Example problem: UVa10487 Closest Sums

    noteImplementation
    int N = 10, a[] = {1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 8, 8, 9, 9}, x = 6;
// lower_bound returns the address of the first element in a that is greater than or equal to x; the computed i is its index
int i = lower_bound(a, a + N, x) - a;
// a[i] (the first element in a that is greater than or equal to x) is the answer in the following two cases:
// 1. even the smallest element in a is greater than or equal to x;
// 2. a contains an element greater than or equal to x, and the first element greater than or equal to x (a[i])
// is closer to x than the first element less than x (a[i - 1]);
// otherwise, a[i - 1] (the first element in a that is less than x) is the answer
if (i == 0 || (i < N && a[i] - x < x - a[i - 1]))
  cout << a[i];
else
  cout << a[i - 1];
    - Use sort and unique to find, in the array aaa, the kkk-th smallest value (note: values that appear multiple times are counted only once, so this problem is not asking for the kkk-th smallest element). Example problem: Luogu P1138 k-th Smallest Integer

    noteImplementation
    int N = 10, a[] = {1, 3, 3, 7, 2, 5, 1, 2, 4, 6}, k = 3;
sort(a, a + N);
// unique returns the address just past the last element of the array after deduplication; the computed cnt is the length of the deduplicated array
int cnt = unique(a, a + N) - a;
cout << a[k - 1];

Chapter 21 · The C++ Standard Library

bitset

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/bitset.md

author: i-Yirannn, Xeonacid, ouuan

Introduction#

std::bitset is a fixed-size container in the standard library that stores 0/1 values. Strictly speaking, it is not part of the STL.

notebitset and the STL

The C++ standard library provides some special container classes, the so-called container adapters (stack, queue, priority queue). In addition, a few classes provide a container-like interface (for example, strings, bitsets, and valarrays). All these classes are covered separately.1 Container adapters and bitsets are covered in Chapter 12.

The C++ standard library provides not only the containers for the STL framework but also some containers that fit some special needs and provide simple, almost self-explanatory, interfaces. You can group these containers into either the so-called container adapters, which adapt standard STL containers to fit special needs, or a bitset, which is a containers for bits or Boolean values. There are three standard container adapters: stacks, queues, and priority queues. In priority queues, the elements are sorted automatically according to a sorting criterion. Thus, the "next" element of a priority queue is the element with the "highest" value. A bitset is a bitfield with an arbitrary but fixed number of bits. Note that the C++ standard library also provides a special container with a variable size for Boolean values: vector.

— Excerpt from The C++ Standard Library 2nd Edition

From this we can see that bitset does not belong to the STL, but is rather a "Special Container" in the standard library. In fact, as a container, it does not satisfy the requirements of STL containers either. And if you call it an adapter, it does not depend on other STL containers as its underlying implementation either.

Since memory is addressed by bytes, i.e. byte, rather than bits, i.e. bit, a variable of type bool, although it can only represent 0/1, still occupies 1 byte of memory.

bitset uses fixed optimizations so that the eight bits of a single byte can separately store 8 bits of 0/1.

For a 4-byte int variable, in the sense of storing only 0/1, a bitset takes up only 132\frac{1}{32}321​ of the space, and when computing some information, the time required is also 132\frac 1{32}321​ of it.

In some cases, bitset can be used to improve the running efficiency of a program. Whether it optimizes the complexity or the constant factor depends on the perspective from which the complexity is measured. The complexity of bitset is commonly written in the following ways: (let the original complexity be O(n)O(n)O(n))

  1. O(n)O(n)O(n): this notation considers that bitset does not optimize the complexity at all.
  2. O(n32)O(\frac n{32})O(32n​): this notation is not quite rigorous (constants should not appear in a complexity), but it reflects that bitset can reduce the required time to 132\frac 1{32}321​.
  3. O(nw)O(\frac n w)O(wn​), where w=32w=32w=32 (the computer's word size); this notation is fairly widely accepted.
  4. O(nlog⁡w)O(\frac n {\log w})O(logwn​), where www is the size of an integer variable on the computer.

In addition, vector<bool>, a specialization of vector, stores data the same way as bitset; the difference is that it supports dynamically allocating space, whereas bitset, like our usual static arrays, has its space allocated at compile time. However, bitset has some handy library functions that are not only convenient, but can also sometimes exploit SIMD to further reduce the constant factor. In addition, parts of the behavior of vector<bool> are inconsistent with vector (for example, for a std::vector<bool> vec, &vec[0] + i is not equal to &vec[i]). Therefore, vector<bool> is generally not used.

Usage#

See std::bitset - cppreference.com.

Header#

#include <bitset>

Specifying the size#

std::bitset<1000> bs;  // a bitset with 1000 bits

Constructors#

  • bitset(): every bit is false.
  • bitset(unsigned long val): set to the binary representation of val.
  • bitset(const string& str): set to the 010101 string str.

Operators#

  • operator []: accesses a specific bit of it.

  • operator ==/operator !=: compare whether the contents of two bitsets are exactly the same.

  • operator &/operator &=/operator |/operator |=/operator ^/operator ^=/operator ~: perform bitwise AND / OR / XOR / NOT operations.

    Note: a bitset can only perform bitwise operations with a bitset; to perform bitwise operations with an integer, you must first convert the integer to a bitset.

  • operator <</operator >>/operator <<=/operator >>=: perform binary left shift / right shift.

In addition, bitset also provides support for C++ stream I/O, which means you can do input and output through cin/cout.

Member functions#

  • count(): returns the number of bits that are true.
  • size(): returns the size of the bitset.
  • test(pos): it serves the same purpose as at() in vector; the difference from the [] operator is the bounds check.
  • any(): returns true if some bit is true, and false otherwise.
  • none(): returns true if all bits are false, and false otherwise.
  • all(): returns true if all bits are true, and false otherwise.
    1. set(): sets the entire bitset to true.
    2. set(pos, val = true): sets one bit to true/false.
    1. reset(): sets the entire bitset to false.
    2. reset(pos): sets one bit to false. Equivalent to set(pos, false).
    1. flip(): flips every bit. (0↔10\leftrightarrow10↔1; equivalent to XOR-ing with a bitset of all 111s)
    2. flip(pos): flips one bit.
  • to_string(): returns the converted string representation.
  • to_ulong(): returns the converted unsigned long representation (long is the same as int on NT and 32-bit POSIX systems, and the same as long long on 64-bit POSIX).
  • to_ullong(): (since C++11) returns the converted unsigned long long representation.

In addition, libstdc++ has some quite useful internal member functions1:

  • _Find_first(): returns the index of the first true in the bitset; if there is no true, it returns the size of the bitset.
  • _Find_next(pos): returns the index of the first true after pos (at a position whose index is strictly greater than pos); if there is no true after pos, it returns the size of the bitset.

Applications#

"LibreOJ β Round #2" Greedy Only Passes the Samples#

This problem can be solved with dp, and the transition equation is very simple:

f(i,j)f(i,j)f(i,j) denotes whether the sum of squares of the first iii numbers can be jjj; then f(i,j)=⋁k=abf(i−1,j−k2)f(i,j)=\bigvee\limits_{k=a}^bf(i-1,j-k^2)f(i,j)=k=a⋁b​f(i−1,j−k2) (OR them together).

But doing it directly is O(n5)O(n^5)O(n5), which (seemingly) does not pass.

We find that this can be optimized with bitset — just left shift and then OR:

noteSubmission: <a href="https://loj.ac/submission/395274">std::bitset</a>
#include <bitset>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

constexpr int N = 101;

int n, a[N], b[N];
bitset<N * N * N> f[N];

int main() {
  int i, j;

  cin >> n;

  for (i = 1; i <= n; ++i) cin >> a[i] >> b[i];

  f[0][0] = 1;

  for (i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    for (j = a[i]; j <= b[i]; ++j) {
      f[i] |= (f[i - 1] << (j * j));
    }
  }

  cout << f[n].count();

  return 0;
}
Since the libstdc++ implementation packs __CHAR_BIT__ * sizeof(unsigned long) bits2, on some platforms this is 323232. Therefore, we can hand-write a bitset (which only needs to support the single operation of OR-ing after a left shift) that packs 646464 bits (__CHAR_BIT__ * sizeof(unsigned long long)) for further optimization:

noteSubmission: <a href="https://loj.ac/submission/395619">hand-written bitset</a>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

constexpr int N = 101;
constexpr int W = 64;

struct Bitset {
  unsigned long long a[N * N * N >> 6];

  void shiftor(const Bitset &y, int p, int l, int r) {
    int t = p - p / W * W;
    int tt = (t == 0 ? 0 : W - t);
    int to = (r + p) / W;
    int qaq = (p + W - 1) / W;

    for (int i = (l + p) / W; i <= to; ++i) {
      if (i - qaq >= 0) a[i] |= y.a[i - qaq] >> tt;

      a[i] |= ((y.a[i - qaq + 1] & ((1ull << tt) - 1)) << t);
    }
  }
} f[N];

int main() {
  int n, a, b, l = 0, r = 0, ans = 0;

  scanf("%d", &n);

  f[0].a[0] = 1;

  for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    scanf("%d%d", &a, &b);

    for (int j = a; j <= b; ++j) f[i].shiftor(f[i - 1], j * j, l, r);

    l += a * a;
    r += b * b;
  }

  for (int i = l / W; i <= r / W; ++i)
    ans += __builtin_popcount(f[n].a[i] & 0xffffffffu) +
           __builtin_popcount(f[n].a[i] >> 32);

  printf("%d", ans);

  return 0;
}
In addition, a brute force with a few prunings can also pass:

noteSubmission: <a href="https://loj.ac/submission/395673">brute force with a few prunings</a>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

constexpr int N = 101;
constexpr int W = 64;

bool f[N * N * N];

int main() {
  int n, i, j, k, a, b, l = 0, r = 0, ans = 0;

  scanf("%d", &n);

  f[0] = true;

  for (i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    scanf("%d%d", &a, &b);
    l += a * a;
    r += b * b;

    for (j = r; j >= l; --j) {
      f[j] = false;

      for (k = a; k <= b; ++k) {
        if (j - k * k < l - a * a) break;

        if (f[j - k * k]) {
          f[j] = true;
          break;
        }
      }
    }
  }

  for (i = l; i <= r; ++i) ans += f[i];

  printf("%d", ans);

  return 0;
}

CF1097F Alex and a TV Show#

Problem Statement#

You are given nnn multisets and four operations:

  1. Set some multiset to a single number.
  2. Set some multiset to two other multisets added together.
  3. Set some multiset to the gcd⁡\gcdgcds of choosing one number from each of two other multisets; that is, A=gcd⁡(x,y)∣x∈B,y∈CA={\gcd(x,y)|x\in B,y\in C}A=gcd(x,y)∣x∈B,y∈C.
  4. Query the number of occurrences of some number in some multiset, modulo 2.

The number of multisets is 10510^5105, the number of operations is 10610^6106, and the range of values is 700070007000.

Approach#

Seeing "in the modulo 222 sense", we can think of using bitset to maintain each multiset.

In that case, operation 111 is a direct assignment, operation 222 is just XOR (because we are working modulo 222), and operation 444 is just a direct lookup; but .. what about operation 333?

We can try to maintain the multiset formed by all the divisors of each multiset; this way, operation 333 is just a direct bitwise AND.

We can precompute, for each number in the range of values, the bitset formed by its divisors; this solves operation 111. Operation 222 is still XOR.

The problem now is how to obtain the number of occurrences of some number in a multiset from the multiset formed by the divisors of that multiset.

Let the original multiset be AAA and the multiset formed by its divisors be A′A'A′; we want the number of occurrences of xxx in AAA. Doing some derivation with Möbius inversion:

\begin{aligned}&\sum\limits_{i\in A}[\frac i x=1]\=&\sum\limits_{i\in A}\sum\limits_{d|\frac i x}\mu(d)\=&\sum\limits_{d\in A',x|d}\mu(\frac d x)\end{aligned}

Since we are working modulo 222, −1-1−1 and 111 are the same, so we only need to check whether dx\frac d xxd​ has a square factor. Therefore, for each number in the range of values, we can precompute the bitset formed by the positions among its multiples that contain no square factor after division by it; when answering a query, just do a bitwise AND first and then count().

In this way, the complexity of a single query is O(vw)O(\frac v w)O(wv​) (v=7000, w=32v=7000,\,w=32v=7000,w=32).

As for the precomputation, an O(vv)O(v\sqrt v)O(vv​) or O(v2)O(v^2)O(v2) precomputation is fairly simple; the log⁡\loglog precomputation is as shown in the code below, and its complexity is a harmonic series, so it is O(vlog⁡v)O(v\log v)O(vlogv).

noteReference code
#include <bitset>
#include <cctype>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

int read() {
  int out = 0;
  char c;
  while (!isdigit(c = getchar()));
  for (; isdigit(c); c = getchar()) out = out * 10 + c - '0';
  return out;
}

constexpr int N = 100005;
constexpr int M = 1000005;
constexpr int V = 7005;

bitset<V> pre[V], pre2[V], a[N], mu;
int n, m, tot;
char ans[M];

int main() {
  int i, j, x, y, z;

  n = read();
  m = read();

  mu.set();
  for (i = 2; i * i < V; ++i) {
    for (j = 1; i * i * j < V; ++j) {
      mu[i * i * j] = 0;
    }
  }
  for (i = 1; i < V; ++i) {
    for (j = 1; i * j < V; ++j) {
      pre[i * j][i] = 1;
      pre2[i][i * j] = mu[j];
    }
  }

  while (m--) {
    switch (read()) {
      case 1:
        x = read();
        y = read();
        a[x] = pre[y];
        break;
      case 2:
        x = read();
        y = read();
        z = read();
        a[x] = a[y] ^ a[z];
        break;
      case 3:
        x = read();
        y = read();
        z = read();
        a[x] = a[y] & a[z];
        break;
      case 4:
        x = read();
        y = read();
        ans[tot++] = ((a[x] & pre2[y]).count() & 1) + '0';
        break;
    }
  }

  printf("%s", ans);

  return 0;
}

Combining with the Sieve of Eratosthenes#

Thanks to the efficiency of bitset's sequential reads and writes, it is very well suited for combining with the Sieve of Eratosthenes to build a table of primes.

The way to use it is also very simple: you only need to replace the boolean array in the Sieve of Eratosthenes with a bitset.

noteSpeed test

The tests were performed using Quick C++ Benchmarks, with GCC 13.2 as the compiler and -std=c++20 -O2 as the compile flags.

Algorithm Function name
Sieve of Eratosthenes + C-style boolean array, not storing the primes found Eratosthenes_CArray
Sieve of Eratosthenes + vector<bool>, not storing the primes found Eratosthenes_vector
Sieve of Eratosthenes + bitset, not storing the primes found Eratosthenes_bitset
Sieve of Eratosthenes + C-style boolean array, storing the primes found Eratosthenes_CArray_sp
Sieve of Eratosthenes + vector<bool>, storing the primes found Eratosthenes_vector_sp
Sieve of Eratosthenes + bitset, storing the primes found Eratosthenes_bitset_sp
Euler's sieve + C-style boolean array Euler_CArray
Euler's sieve + vector<bool> Euler_vector
Euler's sieve + bitset Euler_bitset

  • When the Sieve of Eratosthenes stores the primes found:

    • Test results for N=5×107+1N=5 \times 10^7 + 1N=5×107+1:

      - Test results for N=108+1N=10^8 + 1N=108+1:

      - When the Sieve of Eratosthenes does not store the primes found:

    • Test results for N=5×107+1N=5 \times 10^7 + 1N=5×107+1:

      - Test results for N=108+1N=10^8 + 1N=108+1:

From the test results, we can conclude:

  1. After being optimized with bitset or vector<bool>, the Sieve of Eratosthenes with time complexity O(nlog⁡log⁡n)O(n \log \log n)O(nloglogn) even outperforms Euler's sieve with time complexity O(n)O(n)O(n);
  2. The optimization from using bitset or vector<bool> in Euler's sieve is not significant in most cases;
  3. The optimization effect of bitset is slightly stronger than that of vector<bool>.
noteReference code

You need to install google/benchmark.

#include <benchmark/benchmark.h>
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
using u32 = uint32_t;
using u64 = uint64_t;

#define ERATOSTHENES_STORAGE_PRIME
#define ENABLE_EULER
constexpr u32 N = 5e7 + 1;

#ifndef ERATOSTHENES_STORAGE_PRIME

void Eratosthenes_CArray(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bool is_prime[N];
  for (auto _ : state) {
    fill(is_prime, is_prime + N, true);
    is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime[j] = false;
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(0);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_CArray);

void Eratosthenes_vector(benchmark::State &state) {
  static vector<bool> is_prime(N);
  for (auto _ : state) {
    fill(is_prime.begin(), is_prime.end(), true);
    is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime[j] = false;
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(0);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_vector);

void Eratosthenes_bitset(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bitset<N> is_prime;
  for (auto _ : state) {
    is_prime.set();
    is_prime.reset(0);
    is_prime.reset(1);
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime.reset(j);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(0);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_bitset);

#else

void Eratosthenes_CArray_sp(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bool is_prime[N];
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    fill(is_prime, is_prime + N, true);
    is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime[j] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_CArray_sp);

void Eratosthenes_vector_sp(benchmark::State &state) {
  static vector<bool> is_prime(N);
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    fill(is_prime.begin(), is_prime.end(), true);
    is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime[j] = false;
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_vector_sp);

void Eratosthenes_bitset_sp(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bitset<N> is_prime;
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    is_prime.set();
    is_prime.reset(0);
    is_prime.reset(1);
    for (u32 i = 2; (u64)i * i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i])
        for (u32 j = i * i; j < N; j += i) is_prime.reset(j);
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i)
      if (is_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Eratosthenes_bitset_sp);

#endif

#ifdef ENABLE_EULER

void Euler_CArray(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bool not_prime[N];
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    fill(not_prime, not_prime + N, false);
    not_prime[0] = not_prime[1] = true;
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i) {
      if (!not_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
      for (u32 pri_j : prime) {
        if (i * pri_j >= N) break;
        not_prime[i * pri_j] = true;
        if (i % pri_j == 0) break;
      }
    }
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Euler_CArray);

void Euler_vector(benchmark::State &state) {
  static vector<bool> not_prime(N);
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    fill(not_prime.begin(), not_prime.end(), false);
    not_prime[0] = not_prime[1] = true;
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i) {
      if (!not_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
      for (u32 pri_j : prime) {
        if (i * pri_j >= N) break;
        not_prime[i * pri_j] = true;
        if (i % pri_j == 0) break;
      }
    }
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Euler_vector);

void Euler_bitset(benchmark::State &state) {
  static bitset<N> not_prime;
  for (auto _ : state) {
    vector<u32> prime;
    not_prime.reset();
    not_prime.set(0);
    not_prime.set(1);
    for (u32 i = 2; i < N; ++i) {
      if (!not_prime[i]) prime.push_back(i);
      for (u32 pri_j : prime) {
        if (i * pri_j >= N) break;
        not_prime.set(i * pri_j);
        if (i % pri_j == 0) break;
      }
    }
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(prime);
  }
}

BENCHMARK(Euler_bitset);

#endif

static void Noop(benchmark::State &state) {
  for (auto _ : state) benchmark::DoNotOptimize(0);
}

BENCHMARK(Noop);
BENCHMARK_MAIN();

Chapter 22 · The C++ Standard Library

string

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/string.md

author: johnvp22, Ir1d

What is string#

std::string is a class provided in the standard library <string> (note that this is not the <string.h> library of the C language); it is essentially an alias for std::basic_string<char>.

Why use string#

The C language provides string operations, but strings can only be implemented by way of character arrays. string, on the other hand, is a simple class that is easy to use, and it is widely used in OI contests. Moreover, compared with other STL containers, the constant factor of string can be considered excellent, essentially on a par with character arrays.

string can allocate space dynamically#

Like many STL containers, string can allocate space dynamically. This allows us to read input directly with std::cin, but it is likewise rather slow. This also means we do not have to worry about memory.

string overloads the addition operator and the comparison operators#

The addition operator of string can directly concatenate two strings, or a string and a character. Similar to std::vector, string overloads the comparison operators, which likewise compare in lexicographic order, so we can directly call std::sort to sort several strings.

Usage#

The following introduces the basic operations of string; for details, see the C++ documentation.

Declaration#

std::string s;

Converting to a char array#

In C, there are also many string functions, but their parameters are all of char pointer type. For ease of use, string has two member functions that can convert it to a char pointer—data()/c_str() (before C++11, c_str() guaranteed a null character at the end, while data() did not; after C++11 the two behave identically1), for example:

printf("%s", s);          // Not guaranteed to compile; behavior is undefined
printf("%s", s.data());   // Undefined behavior before C++11, correct output after C++11
printf("%s", s.c_str());  // Guaranteed to output correctly

Getting the length#

Many functions can return the length of a string:

printf("The length of s is %zu", s.size());
printf("The length of s is %zu", s.length());
printf("The length of s is %zu", strlen(s.c_str()));

noteThe complexity of these functions

The complexity of strlen() is always linear in the length of the string.

The complexity of size() and length() was not specified in C++98 and was specified to be constant complexity in C++11. However, on common compilers, even in C++98, the complexity of these two functions is constant.

warningWarning

These three functions (as well as the find function that will be mentioned below) all have return type size_t (unsigned long). Therefore, these return values do not support direct comparison or arithmetic with negative numbers; it is recommended to cast them when needed.

Finding the position of the first occurrence of a character (or string)#

The find(str,pos) function can be used to find the position of the first occurrence of a character/string in the string after pos (inclusive) (if no argument is passed for pos, it defaults to 0). If it does not occur, string::npos is returned (defined as -1, but the type is still size_t/unsigned long).

Example:

string s = "OI Wiki", t = "OI", u = "i";
int pos = 5;
printf("The character I first occurs in s at position %lu\n", s.find('I'));
printf("The character a first occurs in s at position %lu\n", s.find('a'));
printf("The character a first occurs in s at position %d\n", s.find('a'));
printf("The string t first occurs in s at position %lu\n", s.find(t));
printf("Starting from position pos in s, the string u first occurs at position %lu", s.find(u, pos));

Output:

The character I first occurs in s at position 1
The character a first occurs in s at position 18446744073709551615 // This is size_t(-1); the exact value is platform-dependent.
The character a first occurs in s at position -1 // If cast to the int type, it correctly outputs -1
The string t first occurs in s at position 0
Starting from position pos in s, the string u first occurs at position 6

Extracting a substring#

The substr(pos, len) function returns the string composed of at most len characters taken starting from position pos (if the suffix starting from pos is shorter than len, that suffix is taken).

Example:

string s = "OI Wiki", t = "OI";
printf("The substring composed of at most three characters starting from the fourth position of string s is %s\n",
       s.substr(3, 3).c_str());
printf("The substring composed of at most three characters starting from the second position of string t is %s",
       t.substr(1, 3).c_str());

Output:

The substring composed of at most three characters starting from the fourth position of string s is Wik
The substring composed of at most three characters starting from the second position of string t is I

Inserting/deleting characters (or strings)#

insert(index,count,ch) and insert(index,str) are fairly common insertion functions. They respectively mean inserting the string ch count times in a row at index, and inserting the string str.

The erase(index,count) function deletes the count characters of the string starting at position index (inclusive) (if no argument is passed for count, it means deleting all characters at and after position index).

Example:

string s = "OI Wiki", t = " Wiki";
char u = '!';
s.erase(2);
printf("The string obtained after deleting all characters of string s starting from the third position is %s\n", s.c_str());
s.insert(2, t);
printf("The string obtained after inserting string t at the third position of string s is %s\n", s.c_str());
s.insert(7, 3, u);
printf("The string obtained after inserting the string u 3 times in a row at the eighth position of string s is %s",
       s.c_str());

Output:

The string obtained after deleting all characters of string s starting from the third position is OI
The string obtained after inserting string t at the third position of string s is OI Wiki
The string obtained after inserting the string u 3 times in a row at the eighth position of string s is OI Wiki!!!

Replacing characters (or strings)#

replace(pos,count,str) and replace(first,last,str) are fairly common replacement functions. They respectively mean replacing the substring of count characters starting at position pos with str, and replacing the substring that starts at first (inclusive) and ends at last (exclusive) with str, where first and last are both iterators.

Example:

string s = "OI Wiki";
s.replace(2, 5, "");
printf("The string obtained after replacing positions 3~7 of string s with an empty string is %s\n", s.c_str());
s.replace(s.begin(), s.begin() + 2, "NOI");
printf("The string obtained after replacing the first two positions of string s with NOI is %s", s.c_str());

Output:

The string obtained after replacing positions 3~7 of string s with an empty string is OI
The string obtained after replacing the first two positions of string s with NOI is NOI

Chapter 23 · The C++ Standard Library

pair

oi-wiki.org/lang/csl/pair.md

author: sbofgayschool

std::pair is a class template defined in the standard library. It is used to tie two variables together into a "pair", and the two variables may have different data types.

noteClass template

A class template is not itself a class, but a "template" that can produce different classes from different data types.

When it is used, the compiler generates the corresponding class from the data types passed in, and then creates the corresponding instance.

Templates are a relatively advanced language feature of C++ and almost never come up in informatics contests. If you are interested, you can read C++ Primer to learn more advanced C++.

By using pair flexibly, you can easily handle scenarios that require bundling associated data together for storage and processing.

noteStruct

Compared with a custom struct, pair requires no extra definition of a structure or overloaded operators, so it is more convenient to use.

However, the variable names of a custom struct are often clearer (pair can only use first and second to access the two contained variables). Meanwhile, if more than two variables need to be tied together, a custom struct is more suitable.

Usage#

Initialization#

A pair can be initialized directly at the point of definition.

pair<int, double> p0(1, 2.0);

You can also initialize a pair by first defining it and then assigning values.

pair<int, double> p1;
p1.first = 1;
p1.second = 2.0;

The std::make_pair function can also be used. This function takes two variables and returns a pair composed of them.

pair<int, double> p2 = make_pair(1, 2.0);

A commonly used approach is the macro definition #define mp make_pair, which shortens the somewhat lengthy make_pair to mp.

In C++11 and later, make_pair can be used together with auto to avoid declaring data types explicitly.

auto p3 = make_pair(1, 2.0);

For the use of auto in informatics contests, see the explanation in the Iterators section.

Access#

The two variables contained in a pair can be accessed through the members first and second.

int i = p0.first;
double d = p0.second;

They can also be modified.

p1.first++;

Comparison#

pair has all comparison operators predefined, including <, >, <=, >=, ==, and !=. Of course, this requires the data types of the two variables making up the pair to have the == and/or < operators defined.

Among them, the four operators <, >, <=, and >= first compare the first variables of the two pairs, and compare the second variables only when the first variables are equal.

if (p2 >= p3) {
  cout << "do something here" << endl;
}

Since pair defines < and ==, which the STL commonly uses, it can work well with other STL functions or data structures. For example, pair can serve as the data type of a priority_queue.

priority_queue<pair<int, double>> q;

Assignment and Swapping#

The value of a pair can be assigned to another pair of the same type.

p0 = p1;

The swap function can also be used to exchange the values of pairs.

swap(p0, p1);
p2.swap(p3);

Example Applications#

Discretization#

pair can be used to implement discretization with ease.

We can create an array of pairs, taking the value of each piece of original data as the first variable of each pair and the position of the original data as the second variable. After sorting, just assign the rank of each original value (the position it occupies after sorting) to the position where that value originally was.

// a is the original data
pair<int, int> a[MAXN];
// ai is the discretized data
int ai[MAXN];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  // first is the value of the original data, second is its position
  scanf("%d", &a[i].first);
  a[i].second = i;
}
// sort
sort(a, a + n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  // assign the rank of the value to the position where it originally was
  ai[a[i].second] = i;
}

Dijkstra#

As mentioned above, pair can serve as the data type of a priority_queue.

So, in the heap optimization of Dijkstra's algorithm, pair and priority_queue can be used to maintain the nodes, taking the node's current distance to the source as the first variable and the node's number as the second variable.

priority_queue<pair<int, int>, std::vector<pair<int, int>>,
               std::greater<pair<int, int>>>
    q;
... while (!q.empty()) {
  // dis is the node's distance to the source when pushed into the heap, i is the node's number
  int dis = q.top().first, i = q.top().second;
  q.pop();
  ...
}

pair and map#

map is the data structure in C++ that stores key-value pairs. In many cases, the key-value pairs stored in a map are exposed to the outside through pair.

map<int, double> m;
m.insert(make_pair(1, 2.0));

For more on map, please see the relevant parts of Associative Containers and Unordered Associative Containers.

Chapter 24 · Advanced C++

Classes

oi-wiki.org/lang/class.md

author: Ir1d, cjsoft, Lans1ot, JasonkayZK A class is an extension of the struct: not only can it have member elements, it can also have member functions.

In object-oriented programming (OOP), an object is an instance of a class — that is, a variable.

In C++, what the struct keyword defines is also a class; the definition of the struct given above comes from C. For certain historical reasons, C++ kept and extended struct.

Defining a Class#

A class is defined with the class or struct keyword; the examples below use class.

class ClassName {
  ...
};

// Example:
class Object {
 public:
  int weight;
  int value;
} e[array_length];

const Object a;
Object b, B[array_length];
Object *c;

This is much the same as using struct. The example defines a class named Object. The class has two member elements, weight,value; and after the }, an array e of this type is defined.

Defining pointers to a class is done in the same way as for struct.

Access Specifiers#

Unlike the examples in struct, public appears in this example — it is an access specifier.

  • public: every member after this access specifier is publicly accessible; put simply, it can be accessed both inside the class and outside the class.
  • protected: every member after this access specifier can be accessed by members inside the class, by derived classes, or by members of friends, but cannot be accessed from outside the class.
  • private: every member after this access specifier can only be accessed by members inside the class or by members of friends, and cannot be accessed from outside the class or from a derived class.

For a struct, all of its members are public by default. For a class, all of its members are private by default.

noteBasic concepts of friends and derived classes

Friend (friend): applying the friend keyword to some function or class. This allows the decorated entity to access the class's private or protected members without becoming a member function or a member class. Put simply, as long as something carries this class's friend marker, it can access private or protected member elements.

Derived class: C++ allows a class to be used as a base class, and a derived class to be derived from the base class. A derived class (according to certain rules) inherits the member variables and member functions of the base class. This can improve the reusability of code.

Derivation is something like an "is" relationship. For example, a cat (derived class) "is" a mammal (base class).

As for the difference between private and protected above, you can think of it this way: a derived class can access the base class's protected elements (public likewise), but cannot access private elements.

Accessing and Modifying the Values of Member Elements#

The method is the same as for struct

  • For variables, use the . symbol.
  • For pointers, use the -> symbol.

Member Functions#

A member function is, as the name suggests, a function contained in a class.

noteCommon examples of member functions
vector.push_back();
set.insert();
queue.empty();
class Class_Name {
  ... type Function_Name(...) { ... }
};

// Example:
class Object {
 public:
  int weight;
  int value;

  void print() {
    cout << weight << endl;
    return;
  }

  void change_w(int);
};

void Object::change_w(int _weight) { weight = _weight; }

Object var;

This class has a function that prints the member elements of an Object, as well as a function that changes the member element weight.

Just like ordinary functions, member functions can also be declared first and defined later, as in line 14 (the declaration) and after line 17 (the definition).

If you want to call the print member function of var, you can invoke it with var.print().

Operator Overloading#

noteWhat is overloading?

C++ allows programmers to give different definitions to functions or operators with the same name. This is called overloading.

If same-named functions differ pairwise in the kinds of their parameters or in their number (one or both of these), they are regarded as different.

It should be noted that if two same-named functions differ only in the type of their return value, overloading is impossible — in that case the compiler will refuse to compile!

If no ambiguity arises when calling (ambiguity means that, when calling certain same-named functions, it is impossible to uniquely determine the function being called from the kinds and number of the arguments supplied; this often happens with functions that have default parameters), the compiler will decide which function to call based on the arguments supplied at the call.

The process described above is called overload resolution.

Overloaded operators can, to some extent, stand in for functions and simplify code.

An example of operator overloading is given below.

class Vector {
 public:
  int x, y;

  Vector() : x(0), y(0) {}

  Vector(int _x, int _y) : x(_x), y(_y) {}

  int operator*(const Vector& other) const { return x * other.x + y * other.y; }

  Vector operator+(const Vector&) const;
  Vector operator-(const Vector&) const;
};

Vector Vector::operator+(const Vector& other) const {
  return Vector(x + other.x, y + other.y);
}

Vector Vector::operator-(const Vector& other) const {
  return Vector(x - other.x, y - other.y);
}

// Lines 4,5 show assigning values to x,y; see below for the concrete implementation.

This example defines a vector class and overloads the * + - operators, which represent the vector dot product, vector addition, and vector subtraction, respectively.

The template for overloading an operator roughly breaks down into the following parts.

/*overload inside the class definition*/ return type operator symbol(parameters){...}

/*declared inside the class definition, defined outside*/ return type ClassName::operator symbol(parameters){...}

For a class you define yourself, if certain operators are overloaded (generally speaking, only the comparison operator < needs to be overloaded), you can then use the corresponding STL containers or algorithms, such as sort.

To learn more, see item 4 in References.

noteOperators that can be overloaded
+       -       *       /       %       ^       &
|       ~       !       =       <       >       +=
-=      *=      /=      %=      ^=      &=      |=
<<      >>      >>=     <<=     ==      !=      <=
>=      &&      ||      ++      --      ,       ->*
->      ()      []      new     new []  delete  delete []

Setting Initial Values When Instantiating Variables#

To accomplish this, you need to define a default constructor.

class ClassName {
  ... ClassName(...)... { ... }
};

// Example:
class Object {
 public:
  int weight;
  int value;

  Object() {
    weight = 0;
    value = 0;
  }
};

This example defines a default constructor for Object; when we instantiate a variable of type Object, this function initializes all the member elements to 0.

If there is no explicit constructor, the compiler considers the class to have an implicit default constructor. In other words, if no constructor is defined at all, the compiler will automatically generate a default constructor, which initializes the member elements according to their types (the same as defining variables of built-in types).

In this case, the member elements are all uninitialized, and the result of accessing an uninitialized variable is undefined (that is, there is no way to know what value will be returned).

If you need to customize the initial values, you can additionally define (or overload) constructors.

noteOn defining (or overloading) constructors

Generally speaking, a default constructor takes no parameters, and this is what distinguishes it from a constructor. Constructors and default constructors are defined in much the same way, differing only in the number of parameters.

Constructors can be overloaded (though the first one is called a definition). Note that if a constructor has already been defined, the compiler will no longer generate a parameterless default constructor. This may cause an attempt to construct a variable in the default way (i.e., without passing initialization arguments) to fail to compile.

When using C++11 or above, {} can be used to initialize variables.

noteAbout <code>{}</code>

Initializing with {} uses a lightweight proxy object, std::initializer_list, to perform the initialization.

The initialization steps are roughly as follows:

  1. Try to find a default constructor that has std::initializer_list among its parameters; if there is one, it is called (after the call, the searches below are no longer performed; the same applies below).
  2. Try to fill the elements inside {} into the other constructor parameters; if the parameters can be filled in order (default parameters count as well), that default constructor is called.
  3. If there are no private member elements, an attempt is made outside the class to assign values one by one, in the order the elements are defined or in index order.

The process above is only a simplified version of the complete process; see "References item 9" for details.

class Object {
 public:
  int weight;
  int value;

  Object() {
    weight = 0;
    value = 0;
  }

  Object(int _weight = 0, int _value = 0) {
    weight = _weight;
    value = _value;
  }

  // the same as
  // Object(int _weight,int _value):weight(_weight),value(_value) {}
};

// the same as
// Object::Object(int _weight,int _value){
//   weight = _weight;
//   value = _value;
// }
//}

Object A;        // ok
Object B(1, 2);  // ok
Object C{1, 2};  // ok,(C++11)
noteAbout implicit type conversion

Sometimes you may write code like the following

class Node {
 public:
  int var;

  Node(int _var) : var(_var) {}
};

Node a = 1;

It looks quite illogical: an int cannot possibly be converted to the node type. Yet the compiler will not raise an error.

The reason is that when the assignment is carried out, 1 is first used as an argument to call node::node(int), and then the default copy function is called to perform the assignment.

But in most cases, the programmer will want the compiler to report an error. In that case, the explicit keyword can be appended before the constructor. This tells the compiler that the call must be made explicitly.

class Node {
 public:
  int var;

  explicit Node(int _var) : var(_var) {}
};

That is, node a=1 will produce an error, but node a=node(1) will not, because the latter explicitly calls the constructor. Of course, most people would not write code like the latter, but this example is enough to illustrate the role of explicit.

In competitive programming, though, the usual way to avoid such situations is "strengthening the standardization of your code", eliminating them at the source

Destruction#

This is an unavoidable matter. Every variable will head toward destruction when its scope ends.

But for a pointer that already points to dynamically allocated memory, the pointer will not automatically release the memory it points to when it is destroyed; the dynamic memory needs to be released manually.

If the member elements of a struct contain pointers, the same problem is encountered. A destructor is needed to release the dynamic memory manually.

The destructor will be called when the variable is destroyed. The way to overload it is the same as for constructors, but a ~ must be added in front

The default destructor is usually already sufficient for competitive programming; normally we only overload the destructor when the member elements contain pointers.

class Object {
 public:
  int weight;
  int value;
  int* ned;

  Object() {
    weight = 0;
    value = 0;
  }

  ~Object() { delete ned; }
};

Assigning Values to Class Variables#

By default, assignment proceeds according to the rules for assigning the corresponding member elements. You can also use ClassName() or ClassName{} as a temporary variable to perform the assignment.

The former merely calls the copy constructor, while the latter calls the default constructor before calling the copy constructor.

Also, by default, the assignment is a shallow copy carried out between corresponding member elements; if some member element is a pointer, then after the assignment, the member pointers of the two variables have the same address.

// A,tmp1,tmp2,tmp3 are of type Object
tmp1 = A;
tmp2 = Object(...);
tmp3 = {...};

To solve the pointer problem, or to perform more operations, you need to overload the corresponding constructors.

For more on constructors, see item 6 in References.

Chapter 25 · Advanced C++

Namespaces

oi-wiki.org/lang/namespace.md

Overview#

C++'s namespace mechanism can be used to solve the problem of name conflicts in complex projects.

For example: everything in the C++ standard library is defined in the std namespace; if you define a variable called cin, you can access the cin variable you defined via cin, and access the standard library's cin object via std::cin, without worrying about conflicts.

Declaration#

The following code declares a namespace named A:

namespace A {
int cnt;

void f(int x) { cnt = x; }
}  // namespace A

After the declaration, outside this namespace, you can access the function f inside namespace A via A::f(x), and access the variable cnt inside namespace A via A::cnt.

Namespace declarations can be nested, so the following piece of code is also allowed:

namespace A {
namespace B {
void f() { ... }
}  // namespace B

void f() {
  B::f();  // What is actually accessed is A::B::f(); since we are currently inside
           // namespace A, the leading A:: can be omitted
}
}  // namespace A

void f()  // This defines the f function in the global namespace, which conflicts
          // with neither A::f nor A::B::f
{
  A::f();
  A::B::f();
}

The using Directive#

After a namespace is declared, accessing members of the namespace from outside it requires prefixing the member's name with namespace_name::.

Is there a more convenient way that lets us access members of a namespace directly by their member names? The answer is yes: we can use using directives.

The using directive has the following two forms:

  1. using namespace_name::member_name;: this directive lets us omit the namespace in front of a member name and access the member directly by its member name — it is equivalent to importing that member into the current scope.
  2. using namespace namespace_name;: this directive lets us access any member of the namespace directly by its member name — it is equivalent to importing all members of that namespace into the current scope.

Therefore, if using namespace std; is executed, all the names in std will be introduced into the global namespace within the current scope. In this way, we can use cin in place of std::cin, and cout in place of std::cout.

warning<code>using</code> Directives May Cause Name Conflicts!

Because using namespace std; introduces all names in std, declaring a variable or function with the same name as one in std may cause a compilation error due to a name conflict.

Therefore, in engineering projects, the using namespace namespace_name; directive is not recommended.

With using directives, the code in C++ Syntax Basics can be written in these two equivalent ways:

#include <iostream>

using std::cin;
using std::cout;
using std::endl;

int main() {
  int x, y;
  cin >> x >> y;
  cout << y << endl << x;
  return 0;
}
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

int main() {
  int x, y;
  cin >> x >> y;
  cout << y << endl << x;
  return 0;
}

Unnamed Namespaces#

When we define, within a scope, only one namespace whose purpose is to prevent name conflicts, its definition and use can be made very concise. We can use an unnamed namespace.

A namespace defined in the form namespace { /* something ... */ } (omitting the name of the namespace) is called an unnamed namespace. An unnamed namespace in a file is treated as having a unique name, different from all other namespaces, but multiple unnamed namespaces within the same scope are treated as the same namespace. After an unnamed namespace is defined, the names inside it can be found, when used, in the enclosing scope — as if a using namespace directive had been added after the unnamed namespace's definition.

Applications#

Preventing Name Conflicts Between Subtasks#

In some problems that have multiple subtasks, we can define a namespace for each subtask and define, within it, the variables and functions we need to solve that subtask. This way, even if the implementations of two subtasks declare the same names, no conflict arises, so the subtasks do not interfere with each other; this makes debugging somewhat easier and also improves the readability of the program.

Preventing Conflicts with Names Introduced by the Standard Library and the Environment#

Meanwhile, using namespaces can also prevent some names commonly used in competitive programming from conflicting with the standard, as in the example below:

#include <math.h>

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

namespace Sol {
int end;  // std::end is introduced by using namespace std;

int y1;  // y1 is the Bessel function of the second kind defined by POSIX

// Therefore, in general, there is a conflict on Linux but not on Windows

void solve() {
  // Using the end and y1 we declared, unqualified (without ::), inside
  // Sol::solve() does not cause a name conflict; but if the code above were
  // placed in the global namespace, conflicts would arise: end conflicts with
  // std::end only during name lookup (i.e. compiling the code that uses it),
  // while y1 conflicts right at its declaration; and since that conflict
  // depends on the environment, it can go unnoticed on Windows yet cause a
  // compilation error in the Linux judging environment.
}
}  // namespace Sol

int main() { Sol::solve(); }

References#

  • Namespaces - cppreference.com
