Chapter 26 · Advanced C++

Value Categories

oi-wiki.org/lang/value-category.md

Value categories are a very important concept in C++. Although they may not be of much use in competitive programming, understanding them can help us discover and avoid unnecessary copies, thereby improving the efficiency and performance of our code.

The concept of value categories has gone through several rounds of development in C, C++98, C++11, and C++17, gradually becoming a rather complex concept.

Unnecessary Copies#

Let us consider the process of stuffing strings into a vector:

int main() {
  std::vector<std::string> vec;
  vec.reserve(3);
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
    std::string str;
    std::cin >> str;
    vec.push_back(str);
  }
  return 0;
}

We can see that during the transfer, the string is stored once in str and once in vec, so the memory usage doubles.

If we insist on saving this part of the memory, we can implement a crude move operation: define a custom MyString struct with a pointer inside pointing to our string, so that we only need to copy the pointer over and carefully clean up the original object's pointer, preventing it from being destructed by mistake.

struct MyString {
  char *beg, *end;
  // ...
};

void move_to(MyString &src, MyString &dst) {
  dst.beg = src.beg;
  dst.end = src.end;
  src.beg = src.end = nullptr;
}

Since the need for this kind of efficient object transfer is fairly common, and such transfers interact poorly with C++'s construction, destruction, and similar operations, C++11 introduced move semantics into the core of the language.

Value Categories in C#

In the C standard, an object is a concept more general than a variable: it refers to a region of memory and has a memory address. The main properties of an object include: size, effective type, value, and identifier. The identifier is the variable's name, and the value is the meaning of that memory when interpreted according to its type. For example, although the int and float types both occupy 4 bytes, we would interpret the same region of memory with different meanings.

In C, every expression has a type and a value category. Value categories are mainly divided into three kinds:

  • lvalue: an expression that implicitly designates an object. In other words, we can take the address of such an expression.
  • rvalue: an expression that does not designate an object, that is, it denotes a value without a storage location, and we cannot take the address of such a value.
  • function designator: an expression of function type.

Therefore, only a modifiable lvalue (an lvalue that is not const-qualified and is not an array) can appear on the left side of an assignment expression.

For an operator that requires an rvalue as its operand, whenever an lvalue is used as an operand, the lvalue-to-rvalue, array-to-pointer, or function-to-pointer standard conversion is applied to the expression to convert it into an rvalue.

Common misconceptions:

  • An rvalue expression may become an lvalue after further operations. For example, given int *a, the expression a + 1 is an rvalue, but *(a + 1) is an lvalue.
  • Only expressions have value categories; variables do not. For example, given int *a, we cannot say that the variable a is an lvalue, but we can say that it serves as an lvalue in the expression a.

Value Categories in C++98#

C++98 is almost identical to C in terms of value categories, but it adds some new rules:

  • Functions are lvalues, because we can take their addresses.
  • lvalue references (T&) are lvalues, because we can take their addresses.
  • Only const T& can bind to rvalues.

Copy Elision#

C++ allows the compiler to perform copy elision, which can reduce the creation and destruction of temporary objects.

For example, the code below triggers return value optimization (RVO), a form of copy elision: you will only see one construction and one copy construction, even if construction and destruction have side effects.

struct X {
  X() { std::puts("X::X()"); }

  X(const X &) { std::puts("X::X(const X &)"); }

  ~X() { std::puts("X::~X()"); }
};

X get() {
  X x;
  return x;
}

int main() {
  X x = get();
  X y = X(X(X(X(x))));
  return 0;
}

Value Categories in C++11#

C++11 introduced move semantics and rvalue references (T&&), including move constructors and move assignment operators. This gave us a way to make use of temporary objects.

Our move_to above can be rewritten as follows:

struct MyString {
  // ...
  MyString(MyString&& other) {
    beg = other.beg;
    end = other.end;
    other.beg = other.end = nullptr;
  }
};

We now care about one more property of expressions:

  • Whether it has identity: whether it designates an object, that is, whether it has an address.
  • Whether it can be moved from: whether it has functions such as the move constructor and the move assignment operator, giving us a way to make use of these temporary objects.

Therefore, we have three value categories:

  • Has identity, cannot be moved from: lvalue.
  • Has identity, can be moved from: xvalue.
  • No identity, can be moved from: prvalue.
  • No identity, cannot be moved from: such expressions cannot be used.

In addition, C++11 introduced two composite categories:

  • Has identity: the glvalue, i.e., lvalues and xvalues.
  • Can be moved from: the rvalue, i.e., prvalues and xvalues.

std::move#

To go along with move semantics, C++11 also introduced the utility function std::move, whose role is to cast an lvalue to an rvalue so as to trigger move semantics.

int main() {
  std::vector<int> a = {1, 2, 3};
  std::cout << "a: " << a.data() << std::endl;
  std::vector<int> b = a;
  std::cout << "b: " << b.data() << std::endl;
  std::vector<int> c = std::move(b);
  std::cout << "c: " << c.data() << std::endl;
}

Therefore, we only need to change push_back(str) to push_back(std::move(str)) to avoid the copy.

int main() {
  std::vector<std::string> vec;
  vec.reserve(3);
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
    std::string str;
    std::cin >> str;
    vec.push_back(std::move(str));
    // another clever way to write this; requires C++17
    // std::cin >> vec.emplace_back();
  }
  return 0;
}

Since std::string has small string optimization (SSO), in which short strings are stored directly inside the struct itself, you may have to enter fairly long strings before you can observe the invariance of the data pointer.

Value Categories in C++17#

C++17 further simplified value categories:

  • lvalue: has identity, cannot be moved from.
  • xvalue: has identity, can be moved from.
  • prvalue: the initialization of an object.

C++11 extended copy elision to moves; in the code below, there is no move in urvo when the compiler has RVO enabled.

C++17 requires that a prvalue is not materialized unless necessary, and is constructed directly into the storage of its final destination; before the construction, the object does not yet exist. Therefore, in C++17 we no longer have the return step, and there is no need to rely on RVO. This can also be understood as making URVO (Unnamed RVO) mandatory, while NRVO (Named RVO) is still not mandatory.

std::string urvo() { return std::string("123"); }

std::string nrvo() {
  std::string s;
  s = "123";
  std::cout << s;
  return s;
}

int main() {
  std::string str = urvo();  // constructed directly
  std::string str = nrvo();  // not necessarily constructed directly; depends on the optimization
}

Meanwhile, C++17 introduced the temporary materialization mechanism: when we need to access member variables, call member functions, or otherwise encounter situations that require a glvalue, the prvalue can be implicitly converted to an xvalue.

Common Misconceptions#

In the example below:

  • In f1, returning std::move(s) is redundant: it brings no performance improvement, and instead interferes with the compiler's NRVO optimization.
  • In f2, returning std::move(s) is dangerous: the function returns an rvalue reference that points to the local variable s, which has already been destroyed, causing a dangling reference.
std::string f1() {
  std::string s = "123";
  // equivalent to return std::string(std::move(s))
  return std::move(s);
}

std::string&& f2() {
  std::string s = "123";
  return std::move(s);
}

References and Further Reading#

  1. Value categories
  2. Wording for guaranteed copy elision through simplified value categories
  3. Value categories in C++
  4. Everything you need to know about rvalue references, moves, and the value category system in C++
  5. Copy elision

Chapter 27 · Advanced C++

Operator Overloading

oi-wiki.org/lang/op-overload.md

Operator overloading means redefining operators so that they support operations on specific data types. Overloaded operators are a special case of overloaded functions.

When an operator appears in an expression, and at least one of the operator's operands has a class or enumeration type, overload resolution is used to determine which user-defined function satisfying the corresponding declaration should be called.1

In plain terms, if we regard using an "operator" as calling a special function (e.g., treating 1+2 as a call to add(1, 2)), and at least one of this function's parameters (operands) has a class, struct, or enum type, the compiler needs to decide, based on the types of the operands, which custom function should be called.

In C++, we can overload almost all available operators.

noteA list of some overloadable operators

Unary operations: + (positive); - (negative); ~ (bitwise NOT); ++; --; ! (logical NOT); * (dereference); & (address-of); -> (class member access operator); etc.

Binary operations: +; -; & (bitwise AND); [] (subscripting); ==; = (assignment); etc.

Others: () (function call); "" (suffix identifier1, since C++11); new (memory allocation); , (comma operator); <=> (three-way comparison2, since C++20); etc.

Restrictions#

Operator overloading has the following restrictions:

  • Only existing operators can be overloaded; you cannot define new operators yourself.
  • The following operators cannot be overloaded: :: (scope resolution), . (member access), .* (member access through a pointer to member), ?: (the ternary operator).
  • An overloaded operator's precedence, operands, and associativity must not be changed.
  • Overloaded && (logical AND) and || (logical OR) lose short-circuit evaluation.

Implementation#

Operator overloading falls into two cases: overloading as a member function or as a non-member function.

When an operator is overloaded as a member function, an implicit this pointer to the current object is passed as a parameter, so the function has one parameter fewer than the number of operands.

When it is overloaded as a non-member function, the number of the function's parameters is the same as the number of operands.

The basic form is as follows (assuming the operator to be overloaded is @):

class Example {
  // example of a member function
  return type operator@(parameters other than the object itself) { /* ... */ }
};

// example of a non-member function
return type operator@(all parameters participating in the operation) { /* ... */ }

Several examples of overloaded operators are given below.

Basic arithmetic operators#

Below, a two-dimensional vector struct Vector2D is defined, and the corresponding overloads for addition and the dot product are implemented.

noteExample of overloading arithmetic operators
struct Vector2D {
  double x, y;

  Vector2D(double a = 0, double b = 0) : x(a), y(b) {}

  Vector2D operator+(Vector2D v) const { return Vector2D(x + v.x, y + v.y); }

  // note that the type of the return value does not have to be this class
  double operator*(Vector2D v) const { return x * v.x + y * v.y; }
};

Increment/decrement operators#

The increment and decrement operators fall into two categories: prefix (++a) and postfix (a++). To distinguish the prefix and postfix operators, overloading the postfix version requires adding a dummy parameter of type int.

You can think of prefix increment as a call to operator++(a) or a.operator++(), and of postfix increment as a call to operator++(a, 0) or a.operator++(0).

noteExample of overloading the prefix and postfix increment operators separately
struct MyInt {
  int x;

  // prefix version, corresponds to ++a
  MyInt &operator++() {
    x++;
    return *this;
  }

  // postfix version, corresponds to a++
  MyInt operator++(int) {
    MyInt tmp;
    tmp.x = x;
    x++;
    return tmp;
  }
};
One more point: for the built-in increment and decrement operators, the prefix operators return references, while the postfix operators return values. Although overloaded operators are not required to follow this restriction, semantically, the overloaded operators are still expected to keep the types of their return values consistent with those of the built-in operators.

For a type T, the typical definitions of overloaded increment operators are as follows:

Overload definition (taking ++ as an example) Member function Non-member function
Prefix T& T::operator++(); T& operator++(T& a);
Postfix T T::operator++(int); T operator++(T& a, int);

Function call operator#

The function call operator () can only be overloaded as a member function. By overloading the () operator for a class, objects of that class can be called just like functions.

A common application of overloading the () operator is passing a struct that has overloaded the () operator, as a custom comparison function, into priority queues and other STL containers.

Here is an example: given the names and scores of nnn students, sort them in descending order of score, with students of the same score sorted by name in ascending lexicographic order, and output the name and score of the person ranked highest.

Below, a comparison struct is defined that implements a custom ordering for the priority queue.

noteExample of overloading the function call operator
struct student {
  string name;
  int score;
};

struct cmp {
  bool operator()(const student& a, const student& b) const {
    return a.score < b.score || (a.score == b.score && a.name > b.name);
  }
};

// note that the template argument passed in is the name of the struct, not an instance
priority_queue<student, vector<student>, cmp> pq;

Comparison operators#

std::sort and some STL containers need to use the < operator. When using custom types, we need to overload it manually.

The following is an example that implements the same functionality as the previous section

noteExample of overloading comparison operators
struct student {
  string name;
  int score;

  // overload the < operator
  bool operator<(const student& a) const {
    return score < a.score || (score == a.score && name > a.name);
    // the this pointer is omitted above; the full expression is as follows:
    // this->score<a.score||(this->score==a.score&&this->name>a.name);
  }
};

priority_queue<student> pq;
The code above overloads the less-than operator as a member function; of course, overloading it as a non-member function is also possible.

noteOverloading as a non-member function
struct student {
  string name;
  int score;
};

bool operator<(const student& a, const student& b) {
  return a.score < b.score || (a.score == b.score && a.name > b.name);
}

priority_queue<student> pq;
In fact, as long as we have the < operator, the other five comparison operators can easily be implemented as well.

/* clang-format off */

// the implementations below all overload the less-than operator as a non-member function

bool operator<(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { /* overload the less-than operator here */ }
bool operator>(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { return rhs < lhs; }
bool operator<=(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { return !(lhs > rhs); }
bool operator>=(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { return !(lhs < rhs); }
bool operator==(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { return !(lhs < rhs) && !(lhs > rhs); }
bool operator!=(const T& lhs, const T& rhs) { return !(lhs == rhs); }

noteAbout the three-way comparison operator in C++20

If we use C++20 or a later version, we can directly use the defaulted three-way comparison operator to simplify the code.3

auto operator<=>(const T &lhs, const T &rhs) = default;

The default comparison compares the members one by one, in the order in which the member variables are declared.4

You can also use a custom three-way comparison. In this case, you are required to choose the ordering relation embodied in the comparison (std::strong_ordering, std::weak_ordering, or std::partial_ordering), or to return an object such that:

  • if a < b, then (a <=> b) < 0;
  • if a > b, then (a <=> b) > 0;
  • if a and b are equal or equivalent, then (a <=> b) == 0.

For the specific implementation details, refer to Comparison operators #Three-way comparison - cppreference.

References and notes:

Footnotes
  1. Operator overloading - cppreference
  2. User-defined literals - cppreference
  3. Comparison operators #Three-way comparison - cppreference
  4. Default comparisons - cppreference

Chapter 28 · Advanced C++

References

oi-wiki.org/lang/reference.md

Declares a named variable as a reference, that is, an alias to an existing object or function.

A reference can be viewed as a non-null pointer encapsulated by C++; it can be used to pass the object it points to, and it must point to an object at declaration.

A reference is not an object; therefore, there are no arrays of references, pointers to references cannot be taken, and there are no references to references.

noteReference types are not object types

If you want references to be able to perform ordinary operations such as copying and assignment — for example, serving as container elements — you need reference_wrapper, which is usually implemented by maintaining a non-null pointer.

References are mainly divided into two kinds: lvalue references and rvalue references.

noteLvalues and rvalues

For an explanation of lvalues and rvalues, please refer to the value category page.

Lvalue References T&#

The references we usually encounter are lvalue references — references bound to lvalues — while const-qualified lvalue references can bind to rvalues. The following is a piece of sample code from the reference manual.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
  std::string s = "Ex";
  std::string& r1 = s;
  const std::string& r2 = s;

  r1 += "ample";  // modifies r1, which modifies s
  // r2 += "!"; // error: cannot modify through a reference to const
  std::cout << r2 << '\n';  // prints r2, which accesses s, outputting "Example"
}

The most common use of lvalue references is as function parameters, to avoid unwanted copies.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

// the s in the parameters is a reference; no copy happens when calling the function
char& char_number(std::string& s, std::size_t n) {
  s += s;  // 's' and 'str' of main() are the same object;
           // this also shows that an lvalue can appear on the right side of the equals sign
  return s.at(n);  // string::at() returns a reference to char
}

int main() {
  std::string str = "Test";
  char_number(str, 1) = 'a';  // the function's return value is an lvalue and can be assigned to
  std::cout << str << '\n';   // outputs "TastTest" here
}

Rvalue References T&& (C++ 11)#

An rvalue reference is a reference bound to an rvalue; it is used to move objects, and can also be used to extend the lifetime of temporary objects.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

using namespace std;

int main() {
  string s1 = "Test";
  // string&& r1 = s1; // error: cannot bind to an lvalue; std::move or static_cast is needed

  const string& r2 = s1 + s1;  // OK: an lvalue reference to const extends the lifetime
  // r2 += "Test"; // error: cannot modify through a reference to const
  cout << r2 << '\n';

  string&& r3 = s1 + s1;  // OK: an rvalue reference extends the lifetime
  r3 += "Test";
  cout << r3 << '\n';

  const string& r4 = r3;  // an rvalue reference can be converted to a const-qualified lvalue
  cout << r4 << '\n';

  string& r5 = r3;  // an rvalue reference can be converted to an lvalue
  cout << r5 << '\n';
}

Dangling References#

When the object a reference denotes has been destroyed, the reference becomes a dangling reference; accessing a dangling reference is undefined behavior, which may cause the program to crash.

The following are common examples of dangling references:

  • Referencing a local variable

    ```cpp

    include

    int& foo() { int a = 1; return a; }

    int main() { int& b = foo(); std::cout << b << std::endl; // undefined behavior } ```

  • Dangling references caused by deallocation

    ```cpp

    include

    int main() { int ptr = new int(10); int& ref = ptr; delete ptr;

    std::cout << ref << std::endl; // undefined behavior } ```

  • Dangling references caused by memory reallocation

    ```cpp

    include

    int main() { std::string str = "hello";

    const char& ref = str.front();

    str.append("world"); // may reallocate memory, causing the memory ref points to be freed

    std::cout << ref << std::endl; // undefined behavior } ```

    Insertion operations on containers such as std::vector and std::unordered_map may all cause memory reallocation.

When using references, you should always pay attention to the lifetime of the object the reference points to, so as to avoid creating dangling references.

Static analysis tools and good coding habits can usually keep us safe from the problem of dangling references.

Optimization Techniques Related to References#

Eliminating the Copy Overhead of Non-Lightweight Object Parameters#

Common non-lightweight objects include:

  • Containers such as vector, array, and map
  • string
  • Other types that define or inherit custom copy constructors, move constructors, and other special functions

Using references for lightweight objects, on the other hand, brings no benefit: the space occupied by a reference type as a parameter may even be larger than the type itself.

This may bring some performance burden, and may also prevent the compiler from optimizing.

The following count as lightweight objects:

  • Fundamental types such as int and float
  • Smaller aggregate types
  • Iterators of standard library containers

Converting Lvalues into Rvalues#

Use std::move to transfer ownership of an object. This is usually seen between local variables, or between a parameter and a local variable:

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

string world(string str) { return std::move(str) += " world!"; }

int main() {
  // 1
  cout << world("hello") << '\n';

  vector<string> vec0;

  // 2
  {
    string&& size = to_string(vec0.size());

    size += ", " + to_string(size.size());

    vec0.emplace_back(std::move(size));
  }

  cout << vec0.front();
}

But this is not needed at all times — for example, function return value optimization.

Rvalues Extending the Lifetime of Temporaries#

Semantically, temporaries may introduce extra copies or moves; although in most cases the compiler can optimize this away through copy elision, references can force the compiler not to perform these redundant operations, avoiding uncertainty.

References#

  1. C++ language documentation — reference declaration
  2. C++ language documentation — value categories
  3. Does const ref lvalue to non-const func return value specifically reduce copies?

Chapter 29 · Advanced C++

Constants

oi-wiki.org/lang/const.md

C++ provides a complete set of mechanisms for defining read-only entities: variables qualified with const are all read-only; the compiler performs conflict checks at compile time to prevent modification of read-only entities, and may also perform some optimizations.

In general, you should use const to qualify variables and parameters as much as possible, to improve the robustness of your code.

The const Type Qualifier#

Constants#

A variable qualified with const cannot have its value changed after initialization

const int a = 0;  // the type of a is const int

// a = 1; // a constant cannot be modified

References to const and Pointers to const#

Both references to const and pointers to const restrict modification of the value pointed to

int a = 0;
const int b = 0;

int *p1 = &a;
*p1 = 1;
const int *p2 = &a;
// *p2 = 2; // the variable cannot be modified through a pointer to const
// int *p3 = &b; // an int* cannot be used to point to a const int variable
const int *p4 = &b;

int &r1 = a;
r1 = 1;
const int &r2 = a;
// r2 = 2; // the variable cannot be modified through a reference to const
// int &p3 = b; // an int& cannot be used to reference a const int variable
const int &r4 = b;

Another distinction that needs to be made is between the pointer to const (const t*) and the const pointer (t* const), for example the following declarations

int* const p1;  // const pointer: the address it points to cannot be changed after initialization, but the value it points to can
const int* p2;  // pointer to const: the dereferenced value cannot be changed, and it can point to other int variables
const int* const p3;  // const pointer to const: the value cannot be changed, and the address it points to cannot be changed

// using aliases improves readability
using const_int = const int;
using ptr_to_const_int = const_int*;
using const_ptr_to_const_int = const ptr_to_const_int;

Using const in function parameters to qualify the parameter types can prevent variables from being modified by mistake, and also improves the readability of the code

void sum(const std::vector<int> &data, int &total) {
  for (auto iter = data.begin(); iter != data.end(); ++iter)
    total += *iter;  // iter is an iterator; the type after dereferencing is const int
}

const Member Functions#

A member function qualified with const in a type can be used to restrict modification of the members.

#include <iostream>

struct ConstMember {
  int s = 0;

  void func() { std::cout << "General Function" << std::endl; }

  void constFunc1() const { std::cout << "Const Function 1" << std::endl; }

  void constFunc2(int ss) const {
    // func(); // a const member function cannot call a non-const member function
    constFunc1();

    // s = ss; // a const member function cannot modify member variables
  }
};

int main() {
  int b = 1;
  ConstMember c{};
  const ConstMember d = c;
  // d.func(); // a const object cannot call a non-const member function
  d.constFunc2(b);
  return 0;
}

Constant Expression constexpr (C++11)#

A constant expression is an expression whose result can be computed at compile time; constexpr requires that the compiler be able to obtain the value of a function or variable at compile time.

Computing at compile time allows better optimization, such as hard-coding the result into the assembly, which eliminates the run-time computation overhead. Unlike the optimizations that come with const, when a variable qualified with constexpr satisfies the conditions of a constant expression, the compiler is required to compute the result at compile time instead of at run time.

noteA more intuitive understanding is to think of <code>const</code> as 'read-only' and <code>constexpr</code> as 'immutable'
constexpr int a = 10;  // directly defines a constant

constexpr int FivePlus(int x) { return 5 + x; }

void test(const int x) {
  std::array<int, x> c1;            // error: x is not known at compile time
  std::array<int, FivePlus(6)> c2;  // OK: FivePlus is known at compile time
}
The following example gives a good illustration of the difference between const and constexpr: the code uses recursion to compute the Fibonacci sequence and outputs it via control flow.

noteImplementation
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

constexpr unsigned fib0(unsigned n) {
  return n <= 1 ? 1 : (fib0(n - 1) + fib0(n - 2));
}

unsigned fib1(unsigned n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : (fib1(n - 1) + fib1(n - 2)); }

int main() {
  constexpr auto v0 = fib0(9);
  const auto v1 = fib1(9);

  cout << v0;
  cout << ' ';
  cout << v1;
}
notePossible assembly code after compilation (using Compiler Explorer, Clang 19)
fib1(unsigned int):
        push    r14
        push    rbx
        push    rax
        mov     ebx, 1
        cmp     edi, 2
        jb      .LBB0_4
        mov     r14d, edi
        xor     ebx, ebx
.LBB0_2:
        lea     edi, [r14 - 1]
        call    fib1(unsigned int)
        add     r14d, -2
        add     ebx, eax
        cmp     r14d, 1
        ja      .LBB0_2
        inc     ebx
.LBB0_4:
        mov     eax, ebx
        add     rsp, 8
        pop     rbx
        pop     r14
        ret

main:
        push    r14
        push    rbx
        push    rax
        mov     edi, 9
        call    fib1(unsigned int) # the initialization of `v1` performs a function call
        mov     ebx, eax
        mov     r14, qword ptr [rip + std::__1::cout@GOTPCREL]
        mov     rdi, r14
        mov     esi, 55 # `v0` has been replaced by the final computed result
        call    std::__1::basic_ostream<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>::operator<<(unsigned int)@PLT
        mov     byte ptr [rsp + 7], 32
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 7]
        mov     edx, 1
        mov     rdi, r14
        call    std::__1::basic_ostream<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>& std::__1::__put_character_sequence[abi:ne200000]<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>(std::__1::basic_ostream<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>&, char const*, unsigned long)
        mov     rdi, r14
        mov     esi, ebx # reads the value of the variable
        call    std::__1::basic_ostream<char, std::__1::char_traits<char>>::operator<<(unsigned int)@PLT
        xor     eax, eax
        add     rsp, 8
        pop     rbx
        pop     r14
        ret
The fib0 function qualified with constexpr is called with a constant argument at its only call site, so the entire function runs only at compile time. Since the function is never executed at run time, the compiler decides that there is no need to generate assembly code for it.

At the same time, note that in the assembly, v0 has no initialization code: in the code that calls cout to output v0, v0 has been replaced by the final computed result, which shows that the variable's value was already evaluated at compile time, optimizing away the run-time computation. The initialization of v1, on the other hand, is still an ordinary recursive call to fib1.

So constexpr can be used to replace constants defined by macros, avoiding the risks of macro definitions.

In algorithm problems, constexpr can be used to store variables for small data scales, to eliminate the corresponding run-time computation overhead. This is especially common in the 'precomputation' technique, where arrays and other containers qualified with constexpr are used to store the answers.

noteToo much compile-time computation leads to a compilation error

The compiler limits the cost of compile-time computation; if the amount of computation is too large, the code will fail to compile, and you should consider using const.

#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

constexpr unsigned long long fib(unsigned long long i) {
  return i <= 2 ? i : fib(i - 2) + fib(i - 1);
}

int main() {
  // constexpr auto v = fib(32); evaluation exceeded maximum depth
  const auto v = fib(32);
  cout << v;
  return 0;
}
noteThe compilation error Clang gives when using constexpr
<source>:10:20: error: constexpr variable 'v' must be initialized by a constant expression
    10 |     constexpr auto v = fib(32);
    |                    ^   ~~~~~~~~~~~~
<source>:6:25: note: constexpr evaluation exceeded maximum depth of 512 calls
    6 |     return i <= 2 ? i : fib(i - 2) + fib(i - 1);
    |                         ^
<source>:6:25: note: in call to 'fib(32)'
    6 |     return i <= 2 ? i : fib(i - 2) + fib(i - 1);
    |                         ^~~~~~~~~~
<source>:6:25: note: in call to ...

← PreviousReferencesNext →New C++ Features
Chapter 30 · Advanced C++

New C++ Features

oi-wiki.org/lang/new.md

Note: Considering the actual circumstances of algorithm competitions, this page will not study the syntax comprehensively; it only covers the parts that may be applied in algorithm competitions.

The syntax of this page follows the C++11 standard. Where the semantics differ, C++11 is taken as the standard; syntax from C++14, C++17, and so on is mentioned as appropriate and specially noted.

The auto type specifier#

The auto type specifier is used to automatically deduce the type of a variable, etc. For example:

auto a = 1;        // a is of type int
auto b = a + 0.1;  // b is of type double

Note that auto drops references; if you do not want the copy overhead, you need to specify it manually:

int a = 1;
int& b = a;
auto c = b;   // c is of type int, with copy overhead
auto& e = a;  // e is of type int&, with no copy overhead

The decltype specifier#

decltype can deduce a type from an entity or an expression. Note that the two deduce types in different ways, and incorrect use may cause dangling references. It is not commonly used in contests, so only a rough introduction is given here.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
  int a = 1926;
  decltype(a) b;                 // deduced from an entity, b is of type int
  decltype(1 + 1) c;             // deduced from an expression, c is of type int
  decltype((a)) d = a;           // deduced from an expression, d is of type int&!
  std::vector<decltype(b)> vec;  // deduced from an entity, vec is of type std::vector <int>
  return 0;
}

constexpr#

See also Constant expressions constexpr (C++11)

The range-based for loop#

Using a range-based for to traverse an iterable object is as efficient as traversing it with iterators. Both of these are generally more efficient than traversal by index, because there is no need to address elements based on the index.

The following is the syntax of a simple range-based for loop:

for (item_declaration : range_initializer) statement

For example:

std::array<int, 4> arr = {1, 2, 3, 4};
for (int x : arr) {
  std::cout << x << std::endl;
}

The effect of the code produced by the syntax above is equivalent to the following code:

std::array<int, 4> arr = {1, 2, 3, 4};
for (auto px = arr.begin(), ed = arr.end(); px != ed; ++px) {
  std::cout << *px << std::endl;
}

item-declaration#

This declares a variable used to receive the elements of the container on the right; the type of the variable must match the type of the sub-elements inside the container. You can use auto to deduce the type automatically; for complex types, auto& is commonly used to prevent copy overhead.

range-initializer#

The range-initializer can be any kind of iterable object (for example, an array, or an object of a class that defines the begin and end member functions). If an expression is placed there, the expression is also evaluated only once.

Example:

int a[] = {1, 1, 4, 5, 1, 4};
std::vector<int> b{1, 1, 4, 5, 1, 4};
std::map<std::string, int> c{{"114", 114}, {"514", 514}};
for (int i : a) std::cout << i;
for (auto i : b) std::cout << i;
// below, the type of i is std::pair<const std::string, int>&
for (auto& i : c) std::cout << i.first << i.second;
for (auto i : {1, 1, 4, 5, 1, 4}) std::cout << i;

Custom types supporting range-based for#

You only need to provide the begin and end member functions; the return type needs to support comparison, increment, and dereference (the * operator).

Here is an example:

#include <iostream>

struct C {
  int a[4];

  int* begin() { return a; }

  int* end() { return a + 4; }
};

int main() {
  C c = {1, 9, 2, 6};
  for (auto i : c) std::cout << i << " ";
  std::cout << std::endl;
  // output: 1 9 2 6
  return 0;
}

Init-statement (C++20)#

In C++20, an init-statement can also be used to achieve some functionality, such as a loop counter:

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
  std::vector<int> v = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5};

  for (int counter = 0; auto i : v)  // the init-statement (C++20)
    std::cout << counter++ << ' ' << i << std::endl;
}

Structured bindings (C++17)#

Structured bindings are a kind of syntactic sugar provided by C++17, which makes it convenient to extract sub-elements or references to sub-elements, like this:

struct C {
  int x{1}, y{2};
};

int arr[]{4, 5, 6};

auto [c1, c2] = C{};       // c1=1,c2=2; of type int
auto& [a1, a2, a3] = arr;  // a1=arr[0],a2=arr[1],a3=arr[2]; of type int&

Note the following points:

  • The number of variables declared on the left must match the number of sub-elements of the object on the right
  • The type declaration needs to use auto
  • You can use the & modifier to obtain references

You can write it like this when traversing a map container:

std::map<std::string, int> m = {{"k1", 1}, {"k2", 2}};

// use "auto&", no copy overhead
for (auto& [k, v] : m) {
  // the type of k is const std::string&, because the key carries a const qualifier
  // the type of v is int&
  std::cout << k << ' ' << v << std::endl;
}

std::tuple#

Tuples are defined in the header <tuple>; they are a generalization of std::pair and can store multiple values of different types. Let's look at an example:

#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>
#include <vector>

constexpr auto expr = 4 - 1;  // expr = 3

int main() {
  std::vector<int> vec = {1, 9, 2, 6, 0};
  std::tuple<int, int, std::string, std::vector<int>> tup =
      std::make_tuple(817, 114, "514", vec);

  // use get<> to fetch the sub-elements; what is inside the angle brackets must be an integral constant expression
  for (auto i : std::get<expr>(tup)) std::cout << i << " ";
  // the first element is numbered 0, so with std::get<3> we get a std::vector<int>
  return 0;
}

Since C++17, structured bindings can be used to extract the values, like this:

std::vector<int> vec = {1, 9, 2, 6, 0};
std::tuple<int, int, std::string, std::vector<int>> tup =
    std::make_tuple(817, 114, "514", vec);

auto& [a, b, c, d] = tup;  // C++17 Structured binding
std::cout << a << ' ' << b << c << std::endl;
std::cout << d.size() << ' ' << d[2] << std::endl;

Member functions#

Function Description
operator= assigns the contents of one tuple to another
swap swaps the contents of two tuples

Example:

constexpr std::tuple<int, int> tup = {1, 2};
std::tuple<int, int> tupA = {2, 3}, tupB;
tupB = tup;
tupB.swap(tupA);

Non-member functions#

Function Description
make_tuple creates a tuple object whose type is defined from the types of the arguments
std::get accesses the specified element tuple-style
std::tie assigns the values in the tuple to existing variables
operator== etc. compares the values in a tuple in lexicographic order
std::swap the specialized std::swap algorithm

Example:

std::tuple<int, int> tupA = {2, 3}, tupB;
tupB = std::make_tuple(1, 2);
std::swap(tupA, tupB);
std::cout << std::get<1>(tupA) << std::endl;
int x;
std::tie(x, std::ignore) = tupB;
std::cout << x << std::endl;

std::tie assigns the tuple elements to existing variables, and std::ignore can be used to skip elements that are not needed. Structured bindings directly declare new variables (supporting value/reference bindings) and must accept all the elements.

Function objects#

An object that can use the function call operator operator() is called a function object (FunctionObject).

It is not a language feature, but a concept or requirement, which is widely used in the standard library.

Function objects can roughly be divided into two categories:

  1. Function pointers
  2. Objects of classes that have overloaded the operator() operator

A lambda is a typical function object of the second kind: it stores what it captures in member variables and overloads the function call operator.

Lambda expressions#

Please refer to the Lambda expressions page.

std::function#

warningNote the performance overhead

std::function introduces a certain amount of performance overhead; according to Benchmark testing, it usually causes a performance loss of 2 to 3 times or more.

This is because it uses the technique of type erasure, which is usually implemented by means of the virtual function mechanism, and calling a virtual function introduces additional overhead.

Please consider using Lambda expressions or function objects instead.

std::function is a general-purpose function wrapper, defined in the header <functional>.

Instances of std::function can store, copy, and call any Callable object, which includes Lambda expressions, pointers to member functions, or other function objects.

If a std::function does not contain any callable object (for example, when it is default-constructed), calling it will throw the std::bad_function_call exception.

#include <functional>
#include <iostream>

struct Foo {
  Foo(int num) : num_(num) {}

  void print_add(int i) const { std::cout << num_ + i << '\n'; }

  int num_;
};

void print_num(int i) { std::cout << i << '\n'; }

struct PrintNum {
  void operator()(int i) const { std::cout << i << '\n'; }
};

int main() {
  // store a free function
  std::function<void(int)> f_display = print_num;
  f_display(-9);

  // store a lambda
  std::function<void()> f_display_42 = []() { print_num(42); };
  f_display_42();

  // store a call to a member function
  std::function<void(const Foo&, int)> f_add_display = &Foo::print_add;
  const Foo foo(314159);
  f_add_display(foo, 1);
  f_add_display(314159, 1);

  // store a call to a data member accessor
  std::function<int(Foo const&)> f_num = &Foo::num_;
  std::cout << "num_: " << f_num(foo) << '\n';

  // store a call to a function object
  std::function<void(int)> f_display_obj = PrintNum();
  f_display_obj(18);
}

Variadic function templates#

Before C++11, class templates and function templates could only accept a fixed number of template parameters. C++11 allows template parameters of any number and any type.

Only variadic function templates are briefly introduced here.

The function template fun declared in the following code can accept any number of template parameters of any type as its template parameters.

template <typename... Clazz>
void fun(Clazz... paras) {}

paras is a function parameter pack, which accepts zero or more function arguments. Clazz is a template parameter pack, which accepts zero or more template arguments (non-types, types, or templates); when marked with typename, it only accepts types.

It can be understood simply as follows:

  • A template parameter pack is usually some type names (but compile-time constants or template names can also be used)
  • A function parameter pack is usually some variable names

Now the fun function can be called like this:

fun();
fun(1);
fun(1, 2, 3);
fun(1, 0.0, "abc");

Parameter pack expansion#

Parameter pack expansion syntax#

Expanding a parameter pack is very simple: just use ..., and the elements will automatically be separated by ,. For example:

template <class A, class... C>
void func(A arg1, C... arg2) {
  // C is the template parameter pack
  tuple<A, C...>();  // expands to tuple<int, int, double, bool>();

  // arg2 is the function parameter pack
  func(arg2...);  // expands to func( 2, 1.1, true );
}

func(1, 2, 1.1, true);

When expanding a parameter pack, you can also attach the operations you need. For example:

template <class A, class... C>
void func(A arg1, C... arg2) {
  func((arg2 + 1)...);
  // expands to func( (2+1) , (1.1+1), (2.1f+1) );
}

func(1, 2, 1.1, 2.1f);

Terminating function#

The function above cannot run, because the number of parameters keeps decreasing and finally becomes an empty parameter list, which errors out.

We need to specify a termination condition; we can provide an ordinary function, like this:

void func() {}

template <class A, class... C>
void func(A arg1, C... arg2) {
  std::cout << arg1 << std::endl;
  func((arg2 + 1)...);
}

func(1, 2, 1.1, 2.1f);

This way, the template is called when the number of parameters is not 0, and the ordinary function is called for the empty parameter list, so it can run correctly.

Fold expressions (C++17)#

C++17 provides a convenient syntax for handling function parameter packs. Its syntax is as follows (it must be wrapped in parentheses):

  1. ( pack op ... ), which becomes (E1 op (... op (EN-1 op EN)))
  2. ( ... op pack ), which becomes (((E1 op E2) op ...) op EN)
  3. ( pack op ... op init ), which becomes (E1 op (... op (EN−1 op (EN op I))))
  4. ( init op ... op pack ), which becomes ((((I op E1) op E2) op ...) op EN)

A simple demonstration makes it easy to understand:

template <class... C>
void func(C... args) {
  (std::cout << ... << args) << std::endl;
  // syntax 4, equivalent to ↓
  // ( ( ( std::cout << 1 ) << 2.1 ) << true ) << std::endl;
  // Output: 12.11  note that true is printed as 1, because boolalpha is not specified here

  std::cout << (args && ...) << std::endl;
  // syntax 1, equivalent to ↓
  // std::cout << ( 1 && ( 2.1 && true ) ) ) << std::endl;
  // Output: 1
}

func(1, 2.1, true);

Abbreviated function templates (C++20)#

Since C++20, auto ... can be used directly as the parameter type to abbreviate function templates:

void func(auto... args) { (std::cout << ... << args) << std::endl; }

Note that it is essentially still a function template, equivalent to the following:

template <class... T>
void func(T... args) {
  (std::cout << ... << args) << std::endl;
}

The ranges library (C++20)#

The ranges library is an extension of the iterators and generic algorithms library that makes iterators and algorithms more powerful through composition, and reduces errors.

A range is a sequence that can be traversed, including arrays, containers, views, and so on.

When complex operations need to be performed on ranges such as containers, the ranges library can make writing algorithms easier and clearer.

View#

A view is a lightweight object that implements some algorithms through specific mechanisms (such as custom iterators), providing ranges with more ways of traversal to meet needs.

The ranges library has already implemented some commonly used views, roughly divided into two kinds:

  1. Range factories, used to construct some special ranges; using these factories skips the step of manually constructing containers, reduces overhead, and directly generates a range.
  2. Range adaptors, which provide a wide variety of traversal support; they can be called like functions, or connected through the pipe operator | to achieve chained calls.

As range adaptor closure objects, range adaptors are also function objects; they overload operator|, which allows them to be assembled together like pipes.

noteThe pipe operator

The | here should be understood as the pipe operator rather than the bitwise OR operator; this usage comes from pipes in Linux.

Even under complex operations, good readability can be maintained, with the following property:

If A, B, and C are some range adaptor closure objects, R is some range, and the other letters are possible valid arguments, then the expression

R | A(a) | B(b) | C(c, d)

is equivalent to

C(B(A(R, a), b), c, d)

The following takes ranges::take_view and ranges::iota_view as examples:

#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>

int main() {
  const auto even = [](int i) { return 0 == i % 2; };

  for (int i : std::views::iota(0, 6) | std::views::filter(even))
    std::cout << i << ' ';
}
  1. The range factory std::views::iota(0, 6) generates a range of the integer sequence from 0 to 5
  2. The range adaptor std::views::filter(even) filters the previous range, generating a range with only the even numbers left
  3. The two operations are linked with the pipe operator

The code above does not need to allocate extra heap space to store the range generated at each step; the actual generation and filtering operations happen during the traversal (more specifically, in the construction, increment, and dereference of the internal iterators), that is, zero overhead.

At the same time, the lifetime of the externally input range is identical to the lifetime of the internal elements of the range adaptor. If the external range (for example, a container or a range factory) has already been destroyed, then traversing a view of it afterwards has the same effect as dereferencing a dangling pointer, which is undefined behavior.

To avoid the situation above, it should be strictly required that the lifetime of an adaptor lies within the lifetime of any range it uses.

noteWhen a range is destroyed, all elements in the view dangle
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int main() {
  auto view = [] {
    vector<int> vec{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    return vec | std::views::filter([](int i) { return 0 == i % 2; });
  }();

  for (int i : view) cout << i << ' ';  // runtime undefined behavior

  return 0;
}

Constrained Algorithm#

C++20 provides constrained versions of most algorithms in the namespace std::ranges, which can specify a range with an iterator-sentinel pair or a single range as the argument, and support projections and pointer-to-member callable objects. In addition, the return types of most algorithms have been changed to return all potentially useful information computed during the execution of the algorithm.

These algorithms can be understood as improved versions of the old standard library algorithms; they are all function objects, providing friendlier overloads and argument type checking (based on concept). Let's first take the comparison of std::sort and ranges::sort as an example.

#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

int main() {
  vector<int> vec{4, 2, 5, 3, 1};

  sort(vec.begin(), vec.end());  // {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

  for (const int i : vec) cout << i << ", ";
  cout << '\n';

  ranges::sort(vec, ranges::greater{});  // {5, 4, 3, 2, 1}

  for (const int i : vec) cout << i << ", ";

  return 0;
}

ranges::sort and sort have the same algorithm implementation, but the former provides range-based overloads, making the arguments passed more concise. Most of the other algorithms under the std namespace also have corresponding range-based overload versions in the ranges namespace.

Using these range arguments, combined with the views from the previous section, allows us to maintain code readability while performing complex operations. Let's look at an example:

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>

using namespace std;

int main() {
  const auto& inputs = views::iota(0u, 9u);  // produces the integer sequence from 0 to 8
  const auto& chunks = inputs | views::chunk(3);  // splits the sequence into chunks, 3 elements per chunk
  const auto& cartesian_product =
      views::cartesian_product(chunks, chunks);  // computes the Cartesian product of the chunks with themselves

  for (const auto [l_chunk, r_chunk] : cartesian_product)
    // computes the sum of the integers of the two chunks in the Cartesian product
    cout << ranges::fold_left(l_chunk, 0u, plus{}) +
                ranges::fold_left(r_chunk, 0u, plus{})
         << ' ';
}
noteOutput:

6 15 24 15 24 33 24 33 42

  1. C++ Reference Manual

Chapter 31 · Advanced C++

Lambda Expressions

oi-wiki.org/lang/lambda.md

Note: Considering the practical realities of competitive programming, this article will not study the syntax comprehensively; it will only cover the parts that may be applied in competitive programming.

The syntax in this article follows the C++11 standard; syntax from later versions of the standard is mentioned as appropriate and will be specifically marked.

Lambda Expressions#

Lambda expressions take their name from the λ\lambdaλ calculus in mathematics and correspond directly to the lambda abstraction in it. When compiling, the compiler generates an anonymous function object according to the syntax, with the captured variables as its members, and the parameters and function body used to implement the operator() overload.

noteFunction Objects

A function object is a kind of class object, generally implemented by overloading operator(), so that it can be called like a function. Compared with using ordinary functions, function objects have many advantages, such as being able to save state and being passable as arguments to other functions.

The following is one syntax for a lambda:

[capture] (parameters) mutable -> return-type {statement}

A lambda expression is itself a class; when expanded, it looks like the following:

class Lambda_1 {
 private:
  Lambda_1() : capture-list(init-value) { }

 public:
  return-type operator()(parameters) const { statement }

 private:
  mutable capture-list
};

A lambda with an empty capture can be implicitly converted to a function pointer, for example:

void (*f)(int, int) = [](int, int) -> void {};

Below, we introduce each part of the syntax in turn.

statement (function body)#

The function body of a lambda expression is similar to that of an ordinary function: besides being able to access parameters and global variables, it can also access the variables that are captured.

capture (capture clause)#

A lambda begins with a capture clause, which specifies which variables are captured; the capture list can be empty, or it can specify the capture method: variables with the & symbol prefix are accessed by reference, and variables without that prefix are accessed by value.

We can also use the default capture mode to capture all the variables mentioned in the lambda: & means that all captured variables are accessed by reference, and = means that all captured variables are accessed by value.

After a default capture, it is still possible to explicitly specify the capture mode for particular variables.

If you need to access the outer variable a by reference and the outer variable b by value, then the following capture clauses can all do so:

  • [&a, b]
  • [b, &a]
  • [&, b]
  • [b, &]
  • [=, &a]

The capture list can also be used to declare variables, with the types deduced from the initializers, similar to declaring variables with auto.

Here are some common examples:

int a = 0;
auto f0 = []() { return a * 9; };   // Error, cannot access 'a'
auto f1 = [a]() { return a * 9; };  // OK, 'a' is "captured" by value
auto f2 = [&a]() { return a++; };   // OK, 'a' is "captured" by reference
auto f3 = [v = a + 1]() {
  return v + 1;
};  // OK, declares the variable v with an initializer, of the same type as a

// Note: when capturing by reference, make sure a has not been destroyed when the call happens
auto b = f2();  // f2 gets the value of a from the capture list; there is no need to pass a in as a parameter

generalized capture (capture with an initializer) (C++14)#

Since C++14, the capture can not only be used to capture outer variables, but can also be used to declare and initialize new variables, for example:

auto f1 = [val = 520]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type int and initial value 520; the return type is int

auto f2 = [val = 520LL]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type long long and initial value 520; the return type is long long

auto f3 = [val = "520"]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type const char* and initial value "520"; the return type is const char*

auto f4 = [val = "520"s]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, since C++14; requires using namespace std; or using namespace std::literals;
    // defines val with type std::string and initial value std::string("520"); the
    // return type is std::string

auto f5 = [val = std::string("520")]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type std::string and initial value std::string("520");
    // the return type is std::string

auto f6 = [val = std::vector<int>(3, 6)]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type std::vector<int>, size 3, elements filled with 6;
    // the return type is std::vector<int>

auto f7 = [val = 520]() -> int {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type int and initial value 520; the return type is int

auto f8 = [val = 520]() -> long long {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type int and initial value 520; the return type is long long

When defining a new variable, the initial value cannot be omitted; the type of the variable is determined by the type of the initial value, which is equivalent to:

auto val = init-value;

The following is an incorrect way of writing it:

auto f = [val]() { return val; };  // Error: 'val' was not declared in this
                                   // scope, identifier "val" is undefined

The initial value can also be an outer variable, for example:

int value = 520;
auto f = [val = value]() { return val; };
std::cout << f();  // Output: 520

val can also be a reference type, referring to an outer variable; in this way, you can give an alias to an outer variable captured by reference, for example:

int value = 520;

auto f = [&val = value]() {
  return val;
};  // OK, defines val with type int&, return type int; equivalent to int& val = value;

std::cout << f() << '\n';  // Output: 520

value = 1314;

std::cout << f() << '\n';  // Output: 1314

Capturing outer variables and defining new variables can be used at the same time.

If you want to modify a new variable defined in the capture from inside the lambda expression, you need to use the mutable keyword; if it is a reference, this is not needed, for example:

int value = 520;

{
  auto f = [val = value]() mutable -> int {
    return val = 1314;
  };  // mutable is needed
  auto val_f = f();
  std::cout << value << ' ' << val_f << std::endl;  // Output: 520 1314
}

{
  auto f = [&val = value]() -> int { return val = 1314; };  // mutable is not needed
  auto val_f = f();
  std::cout << value << ' ' << val_f << std::endl;  // Output: 1314 1314
}

For details, see mutable (mutable specification).

The lifetime of a variable defined in the capture follows the receiver of the lambda expression — the variable fff in the examples above — because a lambda is in fact a class, and everything in the capture is a private member variable of that class, for example:

int main() {
  auto f = [val = 0]() mutable -> int { return ++val; };  // val is constructed and initialized

  std::cout << f() << '\n';  // Output: 1
  std::cout << f() << '\n';  // Output: 2
  std::cout << f() << '\n';  // Output: 3
}  // val is destroyed along with f

parameters (parameter list)#

In most cases, it is similar to the parameter list of a function, for example:

int x[] = {5, 1, 7, 6, 1, 4, 2};
std::sort(x, x + 7, [](int a, int b) { return (a > b); });
for (auto i : x) std::cout << i << " ";

This will print the x array sorted from largest to smallest.

Since the parameters (parameter list) are optional, if you do not pass parameters to the lambda, its declaration does not include mutable, and there is no trailing return type, the empty parentheses can be omitted.

noteParameters Declared with <code>auto</code>

After C++14, if a parameter is declared with the auto type, a generic lambda expression is constructed.

Explicit Object Parameter (C++23)#

Since C++23, the explicit object parameter can be used in a lambda's parameters.

auto nth_fibonacci = [](this auto self, unsigned n) -> unsigned {
  return n < 2 ? n : self(n - 1) + self(n - 2);
};

cout << nth_fibonacci(10u);

mutable (mutable specification)#

It allows the function body to modify variables captured by value.

int a = 0;
auto by_value = [a]() mutable { ++a; };
auto by_ref = [&a] { ++a; };

by_value();
by_ref();

After by_value() finishes executing, the captured member a of by_value is 1, but the outer variable a is still 0. After by_ref() finishes executing, the value of the outer a becomes 1.

return-type (return type)#

Used to specify the return type of the lambda expression. If it is omitted, the return type will be deduced automatically (the behavior is the same as for a function whose return value is declared with auto).

When there are multiple return statements and the deduced types are inconsistent, a compilation error will occur.

auto lam = [](int a, int b) -> int { return 0; };

auto x1 = [](int i) { return i; };

auto x2 = [](bool condition) {
  if (condition) return 1;
  return 1.0;
};  // Error, inconsistent deduced types

Generic Lambda (C++14)#

Using auto as the parameter type, you can construct a generic lambda.

auto add = [](auto a, auto b) { return a + b; };

In cpp insights you can observe the lambda class definition generated by the compiler:

class add_lambda {
 public:
  template <class T, class U>
  auto operator()(T a, U b) const {
    return a + b;
  }
};

add_lambda add{};

Both parameter declarations of add use auto, corresponding to the two template parameters T and U of the operator() function template of the add_lambda class.

Recursion in Lambdas#

Let us first look at an example that fails to compile:

int n = 10;

auto dfs = [&](int i) -> void {
  if (i == n)
    return;
  else
    dfs(i + 1);  // Error: a variable declared with an auto type specifier
                 // cannot appear in its own initializer
};

Here we are trying to capture dfsdfsdfs in the capture list, but there is a problem: the type of dfsdfsdfs is auto, so the type of dfsdfsdfs is deduced only after the type deduction on the right-hand side of the equals sign completes, while for the lambda to capture dfsdfsdfs, the type of dfsdfsdfs must first be determined before its reference variable can be created — well, this falls into a chicken-and-egg problem.

How can this problem be solved?

  1. Explicitly specify the type of dfsdfsdfs; std::function can be used as a substitute.

    exampleModify the code above to:
    int n = 10;

std::function<void(int)> dfs = [&](int i) -> void {
  if (i == n)
    return;
  else
    dfs(i + 1);  // OK
};

dfs(1);
    warningRecursion implemented with <code>std::function</code> is not recommended

    The type erasure of std::function usually requires allocating extra memory, while the addressing operations caused by indirect calls further reduce performance.

    In the Benchmark test, using the Clang 17 compiler with libc++ as the standard library, the std::function implementation was about 2.5 times slower than the lambda implementation of the recursion.

    noteTest code
    #include <algorithm>
#include <functional>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>

using namespace std;

const auto& nums = [] {
  random_device rd;
  mt19937 gen{rd()};
  array<unsigned, 32> arr{};

  std::iota(arr.begin(), arr.end(), 0u);
  ranges::shuffle(arr, gen);

  return arr;
}();

static void std_function_fib(benchmark::State& state) {
  std::function<int(int)> fib;

  fib = [&](int n) { return n <= 2 ? 1 : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); };

  unsigned i = 0;

  for (auto _ : state) {
    auto res = fib(nums[i]);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(res);

    ++i;

    if (i == nums.size()) i = 0;
  }
}

BENCHMARK(std_function_fib);

static void template_lambda_fib(benchmark::State& state) {
  auto n_fibonacci = [](const auto& self, int n) -> int {
    return n <= 2 ? 1 : self(self, n - 1) + self(self, n - 2);
  };

  unsigned i = 0;

  for (auto _ : state) {
    auto res = n_fibonacci(n_fibonacci, nums[i]);
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(res);

    ++i;

    if (i == nums.size()) i = 0;
  }
}

BENCHMARK(template_lambda_fib);
    2. Obtain dfsdfsdfs not by capturing it, but by passing it as a function parameter.

    exampleModify the code above to:
    int n = 10;

// If a parameter in the parameter list has type auto, the operator() function of
// this Lambda class will be defined as a template function, which can be instantiated later at call time
auto dfs = [&](auto& self,
               int i) -> void  // [&] only captures the variables that are used, so it does not capture auto dfs
{
  if (i == n)
    return;
  else
    self(self, i + 1);  // OK
};

dfs(dfs, 1);
    noteThe difference between <code>auto self</code>, <code>auto&amp; self</code>, and <code>auto&amp;&amp; self</code>:

    In theory, both auto& self and auto&& self use only 888 bytes (the size of a pointer) for parameter passing, and no other copies happen. The specifics depend on the compiler's implementation of lambdas and the corresponding optimizations. Using auto self, on the other hand, causes an object copy; the size of the copy depends on the elements in the capture list, because they are all private member variables of this Lambda class.

    3. You can manually expand the Lambda class, or write something similar, so that the type of dfsdfsdfs can be declared directly.

    exampleModify the code above to:
    int n = 10;

class Lambda_1 {
 public:
  auto operator()(int i) const -> void {
    if (i == n)
      return;
    else
      (*this)(i + 1);  // OK
  }

  explicit Lambda_1(int& __n) : n(__n) {}

 private:
  int& n;
} dfs(n);

dfs(1);
    4. If the lambda does not capture any variables, we can also make use of function pointers.

    If the lambda does not capture any variables, it can be implicitly converted to a function pointer. At the same time, the lambda can then also be declared static, and the function pointer type can also be declared static. This way, the lambda can access the function pointer without needing to capture it, thereby achieving recursion.

    exampleExample
    static unsigned (*fptr)(unsigned);

static const auto lambda = [](const unsigned a) {
  return a < 2 ? a : (*fptr)(a - 2) + (*fptr)(a - 1);
};

static auto init = [] {
  fptr = +lambda;
  // Or
  // fptr = static_cast<unsigned (*)(unsigned)>(lambda);
  return 0;
}();

cout << lambda(10);

    Applications of Lambda Expressions#

As a Predicate for Standard Library Algorithms#

Sorting from largest to smallest:

std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a > b; });

Using std::find_if to find the first element greater than 3:

std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
auto it = std::find_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a) { return a > 3; });

Controlling the Lifetime of Intermediate Variables#

In competitive programming, we encounter scenarios like this one: the initialization of a variable needs to use previously declared variables, and its initialization process in turn generates intermediate variables that take up considerable space.

We want these intermediate variables to be destroyed as soon as possible, to reduce memory consumption. Here, we can use a lambda to control the lifetime of these intermediate variables.

void solution(const vector<int>& input) {
  int b = [&] {
    vector<int> large_objects(input.size());
    int c = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < large_objects.size(); ++i)
      large_objects[i] = i + input[i];

    for (int i = 0; i < input.size(); ++i) c += large_objects[input[i]];

    return c;
  }();

  // ...
}

Compared with using a block scope, a lambda allows us to use a return value, making the code more concise; compared with a function, we do not need to come up with extra names or declare the various captured parameters, making the code more compact.

References#

  • cppreference-lambda
  • Stackoverflow: Overhead with std::function

Chapter 32 · Advanced C++

pb_ds: Introduction · pb_ds

oi-wiki.org/lang/pb-ds/index.md

author: HeRaNO, Xeonacid, saffahyjp

The full name of the pb_ds library is Policy-Based Data Structures.

The pb_ds library encapsulates many data structures, such as hash tables, balanced binary trees, tries, and heaps (priority queues).

Just like vector, set, and map, its components all conform to the relevant STL interface specifications. Some of them (such as the priority queue) contain all the functionality of the corresponding STL components, but offer more than the STL.

pb_ds can only be used with compilers that use libstdc++ as the standard library.

You can use begin() and end() to obtain an iterator and traverse the container

You can increase_key, decrease_key, and erase a single element

Since the main content of the pb_ds library is in the __gnu_pbds namespace, which begins with an underscore, its compliance in NOI series activities had long been uncertain. On September 1, 2021, according to the Supplementary Notice on Restrictions on the Use of Programming Languages in NOI Series Activities, which permits the use of library functions and macros whose names begin with an underscore (except for library functions and macros with explicitly forbidden operations), the compliance of using the pb_ds library in NOI series activities gained a documented basis.

References: The Application of the C++ pb_ds Library in OI

pb_ds: Heaps · pb_ds

oi-wiki.org/lang/pb-ds/pq.md

author: Xeonacid, ouuan, Ir1d, WAAutoMaton, Chrogeek, abc1763613206, Planet6174, i-Yirannn, opsiff, GoodCoder666

__gnu_pbds::priority_queue#

Appendix: official documentation — complexity and constant-factor tests

#include <ext/pb_ds/priority_queue.hpp>
using namespace __gnu_pbds;
__gnu_pbds::priority_queue<T, Compare, Tag, Allocator>

Template Parameters#

  • T: the type of the elements stored
  • Compare: a type providing a strict weak ordering comparison
  • Tag: the five different heaps provided by __gnu_pbds; the Tag parameter defaults to pairing_heap_tag. The five are:
    • pairing_heap_tag: pairing heap The official documentation considers the pairing heap to perform best for non-native elements (such as custom structs/std::string/pair)
    • binary_heap_tag: binary heap The official documentation considers the binary heap to perform best for native elements, but the performance in the author's own tests was not that good
    • binomial_heap_tag: binomial heap The binomial heap performs better than the binary heap on the join operation, but the complexity of its operation of taking the top element is higher than that of the binary heap
    • rc_binomial_heap_tag: redundant-counter binomial heap
    • thin_heap_tag: a tag that is the same as the Fibonacci heap in everything except the complexity of join
  • Allocator: the allocator; since it rarely appears in OI, it will not be covered here

Since this article is only intended for students learning competitive programming, the last four tags will only have their complexities briefly introduced, while the first one will have its member functions and usage explained.

The author's tests of the basic heap operations on a local Core i5 @3.1 GHz on macOS, combined with GNU's official complexity tests and Dijkstra tests, all indicate that: at least for OI contestants, the four tags other than the pairing heap are of little value: either they are useless, or their constant factors are so large that they are worse than the std ones, and they may even cause MLE. Therefore, only the default pairing heap is recommended here. Likewise, the pairing heap also outperforms make_heap() from the algorithm library.

Construction#

You must specify the namespace, because the class name duplicates the one in std.

// __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int>;
// __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>>;
// __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, pairing_heap_tag>;
__gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int>::point_iterator id;  // point-type iterator
// Both modify and push return a point_iterator; its usage is explained in detail below
id = q.push(1);

Member Functions#

  • push(): pushes an element onto the heap and returns an iterator to that element's position.
  • pop(): pops the top element off the heap.
  • top(): returns the top element of the heap.
  • size() returns the number of elements.
  • empty() returns whether it is non-empty.
  • modify(point_iterator, const key): changes the key at the iterator's position to the passed-in key, and sorts the underlying storage structure.
  • erase(point_iterator): erases the key at the iterator's position from the heap.
  • join(__gnu_pbds::priority_queue &other): merges other into *this and clears other.

The tag used determines the time complexity of each operation:

push pop modify erase Join
pairing_heap_tag O(1)O(1)O(1) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) O(1)O(1)O(1)
binary_heap_tag worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n)
binomial_heap_tag worst Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) amortized O(1)O(1)O(1) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n))
rc_binomial_heap_tag O(1)O(1)O(1) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n))
thin_heap_tag O(1)O(1)O(1) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) worst Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) amortized O(1)O(1)O(1) worst Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n) amortized Θ(log⁡(n))\Theta(\log(n))Θ(log(n)) Θ(n)\Theta(n)Θ(n)

Example#

#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <ext/pb_ds/priority_queue.hpp>
#include <iostream>
using namespace __gnu_pbds;
// Since this is aimed at OI contestants, this article uses the common heap: pairing_heap_tag as the example
// For a better reading experience, define the macro as follows:
using pair_heap = __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int>;
pair_heap q1;  // max-heap, pairing heap
pair_heap q2;
pair_heap::point_iterator id;  // an iterator

int main() {
  id = q1.push(1);
  // elements in the heap : [1];
  for (int i = 2; i <= 5; i++) q1.push(i);
  // elements in the heap :  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
  std::cout << q1.top() << std::endl;
  // output : 5;
  q1.pop();
  // elements in the heap : [1, 2, 3, 4];
  id = q1.push(10);
  // elements in the heap : [1, 2, 3, 4, 10];
  q1.modify(id, 1);
  // elements in the heap :  [1, 1, 2, 3, 4];
  std::cout << q1.top() << std::endl;
  // output : 4;
  q1.pop();
  // elements in the heap : [1, 1, 2, 3];
  id = q1.push(7);
  // elements in the heap : [1, 1, 2, 3, 7];
  q1.erase(id);
  // elements in the heap : [1, 1, 2, 3];
  q2.push(1), q2.push(3), q2.push(5);
  // elements in q1 : [1, 1, 2, 3], elements in q2 : [1, 3, 5];
  q2.join(q1);
  // q1 has no elements, elements in q2 : [1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 5];
}

__gnu_pbds Iterator Invalidation Guarantees (invalidation_guarantee)#

In the example above, as well as in some practice (such as writing single-source shortest path and similar algorithms with the pb-ds heaps of this chapter), it is often necessary to store and use iterators into the heap (such as __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int>::point_iterator).

However, for example, with the different Tag parameters of __gnu_pbds::priority_queue, the underlying implementations are not the same, and the conditions under which iterators are invalidated also differ. According to the design of the __gnu_pbds library, there are the following three cases, derived from top to bottom:

  1. Basic invalidation guarantee (basic_invalidation_guarantee): when the container is not modified, point-type iterators (point_iterator), pointers, and references (key/value) remain valid.

  2. Point invalidation guarantee (point_invalidation_guarantee): after the container is modified, point-type iterators (point_iterator), pointers, and references (key/value) remain valid as long as the corresponding elements have not been deleted from the container.

  3. Range invalidation guarantee (range_invalidation_guarantee): after the container is modified, besides the properties of (2), any range-type iterators (including the return values of begin() and end()) are correct. Tags with the range invalidation guarantee include rb_tree_tag and splay_tree_tag for __gnu_pbds::tree, as well as pat_trie_tag for __gnu_pbds::trie.

From running the code below, we can see that except for binary_heap_tag, which has basic_invalidation_guarantee and whose iterators are invalidated after modification, the rest all have point_invalidation_guarantee, which can meet the requirement that point-type iterators (point_iterator) are not invalidated after modification.

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
#include <ext/pb_ds/assoc_container.hpp>
#include <ext/pb_ds/priority_queue.hpp>
using namespace __gnu_pbds;
#include <cxxabi.h>

template <typename T>
void print_invalidation_guarantee() {
  using gute = __gnu_pbds::container_traits<T>::invalidation_guarantee;
  cout << abi::__cxa_demangle(typeid(gute).name(), 0, 0, 0) << endl;
}

int main() {
  using pairing =
      __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, pairing_heap_tag>;
  using binary = __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, binary_heap_tag>;
  using binomial =
      __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, binomial_heap_tag>;
  using rc_binomial =
      __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, rc_binomial_heap_tag>;
  using thin = __gnu_pbds::priority_queue<int, greater<int>, thin_heap_tag>;
  print_invalidation_guarantee<pairing>();
  print_invalidation_guarantee<binary>();
  print_invalidation_guarantee<binomial>();
  print_invalidation_guarantee<rc_binomial>();
  print_invalidation_guarantee<thin>();
  return 0;
}
