Chapter 34 · Advanced C++

pb_ds: Balanced Trees · pb_ds

oi-wiki.org/lang/pb-ds/tree.md

__gnu_pbds::tree#

Appendix: official documentation

#include <ext/pb_ds/assoc_container.hpp>  // tree is defined here, so this header must be included
#include <ext/pb_ds/tree_policy.hpp>
using namespace __gnu_pbds;
__gnu_pbds::tree<Key, Mapped, Cmp_Fn = std::less<Key>, Tag = rb_tree_tag,
                 Node_Update = null_tree_node_update,
                 Allocator = std::allocator<char>>

Template Parameters#

  • Key: the type of the elements stored; if you want to store multiple identical Key elements, you need to use an approach such as std::pair and struct, together with the lower_bound and upper_bound member functions for lookup
  • Mapped: the mapping rule (Mapped-Policy) type; if you want to indicate that the associative container is a set, similar to storing elements in std::set, fill in null_type here — in older versions of g++ this is null_mapped_type; if you want to indicate that the associative container is a set with values, similar to storing elements in std::map, fill in the Value type similar to that of std::map<Key, Value> here
  • Cmp_Fn: the key comparison functor, e.g. std::less<Key>
  • Tag: which underlying data structure type to use; the default is rb_tree_tag. __gnu_pbds provides three different balanced trees, namely:
    • rb_tree_tag: red-black tree; this one is generally used, and the performance of the latter two is generally not as good as the red-black tree's
    • splay_tree_tag: splay tree
    • ov_tree_tag: ordered vector tree; it is just an ordered structure implemented with a vector, similar to implementing a balanced tree with a sorted vector, and its performance depends on whether the data is out to get you
  • Node_Update: the strategy used to update nodes; the default is null_node_update, and to use the order_of_key and find_by_order methods, tree_order_statistics_node_update is required
  • Allocator: the allocator type

Construction#

__gnu_pbds::tree<std::pair<int, int>, __gnu_pbds::null_type,
                 std::less<std::pair<int, int>>, __gnu_pbds::rb_tree_tag,
                 __gnu_pbds::tree_order_statistics_node_update>
    trr;

Member Functions#

  • insert(x): inserts an element x into the tree, returning std::pair<point_iterator, bool>, where the first element is an iterator to the insertion position, and the second element indicates whether the insertion succeeded.
  • erase(x): erases an element/iterator x from the tree. If x is an iterator, it returns an iterator pointing to the one after x (if x is end(), it returns end()); if x is a Key, it returns whether the erasure succeeded (if it does not exist, the erasure fails).
  • order_of_key(x): returns the number of elements strictly less than x (using Cmp_Fn as the comparison logic), i.e. the rank starting from 000.
  • find_by_order(x): returns an iterator to the element corresponding to the rank under the Cmp_Fn comparison.
  • lower_bound(x): returns an iterator to the first element not less than x (using Cmp_Fn as the comparison logic).
  • upper_bound(x): returns an iterator to the first element strictly greater than x (using Cmp_Fn as the comparison logic).
  • join(x): merges the tree x into the current tree, and the tree x is emptied (you must ensure that the comparison functions and element types of the two trees are the same).
  • split(x,b): compares with Cmp_Fn; elements less than or equal to x belong to the current tree, and the rest belong to the tree b.
  • empty(): returns whether it is empty.
  • size(): returns the size.
warningNote

The join(x) function requires that the key range of the merged-in tree and the key range of the tree being merged into be disjoint (that is, all values in the merged-in tree must be entirely greater than/less than all values in the current tree); otherwise a join_error exception is thrown.

To merge two trees whose key ranges overlap, you need to insert the elements of one tree into the other tree one by one.

Example#

// Common Header Simple over C++11
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;
using ull = unsigned long long;
using ld = long double;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
#include <ext/pb_ds/assoc_container.hpp>
#include <ext/pb_ds/tree_policy.hpp>
__gnu_pbds::tree<pair<int, int>, __gnu_pbds::null_type, less<pair<int, int>>,
                 __gnu_pbds::rb_tree_tag,
                 __gnu_pbds::tree_order_statistics_node_update>
    trr;

int main() {
  int cnt = 0;
  trr.insert(make_pair(1, cnt++));
  trr.insert(make_pair(5, cnt++));
  trr.insert(make_pair(4, cnt++));
  trr.insert(make_pair(3, cnt++));
  trr.insert(make_pair(2, cnt++));
  // elements in the tree {(1,0), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1)}

  auto it = trr.lower_bound(make_pair(2, 0));
  trr.erase(it);
  // elements in the tree {(1,0), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1)}

  // output the first of the element at rank 1 among ranks 0 1 2 3
  auto it2 = trr.find_by_order(1);
  cout << (*it2).first << endl;  // output: 3

  // output its rank
  int pos = trr.order_of_key(*it2);
  cout << pos << endl;  // output: 1

  // split trr by it2
  decltype(trr) newtr;
  trr.split(*it2, newtr);
  for (auto i = newtr.begin(); i != newtr.end(); ++i) {
    cout << (*i).first << ' ';  // output: 4 5
  }
  cout << endl;

  // merge the tree newtr into the tree trr, and the tree newtr is emptied.
  trr.join(newtr);
  for (auto i = trr.begin(); i != trr.end(); ++i) {
    cout << (*i).first << ' ';  // output: 1 3 4 5
  }
  cout << endl;
  cout << newtr.size() << endl;  // output: 0

  return 0;
}

References#

  • Tree-Based Containers
  • The implementation of the join function in GCC 14.1.0
  • The implementation of the erase function in GCC 14.1.0

Chapter 35 · Advanced C++

Compiler Optimizations

oi-wiki.org/lang/optimizations.md

author: inclyc

The commonly used programming language in the OI world is C++. Since you have chosen this language, you are destined to deal with compilers and language standards. As everyone knows, C++ is extremely chaotic and evil; this article aims to provide practical compiler-related knowledge, enough for use in contests.

Introduction to Compiler Optimizations#

What Is Optimization#

According to the as-if rule, improvements are made to the program's running speed and the size of its executable file while keeping the semantics unchanged.

Common Compiler Optimizations#

Constant Folding#

Constant folding, also known as constant propagation: if an expression can be determined to be a constant, constant propagation can be performed before its next definition.

int x = 1;
int y = x;  // x = 1, => y = 1
x = 3;
int z = 2 * y;   // z => 2 * y = 2 * 1 = 2
int y2 = x * 2;  // x = 3, => y2 = 6

This code can be transformed at compile time into:

int x = 1;
int y = 1;
x = 3;
int z = 2;
int y2 = 6;

Example: https://godbolt.org/z/oEfY35TTd

Deadcode Elimination#

As the name suggests, code that is not used is deleted.

int test() {
  int a = 233;
  int b = a * 2;
  int c = 234;
  return c;
}

will be transformed into

int test() { return 234; }

Note that this code has first undergone constant folding, so the return value can be determined to be 234; a and b are inactive variables and are therefore deleted.

Loop Rotate#

The loop is transformed from "for" form into "do-while" form, with one more conditional check added in front. This transformation mainly serves as preparation for other transformations.

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
  auto v = *p;
  use(v);
}

is transformed into

if (0 < n) {
  do {
    auto v = *p;
    use(v);
    ++i;
  } while (i < n);
}

Loop Invariant Code Motion#

Based on alias analysis, code inside the loop that has been proven to be invariant (it may involve memory accesses, load/store, and therefore depends on alias analysis) is hoisted out of the loop body, so that there is less code inside the loop body.

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
  auto v = *p;
  use(v);
}

Intuitively, this code can be hoisted into:

auto v = *p;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
  use(v);
}

But in reality, if n <= 0, this loop is never entered, yet we have executed one extra instruction (which may have side effects!). Therefore, loops are usually rotated into do-while form, which makes it convenient to insert a "loop guard". Loop invariant code motion is performed afterwards.

if (0 < n) {  // loop guard
  auto v = *p;
  do {
    use(v);
    ++i;
  } while (i < n);
}

Loop Unroll#

A loop consists of a loop body and various kinds of branch statements, which requires modern CPUs to perform a certain amount of branch prediction. Directly unrolling the loop trades a certain amount of code size for running time.

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  a[i] = i;
}

is transformed into:

a[0] = 0;
a[1] = 1;
a[2] = 2;

Loop Unswitching#

Loop unswitching moves the conditional inside the loop to outside of the loop, and then places two loops under the two external conditions respectively; this can increase the potential for loop vectorization and parallelization (simple loops are usually easier to vectorize).

// clang-format off
void before(int x) {
  for(;/* i in some range */;) {
    /* A */;
    if (/* condition */ x % 2) {
      /* B */;
    }
    /* C */;
  }
}

void after(int x) {
  if (/* condition */ x % 2) {
    for(;/* i in some range */;) {
      /* A */;
      /* B */; // execute B directly, without the loop condition check
      /* C */;
    }
  } else {
     for(;/* i in some range */;) {
      /* A */; 
               // do not execute B
      /* C */;
    }
  }
}

Code Layout Optimizations#

While a program is executing, its execution paths can be divided into cold and hot paths. When the CPU jumps to execute, in the vast majority of cases this is not as fast as executing directly in sequence; the latter is usually called "fallthrough" by compiler writers. Correspondingly, code that is often executed becomes hot code, and the opposite becomes cold code. In OI code, if a section is a special boundary-condition check inside a loop, or exception handling, or similar logic, then that part of the code is cold code.

A basic block is the fundamental structure of control flow; a procedure is composed of a number of basic blocks, forming a directed graph. During the process of generating an executable file, the compiler needs to arrange a layout for placing the basic blocks, and how to arrange the layout is the focus of this optimization.

In principle, placing hot code together should be preferred, and cold code kept apart. The reason is that this makes better use of the instruction cache: the locality of hot code is better.

// clang-format off
int hotpath; // <-- hot!
if (/* boundary condition */ false) {
    // <-- cold!
}
int hotpath_again;  // <-- hot!

Basic Block Placement#

We use labels to express a kind of "pseudo-machine code"; this C++ program has two possible translations:

noteLayout 1
// clang-format off
hotblock1:
    Stmts; // <-- hot!
    if (/* boundary condition does not hold */ true)
        goto hotblock2; // often!     ------+
coldblock:                           /*   |   */
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |  spans a large number of instructions, at a high cost!
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
hotblock2:                          /*    |   */
    Stmts; // <- hot!           <----------+
Another layout is:

noteLayout 2
// clang-format off
hotblock1:
    Stmts; // <-- hot!
    if (/* boundary condition */ false)
        goto coldblock; // rarely happens
hotblock2:                         /*   |  low cost! */
    Stmts; // <- hot!  <-----------------+
coldblock:
    Stmt; // <- cold
    Stmt; // <- cold
    Stmt; // <- cold
    Stmt; // <- cold
    Stmt; // <- cold
We see that in the latter layout, the two hot code blocks are placed together, and the execution efficiency is better.

To tell the compiler whether a branch is likely to be executed, you can use the C++20 [[likely]] and [[unlikely]]:https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/attributes/likely

If the contest has not adopted a standard of C++20 or above, you can make use of __builtin_expect (GNU Extension).

#define likely(x) __builtin_expect(!!(x), 1)
#define unlikely(x) __builtin_expect(!!(x), 0)

if (unlikely(/* some boundary condition check */ false)) {
  // cold code
}

Hot Cold Splitting#

A procedure contains both cold and hot paths, and when the cold code is long, a better approach is to make the cold code a function call instead of blocking the hot path. This also reminds us not to be too clever and make all functions inline. Cold code obstructs execution speed far more than a function call does.

noteA Bad Code Layout
// clang-format off
void foo() {
      // clang-format off
hotblock1:
    Stmts; // <-- hot!
    if (/* boundary condition does not hold */ true)
        goto hotblock2; // often!     ------+
coldblock:                           /*   |   */
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |  spans a large number of instructions, at a high cost!
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
    Stmt; // <- cold                      |
hotblock2:                          /*    |   */
    Stmts; // <- hot!           <----------+
}
noteA Good Code Layout
// clang-format off
void foo() {
hotblock1:
  Stmts;  // <-- hot!
  if (/* boundary condition */ false)
    coldBlock();  // split the cold code out, making the hot path more cache-friendly
hotblock2:
  Stmts;  // <- hot!
}

void coldBlock() {
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
  Stmt;  // <- cold
}
Hot/cold code splitting is actually the reverse operation of function inlining. The existence of this optimization shows us that inlining functions does not necessarily make the program run faster. If the inlined code is cold code, it can even make the program run slower! Some compilers have a compilation option for forced inlining, but using it is not recommended. Inside the compiler there is a static analysis process that computes the probability of each basic block and branch, as well as a cost model related to function calls, and decides whether to inline on that basis; deciding whether to inline yourself is not necessarily better than the compiler's decision.

In fact, without additional information, the compiler usually assumes that the probability of a branch being taken is the same as the probability of it not being taken, and propagates the hotness and coldness of each control-flow path on this basis. Part of PGO (Profile Guided Optimization) is to obtain the program's real branch probabilities in a real environment through several performance tests and experiments; this information can make the code layout better.

Function Inlining#

A function call usually needs registers and the stack to pass arguments; the caller and the callee both need to save some register state, and this process is usually called the calling convention. A function call therefore causes some loss of time, and inlining a function means writing the function directly into the caller's procedure without a real function call.

int add(int x) { return x + 1; }

int foo() {
  int a = 1;
  a = add(a);
}

add() can be inlined into foo():

int foo() {
  int a = 1;
  a = a + 1;  // <-- the body of add(), without argument passing
}

always_inline,__force_inline#

https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html#always-inline-force-inline

Some compilers provide a way to manually inline function calls: adding __attribute__((always_inline)) in front of the function. Using this is not necessarily faster than a function call; at this point the compiler trusts that the programmer has good enough judgment.

Tail Call Optimization#

When a function call is located at the tail position of a function body, this kind of function call is called a tail call. For this special form of call, some special optimizations can be performed. The vast majority of architectures have a Frame Pointer (a.k.a FP) and a Stack Pointer (a.k.a SP), which maintain the call frames of functions; and if the call is at the tail of the function, we can skip keeping the outer function's call record and directly replace it with the inner function.

Replacing Function Calls with Jump Instructions#

Under the vast majority of architectures, a function call needs to save the position of the current program counter $pc and save several caller-saved registers, in order to return to where it left off. A tail call does not need this process and is directly translated into a jump instruction, because a tail recursion never returns to the position where the function was running.

A simple example: https://godbolt.org/z/e7b1safaW

int test(int a);

int tailCall(int x) { return test(x); }
tailCall(int):                           ; @tailCall(int)
        jmp     test(int)@PLT                    ; TAILCALL

Automatic Tail-Recursion Rewriting#

If a function's tail call is to itself, then the function is tail-recursive. Broadly speaking, indirect recursion (recursion formed jointly by two or more functions) in which all the calls are tail calls also falls within the scope of tail recursion. Tail recursion can be optimized by the compiler into a non-recursive form, reducing the extra stack overhead and the cost of function calls. Many competitive programming contestants are keen on writing non-recursive code; without optimizations enabled this can greatly optimize the constants of the code, but with optimizations enabled, the binary quality of recursive code is no different from that of handwritten code.

int fac(int n) {
  if (n < 2) return 1;
  return /* uses */ n * fac(n - 1); /* uses the variable n, so tail-recursion optimization cannot be applied directly! */
}

Note that this function is not tail-recursive, but it can be rewritten as:

int fac(int acc, int n) {
  if (n < 2) return acc;
  return fac(acc * n, n - 1);
}

The new code is tail-recursive.

Modern compilers can automatically complete this process for you: if your code has the chance to be rewritten as tail recursion, the compiler can recognize this form and then complete the rewriting.

Tail-Recursion Elimination -Rpass=tailcallelim#

Since the function is already tail-recursive, the recursive statement can be deleted directly; through a certain amount of static analysis, the function is converted directly into a non-recursive form. We will not dig into how compiler writers achieve this here; from practical experience, for the vast majority of OI code, if a recursive version and a non-recursive version both exist, the code can generally be automatically optimized into the non-recursive version. Here are some concrete examples for the reader:

note<a href="https://godbolt.org/z/8Wb6WEnzv">GCD</a>
int gcd(int a, int b) { return b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a; }
note<a href="https://godbolt.org/z/4enof6Wcb">Fibonacci sequence</a>
// expand the fib(n - 2) term
// fib(n - 1) cannot be transformed into non-recursive form; the optimized code is still exponential
int fib(int n) {
  if (n < 2) return 1;
  return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}
note<a href="https://godbolt.org/z/n64e75xrf">Factorial</a>
// expanded into a scalar loop, then auto-vectorized; the generated code is SIMD
unsigned fac(unsigned n) {
  if (n < 2) return 1;
  return n * fac(n - 1);
}
The assembly of these functions after optimization is completely identical to the non-recursive version; the recursion is directly eliminated. For OI contestants, you can confidently write recursive versions of all kinds of algorithms with O2 enabled — there will be no difference from the non-recursive version. If the function you write cannot itself be rewritten into non-recursive form, the compiler can do nothing about it.

Strength Reduction#

A common compiler optimization. The simplest example is turning x * 2 into x << 1; the second form is quite common in OI. The compiler automatically performs similar optimizations: with optimizations turned on, x * 2 and x << 1 are completely equivalent. Strength reduction converts high-cost instructions into low-cost instructions.

Scalar Operator Transformations#

Replacing Multiplication with Shifts#
int a;
a = x * 2;   // bad!
a = x << 1;  // good!

Note that signed and unsigned numbers differ significantly in terms of shifting and promotion. The sign bit receives special treatment when shifting; there are two types, arithmetic shift and logical shift. This becomes prominent when writing binary search/segment trees and other code that contains a large number of divisions by two: signed integer division cannot be directly optimized into a single right-shift operation.

int l, r;
/* codes */
int mid = (l + r) / 2; /* if the compiler cannot assume l, r are non-negative, worse code is generated */
                       // cannot be optimized to
                       // mid = (l + r) >> 1
                       // counterexample:
                       // mid = -127
                       // mid / 2 = -63
                       // mid >> 1 = -64
int mid = (l + r);
int sign = mid >> 31; /* logical right shift, obtains the sign bit */
mid += sign;
mid >>= 1; /* arithmetic right shift */

Feasible solutions:

  • Use unsigned l, r; — indices should be unsigned in the first place
  • Use shifts in the source code
Replacing Division with Multiplication#
int x = a / 3;

This process can be transformed into x = a * 0x55555556 >> 32; for details, see this Zhihu answer or the original paper.

Index Variable Strength Reduction (IndVars)#

The compiler automatically recognizes the index variables in loops, and converts the related high-cost processes into low-cost ones

int a = 0;
for (int i = 1; i < 10; i++) {
  a = 3 * i;  // bad!
  a = a + 3;  // good!
}

Using a = 3 * i directly here is very common in OI, while the compiler can automatically work out that the equivalent transformation is a = a + 3, replacing the multiplication with the lower-cost addition. The analysis of the iteration process of loop variables is called SCEV (Scalar Evolution).

SCEV can also optimize some loops:

int test(int n) {
  int ans = 1;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    ans += i * (i + 1);
  }
  return ans;
}

This function will be optimized into summation by an O(1)O(1)O(1) formula; see https://godbolt.org/z/ET8d89vvK. Currently, only LLVM-based compilers exhibit this behavior; the GCC compiler is more conservative.

test(int):                               # @test(int)
        test    edi, edi
        jle     .LBB0_1
        lea     eax, [rdi - 1]
        lea     ecx, [rdi - 2]
        imul    rcx, rax
        lea     eax, [rdi - 3]
        imul    rax, rcx
        shr     rax
        imul    eax, eax, 1431655766
        and     ecx, -2
        lea     eax, [rax + 2*rcx]
        lea     eax, [rax + 2*rdi]
        dec     eax
        ret
.LBB0_1:
        mov     eax, 1
        ret

Auto-Vectorization#

Single instruction stream, multiple data stream is a good way to provide single-core parallelism. Using such instructions, the CPU's SIMD registers, which are wider than general-purpose registers, can be exploited — for example, putting 4 integers in at once and then computing. OI contestants do not need to understand the details of auto-vectorization; in general, the Clang compiler does more aggressive auto-vectorization than GCC:

// https://godbolt.org/z/h1hx5sWoE
void test(int *a, int *b, int n) {
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    a[i] += b[i];
  }
}

__restrict type specifier (GNU, MSVC)#

The regions pointed to by two arbitrary pointers may overlap; in that case, a special check is needed to decide whether vector code can be used. The figure below shows an example of pointer overlap:

__restrict, as a kind of convention, makes the compiler assume that the memory regions pointed to by the two pointers never overlap.

void test(int* __restrict a, int* __restrict b, int n) {
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    a[i] += b[i];
  }
}

__restrict is not part of the C++ standard, but it can be used with all the major compilers. This keyword affects the code-generation quality of auto-vectorization; it can be used in extreme constant-factor-optimization situations.

Common Language Misuses Related to Compiler Optimizations#

inline - Inlining#

With O2 enabled, function inlining is usually done automatically by the compiler. The inline in struct definitions is completely redundant; if the contest you are preparing for enables O2, there is no need at all to declare functions inline. If O2 is not enabled, using inline will not make the compiler actually inline either.

The inline keyword is treated in modern C++ as a semantic behavior of linkage and of exported symbols, not as doing function inlining.

register - The False Register Hint#

Modern compilers will simply ignore your register keyword; the register allocation you have in mind is generally not as smart as the compiler directly running its register allocation algorithm. This keyword was deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++171.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/keyword/register

Undefined Behavior and Compiler Optimizations#

The compiler may assume that C++ programs contain no undefined behavior (undefined behavior, UB); therefore, when compiling a program that contains UB, the compiler may produce unexpected results. At the same time, the compiler can also perform more aggressive and liberal optimizations under the assumption that UB does not exist.

Common UB includes:

  1. signed overflow;
  2. using uninitialized variables;
  3. out-of-bounds access;
  4. null pointer dereference;
  5. infinite loops with no side effects.

Other UB, examples, and so on can be understood in detail through further reading.

Signed Overflow#

int f(int x) { return x * 2 / 2; }

The compiler can assume that the program contains no signed overflow, so this function may be optimized into

int f(int x) { return x; }

Examples: https://godbolt.org/z/WKv3W5hvM, https://godbolt.org/z/qqE9nxP1j.

This assumption can be disabled with the -fwrapv option. Examples: https://godbolt.org/z/5x3K5KGnr, https://godbolt.org/z/4r4a4EzMW.

Using Uninitialized Variables#

int f(int x) {
  int a;
  if (x)  // either x nonzero or UB
    a = 42;
  return a;
}

The compiler can assume that the program does not use uninitialized variables, so a is guaranteed to be initialized, and this function may be optimized into

int f(int) { return 42; }

Examples: https://godbolt.org/z/8WYMYYjdG, https://godbolt.org/z/qvGd1nvv9.

Out-of-Bounds Access#

int table[4] = {};

bool exists_in_table(int v) {
  // return true in one of the first 4 iterations or UB due to out-of-bounds
  // access
  for (int i = 0; i <= 4; i++)
    if (table[i] == v) return true;
  return false;
}

The compiler can assume that the program contains no out-of-bounds access, so this function is guaranteed to return before any out-of-bounds access occurs, and thus this function may be optimized into

bool exists_in_table(int) { return true; }

Example: https://godbolt.org/z/xfePeYsE3.

Null Pointer Dereference#

int f(int* p) {
  int x = *p;
  if (!p)
    return x;  // Either UB above or this branch is never taken
  else
    return 0;
}

The compiler can assume that the program contains no null pointer dereference, so !p is always false, and thus this function may be optimized into

int f(int*) { return 0; }

Examples: https://godbolt.org/z/GY1jvsrb5, https://godbolt.org/z/4ronPsnxf.

Infinite Loops with No Side Effects#

noteVerifying Fermat&#x27;s Last Theorem

By Fermat's Last Theorem, the Diophantine equation a3=b3+c3a^3=b^3+c^3a3=b3+c3 has no positive integer solutions. The following program tries to enumerate the integers within [1,1000][1,1000][1,1000] to verify whether the equation holds; if it returns true, it means a set of integer solutions has been found within the range [1,1000][1,1000][1,1000], so Fermat's Last Theorem does not hold.

#include <iostream>

bool fermat() {
  const int max_value = 1000;

  // Endless loop with no side effects is UB
  for (int a = 1, b = 1, c = 1; true;) {
    if (((a * a * a) == ((b * b * b) + (c * c * c))))
      return true;  // disproved :()
    a++;
    if (a > max_value) {
      a = 1;
      b++;
    }
    if (b > max_value) {
      b = 1;
      c++;
    }
    if (c > max_value) c = 1;
  }

  return false;  // not disproved
}

int main() {
  std::cout << "Fermat's Last Theorem ";
  fermat() ? std::cout << "has been disproved!\n"
           : std::cout << "has not been disproved.\n";
}
The compiler can assume that the program contains no infinite loop with no side effects, and thus conclude that the for loop in the fermat() function must terminate at some moment and return true; the program may finally output:

Fermat's Last Theorem has been disproved!

Examples: https://godbolt.org/z/d834MK7bz, https://godbolt.org/z/Eov9nsKqf.

Sanitizer#

A sanity guarantor. It checks at run time whether your program has undefined behavior, array out-of-bounds, null pointers, and so on. In local debugging mode, it is recommended to enable some sanitizers, which can greatly shorten your debugging time. These sanitizers were developed by Google; the vast majority of them can be used in GCC and Clang. Sanitizers are more mature in LLVM, so contestants are recommended to use the Clang compiler locally for related debugging.

Address Sanitizer -fsanitize=address#

https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html

Both GCC and Clang support this sanitizer. It includes the following checks:

  • out-of-bounds access
  • use-after-free
  • use-after-return
  • double-free
  • memory leaks
  • use-after-scope

Applying this check will make your program about 2x slower.

Undefined Behavior Sanitizer -fsanitize=undefined#

https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html

Undefined Behavior Sanitizer (a.k.a UBSan) is used to check for undefined behavior in code. Both GCC and Clang support this sanitizer. It automatically checks your program for undefined behavior. UBSan's checks include:

  • shift overflow, for example a 32-bit integer shifted left by 72 bits
  • signed integer overflow
  • overflow when converting a floating-point number to integer data

UBSan's checks are optional; for their impact on the program, refer to the web address provided.

Miscellaneous#

Compiler Explorer#

Observe the behavior and assembly code of the various compilers here: https://godbolt.org

Further Reading#

  1. The LLVM Project Blog: What Every C Programmer Should Know About Undefined Behavior #1/3
  2. The LLVM Project Blog: What Every C Programmer Should Know About Undefined Behavior #2/3
  3. The LLVM Project Blog: What Every C Programmer Should Know About Undefined Behavior #3/3

References and Notes#

Footnotes
  1. Remove Deprecated Use of the register Keyword (open-std.org)

Chapter 36 · C++ and Other Languages

C++ vs. Other Common Languages

oi-wiki.org/lang/cpp-other-langs.md

This article introduces the differences between C++ and other commonly used languages, focusing on the important or easily overlooked differences between C and C++. Although C++ is almost a superset of C, and mixing C and C++ code is generally no problem either, knowing the relatively important differences between C and C++ can help you avoid running into some strange bugs. If you are a contestant whose primary language is C, this article will also make it easier for you to get started with C++. For the unique features C++ adds over C, you can read the tutorials in the Advanced C++ section. In addition, this article also briefly introduces the differences between Python, Java, and C++.

Differences Between C and C++#

Macros and Templates#

When C++ templates were first designed, one of their uses was to replace macro definitions. Learning template programming is an important step in moving from C to C++. Unlike the textual substitution of macros, templates receive more comprehensive compiler checks at compile time, making it easier to write more robust code. Since C++11, templates have supported variadic template parameter lists, which can be used to replace the variadic functions of C while guaranteeing type safety.

Pointers and References#

In C++ you can still use C-style pointers, but for passing variables it is recommended to use C++'s reference feature to achieve similar functionality. Since the object a reference refers to cannot be null, some problems of accessing a null address can be avoided. However, pointers still have their place thanks to their flexibility. It is worth mentioning that C's NULL null pointer has had a type-safe replacement, nullptr, since C++11. References and pointers can be converted into each other through the * and & operators.

bool#

See also the Boolean type.

Unlike C++, the C language originally did not have a Boolean type.

The C99 standard added the _Bool keyword (as well as the equivalent bool macro) and the two macros true and false. To use the three macros bool, true, and false, you need to include the stdbool.h header in your program. Using _Bool, on the other hand, does not require including any extra header.

bool x = true;  // requires including stdbool.h
_Bool x = 1;    // no need to include stdbool.h

Since C23, true, false, and bool have become keywords in the C language; using them no longer requires including the stdbool.h header, and _Bool is retained as an alternative spelling of bool1.

The following table shows how support for the bool type has changed under the different C language standards (C++'s support is included for comparison):

Language standard bool true/false _Bool
C89 / / reserved2
Since C99, before C23 Macro, equivalent to _Bool, requires the stdbool.h header Macro, true is equivalent to 1, false is equivalent to 0, requires the stdbool.h header Keyword
Since C23 Keyword Keyword Alternative spelling of the bool keyword
C++ Keyword Keyword reserved2

struct#

Although both C and C++ have the concept of a struct, the things they correspond to cannot be mixed! A struct in C is used to describe a fixed memory layout, whereas a struct in C++ is simply a kind of class; the only difference between it and a class is that its members and inheritance behavior default to public, while the default members of an ordinary class are private. This is especially fatal when writing mixed C/C++ code.

In addition, declaring a struct in C++ does not need to be as cumbersome as in C. The C version:

typedef struct Node_t {
  struct Node_t *next;
  int key;
} Node;

The C++ version

struct Node {
  Node *next;
  int key;
};

const#

In C, const only has the function of restricting a variable from being modified, while in C++, with the emergence of many new features, const has also been given many more uses. The successor of C's const in C++ is constexpr; for the usage of const in C++, please see the explanation on the constant page.

Memory Allocation#

C++ added the new and delete keywords for allocating space on the "free store"; this free store can be the heap or the static storage area, and they were introduced to work with "classes". Among them, delete[] can also directly free the memory of a dynamic array, which is very convenient. The new and delete keywords will call the type's constructors and destructors; compared with C's malloc(), realloc(), and free() functions, they have more complete support for types, but their efficiency is not as good as these functions in C.

In short, if the objects you need to dynamically allocate memory for are fundamental types or arrays of them, you can use malloc() for more efficient memory allocation; but if the objects you are creating are of non-fundamental types, it is recommended to use new to obtain safety checks. It is worth noting that although both new and malloc() return pointers, a pointer obtained from new can only be reclaimed with delete, and a pointer obtained from malloc() can likewise only be reclaimed with free(); otherwise there is a risk of memory leaks.

Variable Declaration#

Before C99, variable declarations in C had to be placed at the beginning of a statement block; C++ and C after C99 have no such restriction.

Variable-Length Arrays#

Since C99, the C language supports VLAs (variable-length arrays); C++ has never supported them.

Struct Initialization#

Since C99, the C language has supported designated initialization of structs (although it is an optional feature in C11); C++ did not support designated initialization with an ordering requirement until C++20, and the features supported by C — out-of-order designators, nesting, mixing with ordinary initializers, and designated initialization of arrays — are all unsupported by C++3.

Comment Syntax#

The C++-style single-line comment // was not supported in C before C99.

Differences Between Python and C++#

Python is the most commonly used language in the machine learning community today. Compared with C++, Python's advantages are that it is easy to learn and easy to put into practice. Python has a simpler and more direct syntax — for example, when defining a variable, you do not need to declare the variable's type in advance. However, this simplicity comes at a price. Python sacrifices performance compared with C++. C++ is applicable to almost all platforms, including embedded systems, and has faster execution speed, but Python can only be used on some platforms that support high-level languages. C++ is closer to the underlying hardware, so it can be used to write operating systems.

Differences Between Java and C++#

Both Java and C++ are object-oriented languages that use object-oriented ideas (encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism); since object orientation has many very good properties (inheritance, composition, etc.), both have good reusability. Therefore, compared with Python, Java and C++ are more similar to each other.

The biggest difference between Java and C++ is that Java has the JVM mechanism. The full name of JVM is Java Virtual Machine, which means "Java virtual machine" in Chinese. A very important characteristic of the Java language is platform independence. Using the Java Virtual Machine is the key to achieving this characteristic. If an ordinary high-level language is to run on different platforms, it at least needs to be compiled into different object code. After the Java language virtual machine was introduced, the Java language no longer needs to be recompiled to run on different platforms. The Java language uses the Java Virtual Machine to shield information related to specific platforms, so that the Java compiler only needs to generate object code (bytecode) that runs on the Java Virtual Machine, which can then run unmodified on a variety of platforms.

Because of this characteristic, Java is often used in the development of programs that need to be ported to different platforms. However, also because compiling a Java program has to start from bytecode, Java's performance is not as good as C++'s.

References#

Footnotes
  1. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3054.pdf.
  2. Both C and C++ specify that identifiers beginning with an underscore followed by an uppercase letter are reserved; for details, see https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/identifier.
  3. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/aggregate_initialization

Chapter 37 · C++ and Other Languages

Pascal to C++ First Aid

oi-wiki.org/lang/pas-cpp.md

author: kexploring, Ir1d, lvneg1

Quick C++ Installation and Environment Setup#

All of the following steps are performed on Windows.

Using an IDE#

You can refer to the content on the following pages:

  • Dev-C++
  • Code::Blocks

Using a Code Editor + Compiler + Debugger#

You can refer to the content on the VS Code page. The official Visual Studio Code website has documentation explaining how to set up C++. Generally speaking, VS Code is more convenient to use together with extensions; see the official VS Code website.

A Quick Overview of C++ Syntax#

Every C++ program starts running from the part named main.

Braces mark the start and end of a block statement: { is equivalent to begin in Pascal, and } is equivalent to end.

Note that, as in Pascal, every statement in C++ must end with a semicolon ;. However, no semicolon is needed after a closing brace, and there is no period . to type at the very end of the program.

For comments, // marks a line comment, and /* */ marks a block comment.

Following convention, let's take a look at Hello World.

Hello World: The First C++ Program#

#include <iostream>  // import the iostream library

int main()  // the main part
{
  std::cout << "Hello World!" << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

Then compile and run it, and see the result.

Brief Explanation#

The first line, #include <iostream>, means: import the library named iostream.

notePascal&#x27;s library files

Pascal does actually have library files; it is just that many students have never used them...

Do you see the main on the third line? Execution of the program starts from main.

Next, the most important statement is

std::cout << "Hello World!" << std::endl;

std::cout is the output command. You may have seen some C++ programs that simply write cout.

noteAbout the std:: prefix

For questions about the std:: prefix, see the note "What is std?" at the bottom of the section on cin and cout.

The << in the middle vividly suggests flow — it really is indicating how the output "flows". This line of code means: "Hello World!" is pushed onto the output stream first, and afterwards std::endl is pushed onto the output stream.

std::endl is the output newline command, similar to Pascal's writeln, though there is no coutln in C++. The difference between Pascal and C++ is that write('Hello World!') is equivalent to std::cout << "Hello World!", while writeln('Hello World!') is equivalent to std::cout << "Hello World!" << std::endl.

Here, "Hello World!" is a string. In Pascal, strings always use single quotes ' and cannot use double quotes, whereas strings in C++ must use double quotes. In C++, a character enclosed in single quotes has a different meaning, which will be brought up later.

Alright — by this point, Hello World has just about been explained in full.

Some of you may ask: what does that return 0 at the end mean? What does that int main() mean? Don't worry about it for now. When you first start writing programs, just treat it as boilerplate and write it as such (it was written as boilerplate here too). Since you will not be using the parameters of main when getting started, there is no need to write int main(int argc, char const *argv[]).

Simple Exercises#

  1. Try outputting a different string.
  2. Try learning about escape characters.

A+B Problem: The Second C++ Program#

The classic A+B Problem.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int a, b, c;

  std::cin >> a >> b;

  c = a + b;

  std::cout << c << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

Note: the code contains quite a few blank lines; remove them if you are not used to them.

Brief Explanation#

std::cin is the input command (cin stands for C-in), and >> works in a way similar to the output syntax.

Of the statements newly added here, two are the most important; one is the variable declaration statement.

int a, b, c;

You may be accustomed to declaring variables in Pascal like this:

var
a, b, c: integer;

A declaration in C++ begins directly with a data type name. Here, the leading int (integer type) indicates that variables are about to be declared.

The other most important statement is the assignment statement.

c = a + b;

This is one of the bigger differences in syntax between Pascal and C++: assignment in Pascal is :=, while in C++ it is =; and testing for equality in C++ is ==.

C++ also lets you initialize a variable with a value directly at the point of declaration.

int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0;

Simple Exercises#

  1. Rewrite the code, submit it to an OJ, and get AC.
  2. For more input/output syntax, see the section on scanf and printf, and try to learn about formatted output in C++.

Closing Remarks and Next Steps#

Alright — at this point you have grasped some of the most basic essentials. What remains is to look up the syntax in C++ corresponding to Pascal, and the features that differ.

But before that, it is strongly recommended that you first read Variable scope: global variables and local variables.

Make good use of Alt+← and Alt+→ to jump back and forward.

Syntax#

Variables#

Fundamental Data Types#

C++ and Pascal are largely the same here; the common ones are:

  • bool: the Boolean type
  • int: the integer type
  • float: the single-precision floating-point type
  • double: the double-precision floating-point type
  • char: the character type
  • void: no type

In C++, single quotes are used specifically to represent a single character (the character type), such as 'a', while strings (arrays of characters) must use double quotes.

C++ also has many additional data types; see Fundamental types - cppreference.com.

Declaring Constants#

const double PI = 3.1415926;

If you are not clear on the issues around macro expansion, it is recommended to use constants instead of macro definitions.

Operators#

Refer directly to the content of the Operations page. The appendix also provides comparison tables of operator and math function syntax.

Conditionals#

The if Statement#

if (a = b) and (a > 0) and (b > 0) then
    begin
        b := a;
    end
else
    begin
        a := b;
    end;
if (a == b && a > 0 && b > 0) {
  b = a;
} else {
  a = b;
}

Boolean operations and comparisons:

  • and -> &&
  • or -> ||
  • not -> !
  • = -> ==
  • <> -> !=

Notes:

  1. The precedence of and in Pascal differs from that of && in C++, so in C++ there is no need to wrap the condition in parentheses.
  2. In Pascal, testing for equality uses = and assignment uses :=; in C++, testing for equality uses == and assignment uses =.
  3. If you write a = b instead of a == b inside the parentheses of an if statement, the program will not report an error; rather, it will assign b to a, and make the assignment expression a = b as a whole take on the value of a after the assignment has completed.
  4. In C++ there is no need to agonize over whether to put a semicolon after end.
  5. In C++ Boolean operations, non-Boolean values are automatically converted to Boolean values.
warningCommon pitfall warning

Pay special attention: do not write = where you mean ==!

Because C/C++ is more flexible syntactically than Pascal, if you write if (a=b) in a conditional, the program will keep running along smoothly, since a=b in C++ has a return value.

case and switch#

It is not used very often, so it will not be covered in detail here.

Note: C++ has no 1..n, and no chained inequalities (such as 1 < x < 2).

Loops#

The three kinds of loops below, in six pieces of code, implement the same functionality.

The while Loop#

while is very similar. (The C++ code here is not a complete program; some boilerplate has been omitted. The same applies below.)

var i: integer;

begin
    i := 1;
    while i <= 10 do
        begin
            write(i,' ');
            inc(i); // or i := i + 1;
        end;
end.
int i = 1;
while (i <= 10) {
  std::cout << i << " ";
  i++;
}

The for Loop#

The for statement in C++ is very different.

var i: integer;

begin
    for i:= 1 to 10 do
        begin
            write(i, ' ');
        end;
end.
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  std::cout << i << " ";
}

Notes:

  1. The line for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++){ packs many statements together — there are three statements inside the for.
  2. The first statement, int i = 1;, declares a local variable i and initializes it. (This design is much more sensible than Pascal's.)
  3. The second statement, i <= 10;, serves as the criterion for deciding whether the loop continues.
  4. The third statement, i++, is executed at the end of each loop iteration; it means roughly the same as inc(i) in Pascal, and writing ++i here works just the same. For the difference between i++ and ++i, refer to other resources.

repeat until and do while Loops#

Note that repeat until and do while are different; compare the following code:

var i: integer;

begin
    i := 1;
    repeat
        write(i, ' ');
        inc(i);
    until i = 11;
end.
int i = 1;
do {
  std::cout << i << " ";
  i++;
} while (i <= 10);

Loop Control#

In C++, break works the same as in Pascal: it exits the loop.

continue is likewise the same: it skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one (returning to the top of the loop).

Arrays and Strings#

Variable-Length Arrays: The Standard Library Type Vector#

Refer to the content of the Sequence containers page.

The C++ standard library provides vector, which is equivalent to a variable-length array; the library file must be imported before it can be used.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>  // import the vector library

int main() {
  std::vector<int> a;  // declare the vector a and define a as an empty vector object
  int n;

  std::cin >> n;
  // read a
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int t;
    std::cin >> t;
    a.push_back(t);  // put the number t just read at the end of vector a; this operation's complexity is O(1)
    /* Subscript access cannot be used for assignment here, because at
    declaration time the size of a is still empty; using `a[i] = t;` here would be wrong.
    */
  }

  // print out all the numbers read into a
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    std::cout << a[i] << ", ";  // !Note: the first number in a is a[0];
    // if the index is out of bounds, it will return an unknown value (overflow) and will not report an error
  }
  std::cout << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

Accessing array elements in C++ is similar to Pascal, but there is a very important difference: the first element of an array is a[0], whereas in Pascal you can specify the lower bound yourself.

Strings: The Standard Library Type String#

Refer to the content of the string page.

The C++ standard library provides string; some of the operations it supports are the same as vector's, and it likewise requires importing a library file.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
  std::string s;  // declare the string s

  std::cin >> s;  // read s;
  // when reading, all leading whitespace characters (spaces, newline characters, tab characters) are skipped, and the string that gets read stops at the next whitespace character.

  std::cout << s << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

C-Style Arrays#

Refer to the content of the Array page.

If you need a variable-length array, use vector; do not use C-style arrays.

C-style arrays are intimately tied to pointers, so they will not be expanded upon here.

Important Differences#

Variable Scope: Global Variables and Local Variables#

In C++, variables can be declared almost anywhere. See Variable scope.

When writing Pascal procedures/functions, it is easy to forget to declare the local variables i or j. Since the main program generally contains loops, in most cases i and j end up as global variables; as a result, operating on i inside a procedure/function in this situation is extremely error-prone. Worse still, if you forget to declare such local variables, the compiler raises no error, and the program runs. (Many hard-to-find bugs are born exactly this way.)

So, when using C++, when declaring variables — such as the i used in loops — do not use global variables; use local variables wherever you can. If you do this, you need not worry about variable-name conflicts (e.g. with i) inside functions.

noteAdditional note

Pascal can avoid this problem to some extent: following the approach of C++, have the main program do nothing but call procedures/functions, declare no global variables like i and j that are highly prone to name collisions, and if a loop is needed, write a separate procedure and call it.

C++ Converts Types Automatically#

int i = 2;
if (i) {  // i = 0 evaluates to false; everything else evaluates to true
  std::cout << "true";
} else {
  std::cout << "false";
}

Not only can int be converted to bool — int and float can also be converted into each other. In Pascal you can assign an integer type to a floating-point type, but not the other way around. C++ does not have this problem.

int a;
a = 3.2;      // now a = 3
float b = a;  // now b = 3.0

Whether / is integer division or floating-point division is determined by the types of the dividend and the divisor:

float a = 32 / 10;    // 32/10 evaluates to 3 (integer division); a = 3.0
float b = 32.0 / 10;  // 32.0/10 evaluates to 3.2; b = 3.2

pow(a, b) computes aba^bab; the function returns a floating-point type. If you use it directly to compute powers of integers, you need not worry about it reporting an error, thanks to the automatic conversion:

int a = pow(2, 3);  // compute 2^3

There are also conversions between char and int in both directions.

char a = 48;              // ASCII 48 is '0'
int b = a + 1;            // b = 49
std::cout << (a == '0');  // true is output as 1

In fact, char and bool in C++ are essentially integer types.

For details, refer to the article Implicit conversions - cppreference.com.

Many Statements in C++ Have Return Values: Reading an Unknown Amount of Data as an Example#

Sometimes you need to keep reading until the data ends — for example, computing the sum of a set of numbers whose count is not fixed (the data may span multiple lines), until the end of the file. The way to implement it is:

noteEOF: end of file

EOF, the end-of-file marker, is entered in the command line with Ctrl+Z on Windows (you then also need to press Enter), and with Ctrl+D on Unix-like systems.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
  int sum = 0, a = 0;

  while (std::cin >> a) {
    sum += a;
  }
  std::cout << sum << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

How it works: in while (std::cin >> a), the expression std::cin >> a returns false when there is a problem with the input or the end of the file is encountered, which breaks the loop.

Functions#

C++ has only functions and no procedures — but it has void; it has no function-value variables, but it has return.

Example comparing a Pascal function with a C++ function:

function abs(x:integer):integer;
begin
    if x < 0 then
        begin
            abs := -x;
        end
    else
        begin
            abs := x;
        end;
end;
int abs(int x) {
  if (x < 0) {
    return -x;
  } else {
    return x;
  }
}

In C++, the function declaration int abs defines the function abs() whose return value is of type int (the integer type); the function's return value is the value given by the return statement.

If you don't want a return value (i.e. a Pascal "procedure"), use void. void means "empty" — nothing at all is returned.

var ans: integer;

procedure printAns(ans:integer);
begin
    writeln(ans);
end;

begin
    ans := 10;
    printAns(ans);
end.
#include <iostream>

void printAns(int ans) {
  std::cout << ans << std::endl;

  return;
}

int main() {
  int ans = 10;
  printAns(ans);

  return 0;
}

C++'s return and assigning to the function variable in Pascal have one very big difference. return in C++ returns a value, and once this statement finishes executing, the function is done; in Pascal, on the other hand, assigning to the function variable does not jump out of the function — execution continues. Consequently, if a Pascal function/procedure needs to break off somewhere, an extra command is needed, namely exit. C++ needs no such thing: if you want to break off somewhere, you can use return directly. For example (since I really cannot come up with a short yet practical piece of code, this will have to do for now):

#include <iostream>

void printWarning(int x) {
  if (x >= 0) {
    return;  // this statement here is equivalent to `exit;` in Pascal
  }
  std::cout << "Warning: input a negative number.";
}

int main() {
  int a;

  std::cin >> a;
  printWarning(a);

  return 0;
}

And in a sense, for the earlier abs function, this is the strictly equivalent version:

function abs(x:integer):integer;
begin
    if x < 0 then
        begin
            abs := -x; exit; // !Note this
        end
    else
        begin
            abs := x;  exit; // !Note this
        end;
end;
int abs(int x) {
  if (x < 0) {
    return -x;
  } else {
    return x;
  }
}

noteSpecial reminder

In C++, exit exits the program; do not type exit out of habit — use return!

C++ treats functions and procedures alike as functions, not even sparing main: when you write int main, C++ regards main as an integer-valued function, and the return value here is 0. This is a customary convention: returning 0 indicates that the program exited normally.

Perhaps you have already guessed: the parameters in main(int argc, char const *argv[]) are precisely int argc and char const *argv[]; for what they mean, refer to other resources.

Passing Parameters to Functions#

C++ does not have Pascal's var keyword for making the passed parameters modifiable, but C++ can use references and pointers to achieve the same effect.

var a, b: integer;

procedure swap(var x,y:integer);
var temp:integer;
begin
    temp := x;
    x := y;
    y := temp;
end;

begin
    a := 10; b:= 20;    
    swap(a, b);
    writeln(a, ' ', b);
end.
// code using pointers
#include <iostream>

void swap(int* x, int* y) {
  int temp;
  temp = *x;
  *x = *y;
  *y = temp;
}

int main() {
  int a = 10, b = 20;
  swap(&a, &b);
  std::cout << a << " " << b;

  return 0;
}

Note that the C++ code here involves pointers. Pointers really are quite a hassle; it is recommended to go read the relevant materials.

// code using references
#include <iostream>

void swap(int& x, int& y) {
  int temp;
  temp = x;
  x = y;
  y = temp;
}

int main(int argc, char const* argv[]) {
  int a = 10, b = 20;
  swap(a, b);
  std::cout << a << " " << b;

  return 0;
}

Note that the C++ code here involves reference-related type issues. When calling some STL or template libraries with references, you may run into problems, in which case you need to manually declare type aliases. For the specifics, you can consult C++ Primer, Fifth Edition, or look things up in online resources yourself.

There are other ways to pass parameters to functions in C++; one of them is passing parameters directly through global variables. If you don't know how to use pointers yet, you can start with this method. But its flaw is that there is no stack saving the data, so there is no way to pass parameters in a recursive function. (Unless you write a stack by hand — and note that a hand-written stack is also one way to break through the system stack limit.)

The C++ Standard Library and Reference Materials#

Never reinvent the wheel (unless for practice): before setting out to write some feature yourself, first go check whether that function or data structure already exists.

The C++ Standard Library#

In the C++ standard library, <algorithm> has many useful functions, such as quicksort and binary search, which can be called directly. Refer to the STL algorithms page.

There are also the STL containers, such as arrays, vectors (resizable arrays), queues, stacks, and so on, with many functions attached. Refer to the Introduction to STL containers page.

If you are looking for functions related to string operations, see:

  • std::basic_string - cppreference.com
  • <string>- C++ Reference

Pointers in C/C++ are very flexible things; you can refer to the Pointers page. If you want to understand pointers thoroughly, it is recommended to find a book or a reference manual and read it carefully.

Troubleshooting and Tips#

  • Common mistakes
  • Common tricks

  • cppreference.com: the most important C/C++ reference material

Afterword#

Writing up to this point, many students will feel that this is not "first aid" at all — so many things have gone unmentioned. Well, that cannot be helped.

Although this is meant to be first aid, many topics — such as how to convert a string into a number, or how to search for a character inside a string — do not fit a short, punchy first-aid post either. If all of that were written out, this would become an introductory C++ tutorial. So make full use of this Wiki, reference manuals, and search engines.

One thing that should be pointed out: much of the C++ syntax mentioned above actually comes from the C language, so a title like Pascal to C/C++ First Aid Post would have been more accurate.

Pascal was a very popular language in the second half of the last century, predating C. But as UNIX systems became widespread and Microsoft used C, Pascal has now become history. It did see later development, though — for example, Free Pascal, the open-source compiler project, added object-oriented features (the Delphi language). Apart from its use in informatics competitions, Pascal has one characteristic no other language has: its compiler supports a great many very old machines, such as the Gameboy — that Nintendo game console from the last century. Another of its uses is appearing in textbooks of all kinds in the form of pseudocode (Pascal-style pseudocode).

Finally, the Pascal community is really quite small, while the C/C++ community is large, with many comprehensive manuals and tutorials — so be sure to get a good command of English. There are many, many more programming languages in the world, and computer science as a discipline and a technology is far more than informatics competitions and programming languages.

About Python#

Python is an interpreted language already in wide use around the world. It provides efficient high-level data structures, also makes object-oriented programming simple and effective, and can further be used in competitive programming.

Advantages of Python#

  • Python is an interpreted language: Python requires no compiling or linking, which to some extent cuts down the number of steps.
  • Python is an interactive language: the Python interpreter implements interactive operation, so you can type and execute instructions directly in the terminal.
  • Python is easy to learn and use: Python provides a wealth of data structures and also supports developing large programs.
  • Python is highly compatible: Python supports the Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems alike.
  • Python is highly practical: from simple input and output to scientific computing and even large web applications, you can write a suitable Python program for it.
  • Python produces concise, readable programs: Python code is usually shorter than code in other languages that implements the same functionality.
  • Python supports extension: Python itself is developed in C (namely CPython), and it supports linking the Python interpreter with applications developed in C, extending and controlling such an application with Python.

Points to note when learning Python#

  • The Python versions in main use today are Python 3.7 and above. Python 2, and Python 3 up to 3.6, are no longer supported, but they are still used by some legacy systems and codebases. This page will introduce the newer versions of Python. If you run into Python 2 code, you can try the 2to3 program to convert Python 2 code into Python 3 code.
  • Python's design philosophy and syntax differ considerably from some other languages; it hides many low-level details, which gives it a practical yet elegant style.
  • Python is a highly dynamic interpreted language, so its programs run relatively slowly, especially when using the built-in for loop statement. When using Python, you should make as much use as possible of built-in functions such as filter and map, or of list comprehension syntax, to improve program performance.

Setting up the environment#

See Python 3. Alternatively:

  • Windows: you can also get Python from the Microsoft Store, for free and quickly.

  • macOS/Linux: typically, most Linux distributions already come with Python. If you only plan to learn Python syntax and have no other development needs, there is no need to install Python separately.

    warningNote

    On some systems where Python is installed by default (meaning installed with a package manager), such as Unix systems, you should run python3 in the terminal to open the Python 3 interpreter.2

    Besides that, you can also use tools such as venv, conda, and Nix to manage the Python toolchain and Python packages, creating isolated virtual environments and avoiding dependency problems.

As an interpreted language, Python executes programs somewhat differently from C++, and this difference often does not show up when programming in an IDE, so the different ways of running a program need to be emphasized here.

When you type python3 on the command line, or right after opening IDLE, you have actually entered an interactive programming environment, also called a "REPL" ("Read-Eval-Print Loop"). Beginners can type statements here and immediately see the results, which makes verifying some syntax extremely easy; we will also make heavy use of this form later on.

But to write a complete program, you had better create a new text file (usually with the extension .py) and then run python3 filename.py on the command line; that way you can run the code and see the result.
