Advanced Java

oi-wiki.org/lang/java-pro.md
warningNote

All the content below is written based on Java JDK 8; it is possible that some of it has changed in higher versions.

Faster Input and Output#

Scanner and System.out.print work well at the very beginning, but they become less efficient when processing larger inputs, so we need some ways to speed up IO.

Using Kattio + StringTokenizer for Input#

One of the most commonly used approaches is to use Kattio.java from Kattis to improve IO efficiency.1 This approach wraps StringTokenizer and PrintWriter in one class for convenient use. When actually solving problems during a contest (if the contest organizers allow it), you can use this template directly.

The IO template that should be included in your code is given below. Since the original Kattio from Kattis contains some features that are rarely used, the template below has been adjusted accordingly (the original Kattio uses the MIT license).

class Kattio extends PrintWriter {
    private BufferedReader r;
    private StringTokenizer st;
    // standard IO
    public Kattio() { this(System.in, System.out); }
    public Kattio(InputStream i, OutputStream o) {
        super(o);
        r = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(i));
    }
    // file IO
    public Kattio(String intput, String output) throws IOException {
        super(output);
        r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(intput));
    }
    // returns null when there is no more input
    public String next() {
        try {
            while (st == null || !st.hasMoreTokens())
                st = new StringTokenizer(r.readLine());
            return st.nextToken();
        } catch (Exception e) {}
        return null;
    }
    public int nextInt() { return Integer.parseInt(next()); }
    public double nextDouble() { return Double.parseDouble(next()); }
    public long nextLong() { return Long.parseLong(next()); }
}

The code below briefly demonstrates the use of Kattio:

class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Kattio io = new Kattio();
        // string input
        String str = io.next();
        // int input
        int num = io.nextInt();
        // output
        io.println("Result");
        // make sure to close the IO stream so that the output is written correctly
        io.close();
    }
}

Using StreamTokenizer for Input#

In some cases, using StringTokenizer can lead to an MLE (Memory Limit Exceeded); at such times we need to use StreamTokenizer for input.

import java.io.*;
public class Main {
    // IO code
    public static StreamTokenizer in = new StreamTokenizer(new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in), 32768));
    public static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(System.out));
    public static double nextDouble() throws IOException { in.nextToken(); return in.nval; }
    public static float nextFloat() throws IOException { in.nextToken(); return (float)in.nval; }
    public static int nextInt() throws IOException { in.nextToken(); return (int)in.nval; }
    public static String next() throws IOException { in.nextToken(); return in.sval; }
    public static long nextLong() throws Exception { in.nextToken(); return (long)in.nval;}

    // usage example
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        int n = nextInt();
        out.println(n);
        out.close();
    }
}

Analysis and Comparison Between the Kattio + StringTokenizer Approach and the StreamTokenizer Approach#

  1. StreamTokenizer uses less memory than StringTokenizer, so you can try StreamTokenizer when a Java reference solution MLEs, but StreamTokenizer loses precision, which causes problems when reading in some data;
    • There is a Type in the source code of StreamTokenizer, which decides the type based on the input content. If the input is a string that starts with digits, such as 123oi, it will forcibly treat the type as double, so reading a String type as a double type during input will throw an exception;
    • StreamTokenizer loses precision when reading numbers of size 1e14 or above;
  2. When using PrintWriter, note that you must call close() at the very end of the program to close the output stream, or use flush() to clear the buffer when output is needed; otherwise the content will not be written to the console/file.
  3. Kattio inherits from the PrintWriter class, so its own objects have the functionality of PrintWriter and can directly call the methods of the PrintWriter class for output, while it keeps StringTokenizer as its own member variable to modify. The Main of the second approach keeps both StreamTokenizer and PrintWriter as its own member variables, so there is a slight difference in usage.

In summary, in most situations StringTokenizer is the better choice compared to StreamTokenizer; you can try StreamTokenizer in extreme MLE situations, and StreamTokenizer is powerless when it comes to data beyond the range of int.

BigInteger and Number Theory#

BigInteger is the arbitrary-precision arithmetic class provided by Java, which makes it very convenient to solve big-number problems.

Initialization#

There are two common ways to create a BigInteger:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.math.BigInteger;

class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        BigInteger a = new BigInteger("12345678910");  // create a BigInteger object from the string in decimal form
        out.println(a);  // the value of a is 12345678910 
        BigInteger b = new BigInteger("1E", 16);  // create a BigInteger object from the string in the specified radix
        out.println(b);  // the value of b is 30 
        out.close();
    }
}

Basic Operations#

In the following, this stands for the current BigInteger:

Function Description
abs() Returns the absolute value of this
negate() Returns the negation of this
add(BigInteger val) Returns the sum of this and val
subtract(BigInteger val) Returns the difference of this and val
multiply(BigInteger val) Returns the product of this and val
divide(BigInteger val) Returns the quotient of this and val
remainder(BigInteger val) Returns the remainder of this divided by val
mod(BigInteger val) Returns the value of this modulo val
pow(int val) Returns this raised to the power val
and(BigInteger val) Returns the bitwise AND of this and val
or(BigInteger val) Returns the bitwise OR of this and val
not() Returns the bitwise complement of this
xor(BigInteger val) Returns the bitwise XOR of this and val
shiftLeft(int n) Returns this shifted left by n bits
shiftRight(int n) Returns this shifted right by n bits
max(BigInteger val) Returns the larger of this and val
min(BigInteger val) Returns the smaller of this and val
bitCount() Returns the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of this, excluding the sign bit
bitLength() Returns the length of the binary representation of this, excluding the sign bit
getLowestSetBit() Returns the position of the rightmost 1 bit in the binary representation of this
compareTo(BigInteger val) Compares the values of this and val
toString() Returns the decimal string representation of this
toString(int radix) Returns the string representation of this in the given radix

A usage example is as follows:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.math.BigInteger;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static BigInteger a, b;

    static void abs() {
        out.println("abs:");
        a = new BigInteger("-123");
        out.println(a.abs());  // outputs 123 
        a = new BigInteger("123");
        out.println(a.abs());  // outputs 123 
    }

    static void negate() {
        out.println("negate:");
        a = new BigInteger("-123");
        out.println(a.negate());  // outputs 123 
        a = new BigInteger("123");
        out.println(a.negate());  // outputs -123 
    }

    static void add() {
        out.println("add:");
        a = new BigInteger("123");
        b = new BigInteger("123");
        out.println(a.add(b));  // outputs 246 
    }

    static void subtract() {
        out.println("subtract:");
        a = new BigInteger("123");
        b = new BigInteger("123");
        out.println(a.subtract(b));  // outputs 0 
    }

    static void multiply() {
        out.println("multiply:");
        a = new BigInteger("12");
        b = new BigInteger("12");
        out.println(a.multiply(b));  // outputs 144 
    }

    static void divide() {
        out.println("divide:");
        a = new BigInteger("12");
        b = new BigInteger("11");
        out.println(a.divide(b));  // outputs 1 
    }

    static void remainder() {
        out.println("remainder:");
        a = new BigInteger("12");
        b = new BigInteger("10");
        out.println(a.remainder(b));  // outputs 2 
        a = new BigInteger("-12");
        b = new BigInteger("10");
        out.println(a.remainder(b));  // outputs -2 
    }

    static void mod() {
        out.println("mod:");
        a = new BigInteger("12");
        b = new BigInteger("10");
        out.println(a.mod(b));  // outputs 2 
        a = new BigInteger("-12");
        b = new BigInteger("10");
        out.println(a.mod(b));  // outputs 8 
    }

    static void pow() {
        out.println("pow:");
        a = new BigInteger("2");
        out.println(a.pow(10));  // outputs 1024 
    }

    static void and() {
        out.println("and:");
        a = new BigInteger("3");  // 11 
        b = new BigInteger("5");  // 101 
        out.println(a.and(b));  // outputs 1 
    }

    static void or() {
        out.println("or:");
        a = new BigInteger("2");  // 10 
        b = new BigInteger("5");  // 101 
        out.println(a.or(b));  // outputs 7 
    }

    static void not() {
        out.println("not:");
        a = new BigInteger("2147483647");  // 01111111 11111111 11111111 11111111 
        out.println(a.not());  // outputs -2147483648, whose binary is 10000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 
    }

    static void xor() {
        out.println("xor:");
        a = new BigInteger("6");  // 110 
        b = new BigInteger("5");  // 101 
        out.println(a.xor(b));  // 011, outputs 3 
    }

    static void shiftLeft() {
        out.println("shiftLeft:");
        a = new BigInteger("1");
        out.println(a.shiftLeft(10));  // outputs 1024 
    }

    static void shiftRight() {
        out.println("shiftRight:");
        a = new BigInteger("1024");
        out.println(a.shiftRight(8));  // outputs 4 
    }

    static void max() {
        out.println("max:");
        a = new BigInteger("6");
        b = new BigInteger("5");
        out.println(a.max(b));  // outputs 6 
    }

    static void min() {
        out.println("min:");
        a = new BigInteger("6");
        b = new BigInteger("5");
        out.println(a.min(b));  // outputs 5 
    }

    static void bitCount() {
        out.println("bitCount:");
        a = new BigInteger("6");  // 110 
        out.println(a.bitCount());  // outputs 2 
    }

    static void bitLength() {
        out.println("bitLength:");
        a = new BigInteger("6");  // 110 
        out.println(a.bitLength());  // outputs 3 
    }

    static void getLowestSetBit() {
        out.println("getLowestSetBit:");
        a = new BigInteger("8");  // 1000 
        out.println(a.getLowestSetBit());  // outputs 3 
    }

    static void compareTo() {
        out.println("compareTo:");
        a = new BigInteger("8");
        b = new BigInteger("9");
        out.println(a.compareTo(b));  // outputs -1 
        a = new BigInteger("8");
        b = new BigInteger("8");
        out.println(a.compareTo(b));  // outputs 0 
        a = new BigInteger("8");
        b = new BigInteger("7");
        out.println(a.compareTo(b));  // outputs 1 
    }

    static void toStringTest() {
        out.println("toString:");
        a = new BigInteger("15");
        out.println(a.toString());  // outputs 15 
        out.println(a.toString(16));  // outputs f 
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        abs();
        negate();
        add();
        subtract();
        multiply();
        divide();
        remainder();
        mod();
        pow();
        and();
        or();
        not();
        xor();
        shiftLeft();
        shiftRight();
        max();
        min();
        bitCount();
        bitLength();
        getLowestSetBit();
        compareTo();
        toStringTest();
        out.close();
    }
}

Mathematical Operations#

In the following, this stands for the current BigInteger:

Function Description
gcd(BigInteger val) Returns the greatest common divisor of the absolute values of this and val
isProbablePrime(int val) Returns a Boolean value indicating whether this is prime
nextProbablePrime() Returns the first prime greater than this
modPow(BigInteger b, BigInteger p) Returns the value of this raised to the b-th power, modulo p
modInverse(BigInteger p) Returns the multiplicative inverse of this modulo p

A usage example is as follows:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.math.BigInteger;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static BigInteger a, b, p;

    static void gcd() {  // greatest common divisor 
        a = new BigInteger("120032414321432144212100");
        b = new BigInteger("240231431243123412432140");
        out.println(String.format("gcd(%s,%s)=%s", a.toString(), b.toString(), a.gcd(b).toString()));  // gcd(120032414321432144212100,240231431243123412432140)=20 
    }

    static void isPrime() {  // uses Miller–Rabin to determine whether the number is prime: the larger the parameter, the higher the accuracy and the higher the complexity. The accuracy is (1-1/(val*2)) 
        a = new BigInteger("1200324143214321442127");
        out.println("a:" + a.toString());
        out.println(a.isProbablePrime(10) ? "a is prime" : "a is not prime");  // a is not prime 
    }

    static void nextPrime() {  // find the next prime after this number 
        a = new BigInteger("1200324143214321442127");
        out.println("a:" + a.toString());
        out.println(String.format("a nextPrime is %s", a.nextProbablePrime().toString()));  // a nextPrime is 1200324143214321442199 
    }

    static void modPow() {  // fast exponentiation, faster than the normal version, with internal mathematical optimizations 
        a = new BigInteger("2");
        b = new BigInteger("10");
        p = new BigInteger("1000");
        out.println(String.format("a:%s b:%s p:%s", a, b, p));
        out.println(String.format("a^b mod p:%s", a.modPow(b, p).toString()));//  24 
    }

    static void modInverse() {  // modular inverse 
        a = new BigInteger("10");
        b = new BigInteger("3");
        out.println(a.modInverse(b));  // a ^ (p-2) mod p = 1 
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        gcd();
        isPrime();
        nextPrime();
        modPow();
        modInverse();
        out.close();
    }
}

For background on Miller–Rabin, see the Miller–Rabin primality test.

Primitive Data Types and Wrapper Data Types#

Introduction#

Since primitive types do not have object-oriented features, in order for them to take part in object-oriented development, Java provides a corresponding wrapper class for each of the eight primitive types: Byte, Double, Float, Integer, Long, Short, Character, and Boolean. The correspondence between the two is as follows:

Primitive data type Wrapper data type
byte Byte
short Short
boolean Boolean
char Character
int Integer
long Long
float Float
double Double

Differences#

Here int and Integer are used as the example:

  1. Integer is the wrapper class of int, while int is one of Java's primitive data types.
  2. The Integer type can only be used after being instantiated, while the int type does not need to be.
  3. An Integer actually corresponds to a reference: when you new an Integer, an object is actually generated, whereas an int directly stores the data.
  4. The default value of Integer is null, and it can accept both null and data of the int type; the default value of int is 0, and it cannot accept data of the null type.
  5. Using == to determine whether two Integer variables are the same can give incorrect results — you can only use equals() — while for int you can use == directly.

Boxing and Unboxing#

Here int and Integer are used as the example:

The essence of an Integer is an object, and int is a primitive type; the two types cannot be assigned to each other directly. When a conversion is needed, converting the primitive type into the wrapper type is called boxing, and the reverse is called unboxing.

// primitive type
int value1 = 1;
// boxing: convert into the wrapper type
Integer integer = Integer.valueOf(value1);
// unboxing: convert into the primitive type
int value2 = integer.intValue();

Java 5 introduced the autoboxing and autounboxing mechanism:

Integer integer = 1;
int value = integer;
warningNote

Although the JDK has added the autoboxing and autounboxing mechanism, please choose a suitable type when declaring variables, because the wrapper type Integer can accept null, while the primitive type int cannot accept null. Therefore, unboxing a wrapper type whose value is null will throw an exception. The following code demonstrates this behavior.

Integer integer = Integer.valueOf(null);
integer.intValue();  // throws a java.lang.NumberFormatException

Integer integer = null;
integer.intValue();  // throws a java.lang.NullPointerException

Inheritance#

Creating a new design based on an existing design is exactly inheritance in object-oriented programming. In inheritance, a new class is not produced out of thin air; it is defined on the basis of an already existing class. Through inheritance, the new class automatically acquires all the members of the base class, including member variables and methods, including members of every access attribute, whether public or private. Clearly, defining a new class through inheritance is far simpler, quicker, and more convenient than writing a new class from scratch. Inheritance is one of the important means of supporting code reuse.

In Java, the keyword for inheritance is extends, and Java only supports single inheritance, but a class can implement multiple interfaces.

In Java, all classes are subclasses of the Object class.

When a child class inherits from a parent class, all the members of the parent class, including variables and methods, become members of the child class — except for the constructors. The constructors belong exclusively to the parent class: because their names are exactly the names of the classes, the parent class's constructors do not exist in the child class. Apart from that, the child class inherits all the members of the parent class.

Each member has a different access attribute. The child class inherits all the members of the parent class, but the different access attributes make a difference when the child class uses these members: some members of the parent class directly become part of the child class's outward interface, while others are deeply hidden — even the child class itself cannot access them directly.

The following table lists the access attributes in the child class of parent-class members with different access attributes:

Access attribute of the parent-class member Meaning in the parent class Meaning in the child class
public open to all classes open to all classes
protected accessible only to other classes in the same package, the class itself, and subclasses accessible only to other classes in the same package, the class itself, and subclasses
default (package-private) accessible only to other classes in the same package if the child class is in the same package as the parent class, accessible only to other classes in the same package; otherwise equivalent to private and not accessible
private accessible only to the class itself not accessible

Polymorphism#

In Java, when you assign an object to a variable, the type of the object must match the type of the variable. But because Java has the concept of inheritance, this can be redefined as a variable can hold its declared type, or any subtype of that type.

If a type implements an interface, it can also be called a subtype of that interface.

In Java, variables that hold object types are polymorphic variables. The term "polymorphism" (literally "many forms") means that a variable can hold objects of different types (that is, its declared type or any subtype).

Polymorphic variables:

  1. Java's object variables are polymorphic; they can hold objects of more than one type.
  2. What they can hold are objects of the declared type, or objects of subclasses of the declared type.
  3. When an object of a child class is assigned to a variable of the parent class, upcasting occurs.

Generics#

Generics means that when a class is defined, the concrete types of the attributes in the class or of the method parameters are not fixed; instead, the types are specified when the class is used (or when an object is created). In essence, generics are parameterized types: the data types being operated on are specified as parameters.

Generics provide a mechanism for compile-time type-safety checking, which allows illegal types to be detected at compile time.

Interfaces#

Introduction#

An interface in Java is an abstract type — a collection of abstract methods — usually declared with interface. A class inherits the abstract methods of an interface by implementing the interface.

An interface is not a class. Writing an interface is very similar to writing a class, but they are different concepts. A class describes the attributes and methods of objects; an interface contains the methods that a class is to implement.

Unless the class implementing the interface is an abstract class, the class must define all the methods in the interface.

An interface cannot be instantiated, but it can be implemented. A class that implements an interface must implement all the methods described in the interface, or it must be declared as an abstract class. In addition, in Java an interface type can be used to declare a variable; such variables can become a null pointer, or be bound to an object that implements the interface.

Differences from Classes#

  1. An interface cannot be used to instantiate objects.
  2. An interface has no constructors.
  3. All methods in an interface must be abstract methods; since Java 8, an interface can contain non-abstract methods qualified with the default keyword.
  4. An interface cannot contain member variables, except static and final variables.
  5. An interface is not inherited by a class; rather, it is implemented by a class.
  6. Interfaces support multiple inheritance; classes do not support multiple inheritance.

Declaration#

[visibility] interface InterfaceName [extends OtherInterfaceNames] {
        // declare variables
        // abstract methods
}

Implementation#

...implements InterfaceName[, OtherInterfaceName, OtherInterfaceName..., ...] ...

Lambda Expressions#

Introduction#

Lambda expressions, also known as closures, are the most important new feature of Java 8.

Lambda expressions allow a function to be used as the argument of a method (functions are passed into methods as parameters).

Using lambda expressions can make code more concise and compact.

Syntax#

  • Optional type declaration: there is no need to declare the parameter types, and the compiler can uniformly recognize the parameter values.
  • Optional parentheses for parameters: a single parameter does not need to be wrapped in parentheses, but multiple parameters must be.
  • Optional curly braces: if the body contains a single statement, there is no need to use curly braces.
  • Optional return keyword: if the body has only one expression as its return value, the compiler returns the value automatically; with curly braces, you have to specify that the expression returns a value.

Lambda expressions can be declared as follows:

// 1. takes no parameters and returns 5
() -> 5

// 2. takes one parameter (a number) and returns twice its value
x -> 2 * x

// 3. takes 2 parameters (numbers) and returns their difference
(x, y) -> x – y

// 4. takes 2 int integers and returns their sum
(int x, int y) -> x + y

// 5. takes a String object and prints it to the console, returning no value (it looks like returning void)
(String s) -> System.out.print(s)

Taking a custom comparator that sorts an array of strings by length as an example, a lambda expression can be applied in the following form.

import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] plants = {"Mercury", "venus", "Earth", "Mars", "Jupiter", "Saturn", "Uranus", "Neptune"};
        Arrays.sort(plants, (String first, String second) -> (first.length() - second.length()));
        for (String word : plants) {
            out.print(word + " ");
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

You can also use multiple statements in a lambda expression, as in the example below.

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] plants = {"Mercury", "venus", "Earth", "Mars", "Jupiter", "Saturn", "Uranus", "Neptune"};
        Arrays.sort(plants, (first, second) ->
        {
            // the parameters omit their types; the types can be inferred from the context
            int result = first.length() - second.length();
            return result;
        });
        for (String word : plants) {
            out.print(word + " ");
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

Here -> is a derivation symbol, indicating that the preceding parentheses receive the parameters and derive the return value that follows (in fact, a method is being passed).

Functional Interfaces#

  1. It is an interface, conforming to the definition of a Java interface.
  2. It is an interface that contains only one abstract method.
  3. Because there is only one unimplemented method, a lambda expression can be plugged in automatically.

A functional interface is used as follows:

exampleOutput the strings whose length is a multiple of 2
import java.io.PrintWriter;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] plants = {"Mercury", "venus", "Earth", "Mars", "Jupiter", "Saturn", "Uranus", "Neptune"};
        Test test = s -> {  // the lambda expression as an instance of the functional interface
            if (s.length() % 2 == 0) {
                return true;
            }
            return false;
        };
        for (String word : plants) {
            if (test.check(word)) {
                out.print(word + " ");
            }
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

interface Test {
    public boolean check(String s);
}
exampleImplement the four arithmetic operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division
import java.io.PrintWriter;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static double calc(double a, double b, Calculator util) {
        return util.operation(a, b);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Calculator util[] = new Calculator[4];  // define an array of the functional interface
        util[0] = (a, b) -> a + b;
        util[1] = (a, b) -> a - b;
        util[2] = (a, b) -> a * b;
        util[3] = (a, b) -> a / b;
        double a = 20, b = 15;
        for (Calculator c : util) {
            System.out.println(calc(a, b, c));
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

interface Calculator {
    public double operation(double a, double b);
}

Collection#

Collection is an interface in Java that is implemented by several generic container interfaces. Here, Collection refers to data structures that hold object types.

In Java, the element type of a Collection must be an object type when defined; it cannot be a primitive data type.

The usage of everything below is based on polymorphism in Java, and all of it appears in the form of implementing interfaces.

Commonly used interfaces include List, Queue, Set, and Map.

Defining Containers#

When defining a generic container class, you need to specify the data type at definition time. If you do not specify a data type and add data freely as the Object type, the code will still compile in Java 8, but there will be many warning risks.

For example, the following way of defining it is safe: the container accepts only the Integer type.

List<Integer> list1 = new LinkedList<>();

The following way of defining it, on the other hand, produces warnings.

List list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(1);
list.add(true);
list.add(1.01);
list.add(1L);
list.add("I am String");

Therefore, unless you have special needs, the second approach is not recommended: the compiler cannot help check whether the data being stored is safe. When fetching a value with list.get(index), the type of the data cannot be made clear (the type of every fetched piece of data is Object), so you have to cast it back to the original type manually, and the slightest carelessness can cause a ClassCastException.

If the type is made explicit, such as List<Integer>, the compiler will check the type of the data being put in, and only integer data can be inserted. When declaring a collection variable, you can only use the wrapper type List<Integer> or a custom Class, not a primitive type such as List<int>.

List#

ArrayList#

ArrayList is an array that supports dynamic growth as needed; its default initial length is 10. If the current length is exceeded, it expands by a factor of 32\dfrac{3}{2}23​.

Initialization#
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> list1 = new ArrayList<>();  // create an auto-growing array named list1, with the default initial length (10)
        List<Integer> list2 = new ArrayList<>(30);  // create an auto-growing array named list2, with initial length 30
        List<Integer> list3 = new ArrayList<>(list2);  // create an auto-growing array named list3, using list2's elements and size as its own initial values
    }
}

LinkedList#

LinkedList is a doubly linked list.

Initialization#
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Integer> list1 = new LinkedList<>();  // create a doubly linked list named list1 
        List<Integer> list2 = new LinkedList<>(list1);  // create a doubly linked list named list2, adding all the elements of list1 into it 
    }
}

Common Methods#

In the following, this stands for the current List<Integer>:

Function Description
size() Returns the length of this
add(Integer val) Inserts the element val at the end of this
add(int idx, Integer e) Inserts the element e at position idx of this
get(int idx) Returns the value at position idx in this; throws an exception if out of bounds
set(int idx, Integer e) Changes the value at position idx in this to e

Usage examples and comparison of differences:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static List<Integer> array = new ArrayList<>();
    static List<Integer> linked = new LinkedList<>();

    static void add() {
        array.add(1);  // time complexity is O(1) 
        linked.add(1);  // time complexity is O(1) 
    }

    static void get() {
        array.get(10);  // time complexity is O(1) 
        linked.get(10);  // time complexity is O(11) 
    }

    static void addIdx() {
        array.add(0, 2);  // worst-case time complexity is O(n)
        linked.add(0, 2);  // worst-case time complexity is O(n)
    }

    static void size() {
        array.size();  // time complexity is O(1)
        linked.size();  // time complexity is O(1)
    }

    static void set() {  // the return value of this method is the element originally at that position
        array.set(0, 1);  // time complexity is O(1)
        linked.set(0, 1);  // worst-case time complexity is O(n)
    }

}

Traversal#

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static List<Integer> array = new ArrayList<>();
    static List<Integer> linked = new LinkedList<>();

    static void function1() {  // naive traversal
        for (int i = 0; i < array.size(); i++) {
            out.println(array.get(i));  // traverse the auto-growing array; the complexity is O(n)
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < linked.size(); i++) {
            out.println(linked.get(i));  // traverse the doubly linked list; the complexity is O(n^2), because LinkedList's get(i) has complexity O(i)
        }
    }

    static void function2() {  // enhanced for loop traversal 
        for (int e : array) {
            out.println(e);
        }
        for (int e : linked) {
            out.println(e);  // the complexity is O(n) for both 
        }
    }

    static void function3() {  // iterator traversal 
        Iterator<Integer> iterator1 = array.iterator();
        Iterator<Integer> iterator2 = linked.iterator();
        while (iterator1.hasNext()) {
            out.println(iterator1.next());
        }
        while (iterator2.hasNext()) {
            out.println(iterator2.next());
        }  // the complexity is O(n) for both 
    }

}
warningNote

Do not remove elements from a List while traversing it with for or foreach, or an exception will be thrown.

The reason is simple: list.size() has changed, but the number of iterations already performed in the loop does not change accordingly. The data that was expected at the next index becomes the data at the current index because of the removal, so when the next loop iteration runs, what gets operated on becomes the data that was originally expected at the index after next; in the end, the data being operated on does not match what was expected.

Queue#

LinkedList#

You can use LinkedList to implement an ordinary queue; underneath, it is a linked list simulating a queue.

Initialization#
Queue<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>();

Underneath, LinkedList implements the List interface and the Deque interface, and the Deque interface inherits from the Queue interface, so LinkedList can implement both List and Queue at the same time.

ArrayDeque#

You can use ArrayDeque to implement an ordinary queue; underneath, it is an array simulating a queue.

Initialization#
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

Underneath, ArrayDeque implements the Deque interface, and the Deque interface inherits from the Queue interface, so ArrayDeque can implement Queue.

Differences Between LinkedList and ArrayDeque in Implementing the Queue Interface#

  1. Data structure: in terms of data structure, both ArrayDeque and LinkedList implement the Java Deque double-ended queue interface. But ArrayDeque does not implement the Java List interface, so it does not have index-position-based behavior.
  2. Thread safety: neither ArrayDeque nor LinkedList considers thread synchronization, and thread safety is not guaranteed.
  3. Underlying implementation: underneath, ArrayDeque is based on a dynamic array, while LinkedList is based on a doubly linked list.
  4. Traversal speed: ArrayDeque is a contiguous block of memory, so based on the principle of locality it can hit CPU cache lines better, while LinkedList is scattered memory space, which is unfriendly to cache lines.
  5. Operation speed: the stack and queue behaviors of both ArrayDeque and LinkedList are O(1)O(1)O(1) time complexity; pushing and enqueuing on an ArrayDeque may trigger a capacity expansion, but from the amortized analysis point of view it is still O(1)O(1)O(1) time complexity.
  6. Extra memory consumption: ArrayDeque has idle space outside the array's head pointer and tail pointer, while LinkedList adds predecessor and successor pointers to its nodes.

PriorityQueue#

PriorityQueue is a priority queue; by default it is a min-heap.

Initialization#
Queue<Integer> q1 = new PriorityQueue<>();  // min-heap
Queue<Integer> q2 = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> {return y - x;});  // max-heap

Common Methods#

In the table below, the queue is defined as Queue<Integer>.

Function Description
size() Returns the current length of the queue
add(Integer val) Inserts val into the queue; throws an exception if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions
offer(Integer val) Inserts val into the queue; if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions, the insertion fails, but no exception is thrown
isEmpty() Checks whether the queue is empty; returns true if it is
peek() Returns the element at the head of the queue, or null if the queue is empty
poll() Returns and removes the element at the head of the queue, or null if the queue is empty

Usage examples and comparison of differences:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static Queue<Integer> q1 = new LinkedList<>();
    static Queue<Integer> q2 = new PriorityQueue<>();

    static void add() {  // add and offer are functionally identical; the difference is whether an exception is thrown 
        q1.add(1);  // time complexity is O(1) 
        q2.add(1);  // time complexity is O(logn) 
    }

    static void isEmpty() {
        q1.isEmpty();  // time complexity is O(1) 
        q2.isEmpty();  // space complexity is O(1) 
    }

    static void size() {
        q1.size();  // time complexity is O(1) 
        q2.size();  // returns the length of q2 
    }

    static void peek() {
        q1.peek();  // time complexity is O(1) 
        q2.peek();  // time complexity is O(logn) 
    }

    static void poll() {
        q1.poll();  // time complexity is O(1) 
        q2.poll();  // time complexity is O(logn) 
    }
}

Traversal#

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.Queue;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static Queue<Integer> q1 = new LinkedList<>();
    static Queue<Integer> q2 = new PriorityQueue<>();

    static void test() {
        while (!q1.isEmpty()) {  // the complexity is O(n) 
            out.println(q1.poll());
        }
        while (!q2.isEmpty()) {  // the complexity is O(nlogn) 
            out.println(q2.poll());
        }
    }

}

Deque#

Deque is the double-ended queue of Java; we usually use it to perform both queue operations and stack operations.

Main Functions#

In the table below, the queue is defined as Deque<Integer>.

Function Description
addFirst(Integer val) Inserts val at the head of the queue; throws an exception if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions
offerFirst(Integer val) Inserts val at the head of the queue; if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions, the insertion fails, but no exception is thrown
removeFirst() Returns and removes the element at the head of the queue; throws an exception if the queue is empty
pollFirst() Returns and removes the element at the head of the queue, or returns null if the queue is empty
peekFirst() Returns the element at the head of the queue, or returns null if the queue is empty
push(Integer val) Inserts val at the head of the queue; equivalent to addFirst
pop() Returns and removes the element at the head of the queue; equivalent to removeFirst
remove() Removes the element at the head of the queue; equivalent to removeFirst
poll() Removes the element at the head of the queue; equivalent to pollFirst
addLast(Integer val) Inserts val at the tail of the queue; throws an exception if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions
offerLast(Integer val) Inserts val at the tail of the queue; if doing so violates the queue's capacity restrictions, the insertion fails, but no exception is thrown
removeLast() Returns and removes the element at the tail of the queue; throws an exception if the queue is empty
pollLast() Returns and removes the element at the tail of the queue, or returns null if the queue is empty
peekLast() Returns the element at the tail of the queue, or returns null if the queue is empty
add(Integer val) Inserts val at the tail of the queue; equivalent to addLast
offer(Integer val) Inserts val at the tail of the queue; equivalent to offerLast

Stack Operations#

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    static int[] a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        for (int v : a) {
            stack.push(v);
        }
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) { // outputs 5 4 3 2 1
            System.out.println(stack.pop()); 
        }
    }
}

Deque Operations#

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class Main {
    static Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();

    static void insert() {
        deque.addFirst(1);
        deque.addFirst(2);
        deque.addLast(3);
        deque.addLast(4);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        insert();
        while (!deque.isEmpty()) { // outputs 2 1 3 4
            System.out.println(deque.poll());
        }
        insert();
        while (!deque.isEmpty()) { // outputs 4 3 1 2
            System.out.println(deque.pollLast());
        }
    }
}

Set#

Set is a data structure that keeps the elements in the container free of duplicates.

HashSet#

A Set that inserts at random positions.

Initialization#
Set<Integer> s1 = new HashSet<>();

LinkedHashSet#

A Set that preserves insertion order.

Initialization#
Set<Integer> s2 = new LinkedHashSet<>();

TreeSet#

A Set that keeps the elements in the container ordered, ascending by default.

Initialization#
Set<Integer> s3 = new TreeSet<>();
Set<Integer> s4 = new TreeSet<>((x, y) -> {return y - x;});  // descending order 
Further Usage of TreeSet#

These methods are newly created and implemented by TreeSet; we cannot call the following methods through the Set interface, so we create it as follows:

TreeSet<Integer> s3 = new TreeSet<>();
TreeSet<Integer> s4 = new TreeSet<>((x, y) -> {return y - x;});  // descending order

In the table below, this stands for the current TreeSet<Integer>.

Function Description
first() Returns the first element in this, or null if there is none
last() Returns the last element in this, or null if there is none
floor(Integer val) Returns the first element in this less than or equal to val, or null if there is none
ceiling(Integer val) Returns the first element in this greater than or equal to val, or null if there is none
higher(Integer val) Returns the first element in this greater than val, or null if there is none
lower(Integer val) Returns the first element in this less than val, or null if there is none
pollFirst() Returns and removes the first element in this, or null if there is none
pollLast() Returns and removes the last element in this, or null if there is none

Example code:

import java.util.TreeSet;

public class Main {
    static int[] a = {4,7,1,2,3,6};

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TreeSet<Integer> set = new TreeSet<>();
        for(int v:a) {
            set.add(v);
        }
        Integer a2 = set.first();
        System.out.println(a2); // returns 1
        Integer a3 = set.last();
        System.out.println(a3); // returns 7
        Integer a4 = set.floor(5);
        System.out.println(a4); // returns 4
        Integer a5 = set.ceiling(6);
        System.out.println(a5); // returns 6
        Integer a6 = set.higher(7);
        System.out.println(a6); // returns null
        Integer a7 = set.lower(2);
        System.out.println(a7); // returns 1
        Integer a8 = set.pollFirst();
        System.out.println(a8); // returns 1
        Integer a9 = set.pollLast();
        System.out.println(a9); // returns 7
    }
}

Common Set Methods#

Function Description
size() Returns the current size of the set
add(Integer val) Inserts val into the set
contains(Integer val) Checks whether the set contains the element val
addAll(Collection e) Adds all the elements in the container e into the current set
retainAll(Collection e) Removes the elements of the current set that do not appear in the container e, that is, it computes the intersection of the current set and e
removeAll(Collection e) Removes the elements of the current set that appear in the container e, that is, it computes the difference of the current set and e 
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static Set<Integer> s1 = new HashSet<>();
    static Set<Integer> s2 = new LinkedHashSet<>();

    static void add() {
        s1.add(1);
    }

    static void contains() {  // check whether the set contains an element with value 2; returns true if so, false otherwise 
        s1.contains(2);
    }

    static void test1() {  // the union of s1 and s2 
        Set<Integer> res = new HashSet<>();
        res.addAll(s1);
        res.addAll(s2);
    }

    static void test2() {  // the intersection of s1 and s2 
        Set<Integer> res = new HashSet<>();
        res.addAll(s1);
        res.retainAll(s2);
    }

    static void test3() {  // the difference: s1 - s2 
        Set<Integer> res = new HashSet<>();
        res.addAll(s1);
        res.removeAll(s2);
    }
}

Traversal#

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static Set<Integer> s1 = new HashSet<>();
    static Set<Integer> s2 = new LinkedHashSet<>();

    static void test() {
        for (int key : s1) {
            out.println(key);
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

Map#

Map is a data structure that maintains key-value pairs <Key, Value>, where Key is unique.

HashMap#

A Map that inserts at random positions.

Initialization#
Map<Integer, Integer> map1 = new HashMap<>();

LinkedHashMap#

A Map that preserves insertion order.

Initialization#
Map<Integer, Integer> map2 = new LinkedHashMap<>();

TreeMap#

A Map that keeps keys ordered, ascending by default.

Initialization#
Map<Integer, Integer> map3 = new TreeMap<>();
Map<Integer, Integer> map4 = new TreeMap<>((x, y) -> {return y - x;});  // descending order

Common Methods#

In the following, this stands for the current Map<Integer, Integer>:

Function Description
put(Integer key, Integer value) Inserts <key, value> into this
size() Returns the size of this
containsKey(Integer key) Checks whether there exists an element in this whose key is key
get(Integer key) Returns the value corresponding to the element in this whose key is key
keySet() Returns the keys of all the elements in this as a set

Usage example:

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    static Map<Integer, Integer> map1 = new HashMap<>();
    static Map<Integer, Integer> map2 = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    static Map<Integer, Integer> map3 = new TreeMap<>();
    static Map<Integer, Integer> map4 = new TreeMap<>((x,y)->{return y-x;});

    static void put(){  // return the element with key 1 and value 1
        map1.put(1, 1);
    }
    static void get(){  // return the value with key 1
        map1.get(1);
    }
    static void containsKey(){  // check whether there is a key-value pair with key 1
        map1.containsKey(1);
    }
    static void KeySet(){
        map1.keySet();
    }
}

Traversal#

import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    static Map<Integer, Integer> map1 = new HashMap<>();

    static void print() {
        for (int key : map1.keySet()) {
            out.println(key + " " + map1.get(key));
        }
    }
}

Of course, the types of the keys and values can also be changed. For example, a Map can also be defined as:

Map<String, Set<Integer>> map = new HashMap<>();

Arrays#

Arrays is a utility class for array operations in java.util. All of its methods are static methods, which can be called directly through the class name.

Arrays.sort()#

Arrays.sort() is the method for sorting arrays; its main overloaded methods are as follows:

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;

public class Main {
    static int[] a = new int[10];
    static Integer[] b = new Integer[10];
    static int firstIdx, lastIdx;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Arrays.sort(a);  // 1 
        Arrays.sort(a, firstIdx, lastIdx);  // 2 
        Arrays.sort(b, new Comparator<Integer>() {  // 3 
            @Override
            public int compare(Integer o1, Integer o2) {
                return o2 - o1;
            }
        });
        Arrays.sort(b, firstIdx, lastIdx, new Comparator<Integer>() {  // 4 
            @Override
            public int compare(Integer o1, Integer o2) {
                return o2 - o1;
            }
        });
        // since Java 8 has lambda expressions, the third overload and the fourth overload can also be written as 
        Arrays.sort(b, (x, y) -> {  // 5 
            return y - x;
        });
        Arrays.sort(b, (x, y) -> {  // 6 
            return y - x;
        });
    }
}

The meanings of the overloads corresponding to the numbers:

  1. Sorts array a, ascending by default.
  2. Sorts specified positions of array a, ascending by default; the sorting range is the half-open interval [firstIdx, lastIdx).
  3. Sorts array a in a custom way: the second parameter - the first parameter gives descending order, and the first parameter - the second parameter gives ascending order. When a custom sorting comparator is used, the array element type must be an object type.
  4. Performs a custom sort on specified positions of array a; the sorting range is the half-open interval [firstIdx, lastIdx). When a custom sorting comparator is used, the array element type must be an object type.
  5. Same idea as 3, but the code is shortened by using a lambda expression.
  6. Same idea as 4, but the code is shortened by using a lambda expression.

noteThe underlying function of <code>Arrays.sort()</code>
  1. When the element type of the array passed to Arrays.sort is a primitive data type (byte, short, char, int, long, double, float), the default is DualPivotQuicksort (dual-pivot quicksort), whose worst-case complexity can reach O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2).
  2. When the element type of the array passed to Arrays.sort is not a primitive data type, the default is legacyMergeSort and TimSort (merge sorts), whose complexity is O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn).
This can be verified with the following code:

example<a href="https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1646/B">Codeforces 1646B - Quality vs Quantity</a>

There are nnn integers, and you need to split them into two groups: is it possible for one of the groups to be shorter than the other while having a sum greater than it?

noteExample solution code
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.InputStreamReader;
import java.io.PrintWriter;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.StringTokenizer;

public class Main {
    static class FastReader {
        StringTokenizer st;
        BufferedReader br;

        public FastReader() {
            br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
        }

        String next() {
            while (st == null || !st.hasMoreElements()) {
                try {
                    st = new StringTokenizer(br.readLine());
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    e.printStackTrace();
                }
            }
            return st.nextToken();
        }

        int nextInt() {
            return Integer.parseInt(next());
        }

        long nextLong() {
            return Long.parseLong(next());
        }

        double nextDouble() {
            return Double.parseDouble(next());
        }

        String nextLine() {
            String str = "";
            try {
                str = br.readLine();
            } catch (IOException e) {
                e.printStackTrace();
            }
            return str;
        }
    }

    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);
    static FastReader in = new FastReader();

    static void solve() {
        int n = in.nextInt();
        // changing the array type from Integer to int here would cause a TLE
        Integer[] a = new Integer[n + 10];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            a[i] = in.nextInt();
        }
        Arrays.sort(a, 1, n + 1);
        long left = a[1];
        long right = 0;
        int x = n;
        for (int i = 2; i < x; i++, x--) {
            left = left + a[i];
            right = right + a[x];
            if (right > left) {
                out.println("YES");
                return;
            }
        }
        out.println("NO");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int t = in.nextInt();
        while (t-- > 0) {
            solve();
        }
        out.close();
    }
}

Arrays.binarySearch()#

Arrays.binarySearch() is a method that performs a binary search over a contiguous interval of an array; the precondition is that the array must be sorted. The time complexity is O(log⁡n)O(\log_n)O(logn​), and the main overloaded methods are as follows:

import java.util.Arrays;

public class Main {
    static int[] a = new int[10];
    static Integer[] b = new Integer[10];
    static int firstIdx, lastIdx;
    static int key;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Arrays.binarySearch(a, key);  // 1 
        Arrays.binarySearch(a, firstIdx, lastIdx, key);  // 2 
    }
}

The source code is as follows:

private static int binarySearch0(int[] a, int fromIndex, int toIndex, int key) {
    int low = fromIndex;
    int high = toIndex - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = (low + high) >>> 1;
        int midVal = a[mid];

        if (midVal < key)
            low = mid + 1;
        else if (midVal > key)
            high = mid - 1;
        else
            return mid; // key found
    }
    return -(low + 1);  // key not found.
}

The meanings of the overloads corresponding to the numbers:

  1. Binary-searches array a for key; if it exists, its index is returned. If it does not exist, a negative number is returned.
  2. Binary-searches array a for key; if it exists, its index is returned, with the search range being the half-open interval [firstIdx,lastIdx). If it does not exist, a negative number is returned.

Arrays.fill()#

The Arrays.fill() method assigns the elements at consecutive positions of an array a uniform value. The parameters it accepts are the array, fromIndex, toIndex, and the number to fill in. After the method is executed, all the elements in the half-open interval [firstIdx,lastIdx) of the array equal the number to fill in.

Collections#

Collections is a utility class for collection operations in java.util. All of its methods are static methods, which can be called directly through the class name.

Collections.sort()#

The underlying principle of Collections.sort() is to convert all the elements into an array and call Arrays.sort(), then assign them back to the original collection after the sorting is done. Also, because the element type of a Collection in Java is always an object type, it is always merge sort that processes it.

This method cannot sort a specified interval of a collection.

The underlying source code:

default void sort(Comparator<? super E> c) {
    Object[] a = this.toArray();
    Arrays.sort(a, (Comparator) c);
    ListIterator<E> i = this.listIterator();
    for (Object e : a) {
        i.next();
        i.set((E) e);
    }
}

Collections.binarySearch()#

Collections.binarySearch() performs a binary search over a specified interval in a collection, with the same functionality as Arrays.binarySearch().

Collections.binarySearch(list, key);

This method cannot search a specified interval.

Collections.swap()#

The function of Collections.swap() is to swap the elements at two specified positions in a collection.

 Collections.swap(list, i, j);

Miscellaneous#

Numeric Comparison Issues#

In Java, if they are plain numeric types, -0.0 = 0.0; if they are object types, then -0.0 != 0.0. This becomes a nuisance when you try to count the number of slopes with a Set. The solution provided is to add 0.0 to the value of every slope before it is added to the Set.

import java.io.PrintWriter;

public class Main {
    static PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(System.out);

    static void A() {
        Double a = 0.0;
        Double b = -0.0;
        out.println(a.equals(b));  // false 
    }

    static void B() {
        Double a = 0.0;
        Double b = -0.0 + 0.0;
        out.println(a.equals(b));  // true 
    }

    static void C() {
        double a = 0.0;
        double b = -0.0;
        out.println(a == b);  // true 
    }


    public static void main(String[] args) {
        A();
        B();
        C();
        out.close();
    }
}
